Abu Ishaq said: "The One who is exalted above the injustice of His servants."

Likewise His name al-'Aziz, the One who possesses perfect might, and from the perfection of His might is His freedom from every evil, defect and shortcoming, for that contradicts perfect might. Likewise His name al-'Ali, the One who is exalted above every defect, evil and deficiency, and from the perfection of His loftiness is that nothing be above Him, rather He is above all things. Likewise His name al-Hamid, the One to whom all praise belongs. The perfection of His praise requires that no evil, no injury and no deficiency be attributed to Him, neither in His names, nor in His acts, nor in His attributes. So His Most Beautiful Names prevent the attribution of evil, injury and injustice to Him, even though He, glorified is He, is the Creator of all things. He is the Creator of the servants and their acts, movements and speech. When the servant does a reprehensible act that is forbidden, he has done evil, injury and wrong, and the Lord, glorified is He, is the One who made him the doer of it. This making is from Him justice, wisdom and rightness. So His making him the doer is good, and the done thing is evil and ugly. Thus by this making He has placed the thing in its place, for the far-reaching wisdom He has in it, for which He is praised. It is good, wisdom and benefit, even though its occurrence from the servant is a defect, a deficiency and an evil. This is an intelligible matter in the case of witnesses. When a skilled craftsman takes a crooked piece of wood, a broken stone and a deficient brick and places them in a place that suits and fits them, this is from him justice and rightness for which he is praised, even if there is crookedness, deficiency and defect in the material, for which the material is blamed. Whoever places wicked things in their proper place and fitting station, that is wisdom, justice and rightness. Foolishness and injustice are only when one places a thing in other than its place. Whoever places the turban on the head, the sandal on the foot, the kohl in the eye and the refuse in the dustbin has placed the thing in its place, and has not wronged the sandal or the refuse, since this is their place. Among His names, glorified is He, are al-'Adl (the Just) and al-Hakim (the Wise), who does not place a thing except in its place. So He is the Benefactor, the Generous, the Wise, the Just, in all that He created and in all that He placed in its station and prepared for it. He, glorified is He, possesses creation and command. Just as in His command He commands only the better of two matters, and commands the attainment and perfection of benefits and the elimination and minimization of harms, and when two matters conflict, He prefers the better and more beneficial of them. There is no command in the Sharia that is performed except that its existence for the one commanded is better than its non-existence, and no prohibition of an act except that its non-existence is better than its existence. If you say: if its existence is better than its non-existence, how is it that He does not will its existence? And if its non-existence is better than its existence, how does He will its existence? The general will overturns this universal rule for you. I say: It does not overturn it, because its existence, though better than its non-existence, may entail the loss of something beloved to Him that is dearer to Him than the occurrence of this commanded thing, in this respect, and the non-existence of the forbidden thing, though better than its existence. Its existence may be a means and cause to something dearer to Him than its non-existence. The full establishment of this will come, God willing, in the chapter on the convergence and divergence of the Divine Decree and the Sharia. When the Lord, glorified is He, commands something, He loves it, is pleased with it, wills it and clarifies it. He does not love anything except that its existence is better than its non-existence, and what He forbids He hates and detests, and He does not hate anything except that its non-existence is better than its existence. This is considered with respect to the essence of this and that. As for considering its leading to what He loves and dislikes, it has a different ruling. For this reason He, glorified is He, commanded His servants to take the best of what was sent down to them. So the best is what is commanded, and it is better than what is forbidden. If this is His practice in His command and His law, then likewise is His practice in His creation, His decree and His predestination. What He wills to create or to do, its creation and doing is better for Him than not creating it and not doing it, and vice versa. Whatever its non-existence is better than its existence, its existence is evil, and He does not do it, rather He is exempt from it, and evil does not belong to Him.

If you say: why then did He create it, when it is evil?

I say: His creating it and doing it is good, not evil. For creation and act subsist in Him, glorified is He, and evil cannot subsist in Him or be attributed to Him. Whatever evil is in the created thing is due to its non-attribution and non-relation to Him. Creation and act are attributed to Him, so it is good. Everything He willed is good, and what He did not will to exist remains in its original non-existence, which is evil, for all evil is non-existence. Its cause is ignorance, which is the absence of knowledge, or injustice, which is the absence of justice. What follows from that of pains is from the lack of readiness of the substrate and its non-acceptance of the causes of goods and pleasures.

If you say: many people state that all good is from existence and its concomitants, and all evil is from non-existence and its concomitants, and existence is good, and pure evil is only non-existence.

I say: This statement is ambiguous. If it is meant that everything Allah created and brought into existence contains good, and its existence is better than its non-existence, and what He did not create and did not will remains in its non-existence, and there is no good in it, since if there were good in it He would have done it, for good is in His hand, then this is correct. Existence-based evil is the absence of good. But if it is meant that everything that entails existence is good, and everything that entails non-existence is evil, then this is not correct. Existence may entail an inferior evil, and non-existence may entail a superior good. The first example is fire, rain, heat, cold, snow, and the existence of animals. This exists and entails a partial evil, overwhelmed in comparison with the good in its existence. Likewise the commanded thing may entail pain and hardship, which is a partial evil overwhelmed in comparison with the good in it.

(Section)

The truth of the matter is that evil is of two kinds: pure real evil from every aspect, and relative, comparative evil from one aspect and not another. The first does not enter existence, for if it entered existence it would not be pure evil. The second is what enters existence. Things said to be evils are either non-existential or existential. If they are non-existential, they are either the absence of things necessary to the thing in its existence, or necessary to it in the continuation of its existence and survival, or necessary to it in its perfection. Or they are not necessary to it in its existence, its survival or its perfection. And if their existence is better than their non-existence, these are four categories:

The first, like sensation, movement and soul for the animal.
The second, like the power of nourishment and growth for the nourished, growing animal.
The third, like its health, hearing, sight and strength.
The fourth, like knowledge of the subtleties of known things, whose knowledge is better than ignorance, and which are not necessary to it.

As for existential things, the existence of everything that opposes life, survival and perfection, like diseases and their causes, pains and their causes, and existential obstacles that prevent the attainment of good and its arrival at the receptive substrate prepared for it, like corrupt humours that prevent nourishment from reaching the body's organs and benefiting from it, and like false beliefs and corrupt wills that prevent their opposites from reaching the heart.

Having known this, the evil in itself is the absence of what is necessary to a thing in its existence, survival or perfection. And this absence has concomitants that are also evil, for the absence of knowledge and justice entails ignorance and injustice, which are existential evils.

The absence of health and balance entails pain and harm, which are existential evil.

As for the absence of things that one can do without, like the absence of excessive wealth, and knowledge whose ignorance does no harm, this is not evil in reality, nor is its existence a cause of evil. For knowledge as such is knowledge, and wealth as such is wealth; neither was placed as a cause of evil. Evil only follows from the absence of a quality that calls for good, like the absence of chastity, patience and justice in regard to wealth, so evil befalls the wealthy man in his wealth through the absence of these qualities. Likewise the absence of wisdom and the placing of a thing in its place, and the absence of the will for wisdom in the case of the man of knowledge, entails that evil follows him because of that.

So it became clear that evil follows only from an absence. Otherwise, the existent as such is not evil nor a cause of evil. Existential things are not evils in themselves, but accidentally, insofar as they include the absence of necessary or beneficial things. For you will not find any act that is evil except that it is a perfection relative to some things, while its evil aspect is relative to other things. An example: injustice proceeds from a power that seeks dominance and subjugation, which is the irascible faculty whose perfection is in overpowering, and for this it was created. So there is no evil in the effect of this power as such. Evil is only the non-effect of its effect altogether, so it becomes weak, impotent and subjugated. The existential evil that occurs is an evil relative to the one wronged, through the loss of his soul, property or disposal, and relative to the wrongdoer not as to dominance and mastery, but as to placing dominance, subjugation and mastery in other than their place, shifting them from their proper locus to another locus. Had he used the force of anger to subdue the aggressive harmful rational and animal beings, it would have been good. But it was diverted to another locus, placing subjugation and dominance in place of justice and equity, and severity in place of mercy. So the evil was not in the existence of this power, nor in the effect of its effect as such, but in running it outside its course. An example: water flowing in a river to a land it waters and benefits. Its perfection is in its flow until it reaches it. If it is diverted from its channel and path to a land it harms, ruining its dwellings, the evil lies in diverting it from what it was prepared for and in its not reaching it. Likewise the will and anger are given to the servant so that through them he may attain what benefits him and subdue what harms and destroys him. If they are used for that, it is their perfection and good. If they are turned from that to using this power in other than its place, and this in other than its place, that becomes a relative comparative evil. Likewise fire's perfection is in burning. If it burns what should be burned, it is good. If it encounters what should not be burned and destroys it, it is a relative evil relative to the particular locus. Likewise killing, for example, is the use of a cutting instrument to separate the bodily connection. The human power to use the instrument is good, the instrument's being able to act is good, and the locus's being able to receive that is good. The evil is only relative and comparative, namely placing this effect in other than its place and diverting it from the locus that leads to other things. This is relative to the agent.

As for relative to the affected party, it is also a relative evil, namely what he undergoes of pain and the loss of life. This may be good for him in another respect and good for others. Likewise intercourse: the power of the agent and the receptivity of the locus is a perfection, but the evil lies in diverting it from the locus suited to it to a locus that is not fitting nor suitable. Likewise the movement of the tongue and movements of the limbs all proceed in this course. Thus it became clear that the entry of evil into existential things is only through relation and comparison, not that they are evil by their existence or essence. Likewise prostration is not evil in its essence and existence. When it is directed to other than Allah, it becomes evil by this relation and comparison. Likewise everything whose existence is disbelief and polytheism became evil only through its being directed to what made it so, like venerating idols. Veneration as such is not praised or blamed except with regard to its object. If it is veneration of Allah and His Book, His religion and His Messenger, it is pure good. If it is veneration of an idol or of Satan, its direction to this locus made it evil, just as the direction of prostration to other than Allah made it so.

(Section)

Among what should be known is that things composed of their materials gradually, like plants and animals, either suffer a deficiency that is an evil at their beginning or after their formation. The first is that causes afflict their matter that make it ill-tempered and deficient in readiness, so evil and deficiency occur in their creation through that cause. This is not because the agent withheld from it and removed from it an existential matter by which its perfection is attained. Rather, it is because the affected thing did not accept perfection and completion, and its non-acceptance is a non-existential matter, not something by the agent. What is by the agent is the existential good by which its perfection, completion and deficiency are received. The evil that occurred in it is from the absence of supply with the cause of perfection, so it remained in its original non-existence. By this the secret of His saying, Exalted is He, is understood: ﴿You see in the creation of the Most Merciful no inconsistency﴾.

For what He created is an existential matter, by which the perfection and completion of the created thing is attained. As for its defect and deficiency, they come from its non-acceptance, and non-acceptance is not a created thing related to the agent's act. So existential creation contains no inconsistency, and inconsistency only occurred through this creation, for the Creator, glorified is He, did not create in it a readiness, so inconsistency occurred in it from the absence of creation, not from the creation itself. Ponder this.

And what is attributed to the Lord, glorified is He, is creation.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 3, verse 26 (part 2 of 3):

As for non-existence, it is not an agent of anything. So when, in the matter of the foetus in the womb, there is not completed what its completion requires and the soundness and proper proportion of its limbs, disparity occurs in it; and likewise with plants.

(Section)

As for the second, namely that the evil which arises after its coming into being and bringing into existence, it is also of two kinds. The first is that the support by which it is perfected after its existence is cut off from it, as the support of water is cut off from a plant and the support of food from an animal. This is an evil attributed to non-existence as well, being the non-existence of that by which it would be perfected. The second is the occurrence of an opposing, contrary thing, and this too is of two kinds. The first is the presence in the locus of an obstacle that prevents suitable causes from taking effect in it, as corrupt humours subsist in the body and prevent food from having its effect on it and its benefit from it, and as corrupt wills and beliefs subsist in the heart and prevent it from benefiting from guidance and knowledge. This evil, although it is existent and its causes are existent, is also from the absence of the power and the will by which that obstacle is repelled. For if a power and a will existed that repelled it, the locus would not be affected by it. An example: the overpowering and dominance of the humours comes from the absence of the power that ripens them or the power that expels what needs to be expelled; and likewise the dominance of corrupt wills comes from the weakness of the power of chastity and patience, and the dominance of false beliefs from the lack of knowledge corresponding to its object. So every evil and deficiency only arises from the absence of the cause of its opposite, and the absence of the cause of its opposite is not an agent of it; rather it suffices for it that it remains in its original non-existence. The second is an obstacle from outside, such as extreme cold, burning, drowning and the like, which afflict animals and plants so that corruption arises in them. This is undoubtedly an existent evil, attributed to an existent cause, but it is a relative, comparative evil, and it is good from another aspect. For the existence of that heat, cold and water entails benefits and general goods, in comparison with which this evil is partial. Thus suspending those causes in order to avert this partial evil entails a greater evil, namely the loss of those goods that arise from them. For what arises from the sun, wind, rain, snow, heat and cold of the benefits of creation is many times more than what arises from them of partial corruptions, which are in comparison with those benefits like a drop in an ocean. This would be so even if its evil were real; how much more so when it is good from one aspect and evil from another, even if many people do not know the aspect of its good. The Lord, glorified is He, did not measure it in vain, nor create it for nothing. At this point it is said: existence is either good in every respect, or evil in every respect, or good in one respect and evil in another. The last has three divisions: one whose good outweighs its evil, its reverse, and one whose good and evil are equal. As for that which has neither good nor evil, these are six divisions, and there are no more. Some of them occur and some do not. As for the first division, namely pure good in every respect with no evil in any respect, it is the most noble of existents absolutely, and the most perfect and sublime, and every perfection and good in them is derived from its goodness and perfection in itself. They draw from it, and it does not draw from them; they are needy of it, and it is independent of them. Each of them asks it for its perfection. The angels ask it for what they have no life without, and for help in its remembrance, its thanks, the goodness of its worship, the execution of its commands, and the discharge of what has been entrusted to them of the interests of the upper and lower worlds; they ask it to forgive the children of Adam. The messengers ask it to help them in delivering its messages and conveying them, to grant them victory over their enemies, and other interests of theirs in this life and the next. All the children of Adam ask it for their interests in their variety and diversity. All animals ask it for their sustenance, their food and their strength, and what sustains them, and ask it for protection. Trees and plants ask it for their nourishment and what perfects them. The whole cosmos asks it for its continuance and its condition: ﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth asks Him; every day He is upon some task﴾. So the palms of the whole world are extended to Him in request and asking, and His hand is outstretched to them in giving and bounty. His right hand is full; it is not diminished by expenditure, the night and day flowing from it. His giving and goodness are lavished upon the righteous and the wicked. To Him belongs every perfection and from Him comes every good. To Him is all praise, to Him is all thanks, in His hand is all good, and to Him all affairs return. Blessed is His name, blessed are His attributes, blessed are His acts, blessed is His essence; all blessing is His and from Him. Nothing He is asked for as good diminishes His treasuries, despite the abundance of His giving and His generosity. If every perfection in the world were fashioned into one single form, and the whole world were upon that form, its relation to His perfection, majesty and beauty would be less than the relation of a feeble lamp to the sun itself.

(Section)

As for the remaining five divisions, only those enter existence whose benefit, wisdom and good in their bringing into being outweigh the harm. The four divisions do not enter existence. As for pure evil with no good in it, that has no reality; it is simply pure non-existence.

If it is said: then Iblis is pure evil, and disbelief and polytheism likewise, and yet they have entered existence. What good is there in Iblis and in the existence of disbelief?

It is said: in the creation of Iblis there are wisdoms and benefits and goods that follow from his existence, which none knows but God, as we shall point out some of them. God, exalted is He, did not create him in vain, nor did He intend by his creation the harming and destruction of His servants. How many a dazzling wisdom, overwhelming proof, manifest sign and abundant blessing there is in God's creation! And he, although he is for religions and faith like poisons for bodies, yet in the existence of poisons there are benefits and wisdoms greater than their loss.

As for that which has neither good nor evil, it also does not enter existence, for it is futile, and God is exalted above it. And if the existence of this division is impossible, then the entry into existence of what evil outweighs good is even more deserving of impossibility. Whoever reflects on this existence knows that good in it predominates, and that illnesses, though many, are fewer than health; pleasures are more than pains; well-being is greater than affliction; and drowning, burning, demolition and the like, though many, are less than safety. And if this division whose good predominates were not to exist on account of the evil that befalls it, the predominant good would be lost, and the loss of the predominant good is a predominant evil. An example of this is fire: in its existence there are many benefits and in it are harms, but when we weigh its benefits against its harms, its harms have no proportion to its benefits. Likewise rain, winds, heat and cold. In sum, the elements of this lower world have their good mixed with their evil, but their good predominates; as for the upper world, it is free of that.

If it is said: why did the Wise Creator not create this world free of evil, such that it would be pure goods?

If you say: wisdom required the creation of this world with pleasure mixed with pain and good mixed with evil, then it was possible to create it in a state in which there would be no evil, like the upper world.

Granted that the existence of what has more good than evil is better than its non-existence, what good and benefit is there in the existence of the very head of all evil, its source and the exemplar of its people, Iblis; and what good is there in his remaining until the end of time; and what predominant good occurs in a creation in which ninety-nine go to the Fire and one to Paradise; and what predominant good was achieved by the expulsion of the two parents from Paradise, so that what befell their offspring befell them, whereas had they remained in Paradise, evil would have been lifted entirely?

And if He created them for His worship, how did His wisdom require that He turn them away from us, and grant success to only a few of mankind? What predominant good is there in the creation of disbelief, wickedness, disobedience, injustice and transgression? What good is there in causing pain to those not charged with obligation, such as children and the insane?

If you say its purpose is compensation, I will object to you with the pain inflicted on animals. Then what good is there in the creation of the Dajjal, and in enabling him to appear and to tempt people by him? And since wisdom required that, what good is achieved by enabling him to display those extraordinary and wondrous acts? And what good is there in sorcery and what follows from it of corruptions and harms? And what good is there in dressing people in factions and making some of them taste the violence of others? And what good is there in the creation of poisons, of venomous creatures, and of beasts that are harmful by their nature? And what good is there in the ruin of this structure after its creation in the finest form, and its return to the most abject age after its uprightness and soundness? Likewise the ruin of this abode and the effacing of its traces. If the existence of all that were a predominant good, then its abolition would be the abolition of a predominant good. Set all this aside: what predominant or subordinate good is there in the Fire, which is the house of the greatest evil and the greatest affliction? You have no escape from these questions except by closing the door of wisdom and causation and attributing the cosmos to pure will, or by saying that the Lord acts by essential necessity and not by His choice and will. These questions are only directed at one who holds that there is a chooser acting by choice. That is why those who say this have resorted to denying causation altogether; they have chosen one of the two positions and sided with one of the two parties. Otherwise, how will you reconcile the affirmation of wisdom and causation with these matters? The answer, after we say "Glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, and God is greatest," lies rather in the realisation of these words as a sufficient answer: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain; glory be to You; so protect us from the punishment of the Fire.﴾

﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play. We did not create them except with truth﴾, and ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in vain; that is the assumption of those who disbelieve, so woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire﴾. ﴿Did you suppose that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us? Exalted is God, the True King; there is no god but He, Lord of the Noble Throne.﴾

﴿God is the One who created seven heavens and of the earth their like; the command descends among them, that you may know that God is over all things competent, and that God has encompassed all things in knowledge.﴾ ﴿God made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of standing for mankind, and the Sacred Month and the offerings and the garlands; that is that you may know that God knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, and that God is Knowing of all things.﴾ ﴿The handiwork of God, who perfected all things.﴾ ﴿He who perfected everything He created.﴾ ﴿You see in the creation of the Most Merciful no disparity.﴾

Rather, it is in the utmost proportion, arranged in the most perfect manner and the nearest to attaining praiseworthy ends and sought wisdoms. Those wisdoms and ends, which God alone knows in detail, and which He has let whomever He wills of His servants know of the least of the least, could not be attained except through these causes and beginnings. The near angels asked Him about the kind of these questions and their root, and He said: ﴿Indeed I know what you do not know.﴾ They acknowledged to Him perfect knowledge and wisdom, and that in all His acts He is upon a straight path, and they said: ﴿Glory be to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us; indeed You are the Knowing, the Wise.﴾ And when He showed them some of His wisdom concerning what they had asked about, and that they had not known, He said: ﴿Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you have been concealing?﴾

(Benefit)

God, exalted is He, attributed good to Himself and not evil, as He said: ﴿Say: O God, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty from whom You will; You honour whom You will and You humble whom You will; in Your hand is the good; indeed You are over all things competent.﴾

And whoever said the meaning is "in Your hand is the good and the evil" erred, for three reasons.

The first: there is nothing in the wording indicating this supposed omitted element; rather its mention is omitted either deliberately or to make clear that it is not intended.

The second: what is in God's hand consists of two kinds, bounty and justice, as in the authentic hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The right hand of God is full; the night and day's giving does not diminish it. Have you considered what He has spent since He created creation? It has not diminished what is in His right hand. And in His other hand is the scale; He lowers and raises." So bounty is in one hand and justice in the other, and both are good with no evil in them in any respect.

The third: the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying "Here I am at Your service, and I am at Your disposal, and the good is in Your hands, and evil is not attributed to You" is like an explanation of the verse. He distinguished between good and evil, placing one in the hands of the Lord, exalted is He, and cutting off the attribution of the other to Him, while affirming that He is the Creator of everything.

(Section)

"Allahumma": there is no dispute that the word "Allahumma" means "O God." For this reason it is used only in supplication. One does not say "Allahumma Ghafur Rahim" (O God, Forgiving, Merciful); one says "Allahumma ighfir li warhamni" (O God, forgive me and have mercy on me).

The grammarians differed concerning the doubled mim at the end of the name.

Sibawayh said: it was added as a substitute for the vocative particle. For this reason it is not permissible in chosen speech to combine the two, so one does not say "ya Allahumma" except in rare cases, such as the poet's saying:

"When a calamity befalls me, I say: O Allah, O Allah."

Such a letter is called a substitute ('iwad), since it is not in the place of the omitted element. If it is in the place of the omitted element, it is called a replacement (badal), like the alif in "qama" and "baa'a," for it is a replacement for waw and ya. In his view it is also not permissible to describe this name with an adjective; one does not say "ya Allahumma al-Rahim irhamni," nor is it replaced by anything.

The damma on the ha' is the damma of the single vocative noun. The mim is given a fatha because of its quiescence and the quiescence of the mim before it. This is one of the peculiarities of this name, just as it is peculiar in taking the ta' in the oath, in the vocative particle entering upon it together with the definite article, in cutting off its hamzat al-wasl in the vocative, and in obligatorily emphasising its lam without a preceding emphatic letter. This is the summary of the school of al-Khalil and Sibawayh.

It was said: the mim is a substitute for an omitted whole sentence. The estimate is: "Ya Allah, amman bi-khayr," meaning "aim at us with good," then the prepositional phrase was omitted and the object was omitted, leaving in the estimate: "Ya Allah, umm." Then the hamza was dropped due to the frequent occurrence of this name on their tongues in supplication, leaving "ya Allahumma." This is the view of al-Farra'.

The proponent of this view permits the entry of "ya" upon it, and cites the poet's saying: "Ya Allahumma, ma turadd 'alayna sahan musallaman," and the verse mentioned earlier and others.

The Basrans rejected this on several grounds.

First: these estimates have no evidence for them, and analogy does not require them, so one should not turn to them without evidence.

Second: the original is non-elision, so estimating these many omitted elements contradicts the original.

Third: the one who supplicates with this may invoke evil upon himself and others, so this estimate is not valid for it.

Fourth: the widespread, eloquent usage indicates that the Arabs did not combine "ya" and "Allahumma," whereas had its origin been what al-Farra' mentioned, combining them would not be forbidden; rather its usage would be eloquent and widespread. The reality is otherwise.

Fifth: it is not impossible for the supplicant to say, "Allahumma, amminna bi-khayr." Had the estimate been as he mentioned, combining them would not be permissible, because it would combine the substitute and what it substitutes.

Sixth: the one who supplicates with this name does not have that in mind; rather his attention is simply directed to the desired matter after mentioning the name.

Seventh: had the estimate been that, "Allahumma" would be a complete sentence on which silence is good, since it contains the vocative noun and an imperative verb. That is false.

Eighth: had the estimate been what he mentioned, the imperative verb would be written alone and not joined to the vocative noun, as one says "ya Allah qah," "ya Zayd 'ah," "ya 'Amr fah." For the verb is not joined to the noun before it so as to be written as a single word. This has no parallel in writing, and the agreement on joining the mim to the name of God is evidence that it is not an independent verb.

Ninth: it is not valid nor good in supplication for the servant to say, "Allahumma, ammani bi-kadha"; rather this is objectionable in both wording and meaning. One does not say "aim me at such-and-such" except to one who is liable to error and forgetfulness, who is told "aim me." As for one who acts only by his will and neither errs nor forgets, one does not say to him "aim at such-and-such."

Tenth: it is permissible to use this word in a position where no supplication follows it, such as the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying in supplication: "Allahumma laka al-hamd, wa ilayka al-mushtaka, wa anta al-musta'an, wa bika al-mustaghath, wa 'alayka al-tukan, wa la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah." And his saying: "Allahumma, inni asbahtu ushhiduka wa ushhidu hamalata 'arshika, wa malaikataka wa jami'a khalqika, annaka anta Allah la ilaha illa anta wahdaka la sharika laka, wa anna Muhammadan 'abduka wa rasuluka." And the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿Say: O God, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty from whom You will; You honour whom You will and You humble whom You will.﴾ And His saying:

Ibn al-Qayyim's Commentary on Surah 3, Verse 26 (Part 3 of 3)

﴿Say, "O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they used to differ."﴾

And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his bowing and prostration: "Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You. O Allah, forgive me."

All of this does not permit the interpretation they mentioned. And Allah knows best.

It has been said: the letter mim (م) was added for emphasis and magnification, like its addition in zarqam (intensely blue) and ibnam (in ibn).

This view is correct, but it needs a complement. Its proponent perceived a correct meaning which must be explained.

It is that the letter mim indicates plurality and requires it, and its point of articulation (makhraj) requires this.

This is consistent with the principle of those who affirm a correspondence (munasabah) between the form of a word and its meaning, which is the doctrine of the masters of the Arabic language. Abu al-Fath Ibn Jinni devoted a chapter to it in al-Khasa'is, and he attributed it to Sibawayh, and he supported it with various kinds of correspondence between word and meaning.

Then he said: "For a while I would encounter a word whose origin I did not know, and I would find its meaning from the strength of its sound and the suitability of those letters to that meaning. Then I would uncover it and find it as I had understood it, or close to it."

I related this from Ibn Jinni to Shaykh al-Islam, and he said: "This happens to me frequently too." Then he mentioned to me a very beneficial section on the correspondence between word and meaning, and the suitability of vowels (harakat) to the meaning of the word, and that they generally give the strongest vowel, the damma, to the stronger meaning, the light fatha to the lighter meaning, and the middle vowel to the intermediate meaning. So they say: 'azza ya'uzzu (with fatha on the 'ayn) when a thing is hard, and ard 'azaz (a hard land). And they say: 'azza ya'izzu (with kasra) when it becomes unassailable.

The unassailable is above the hard, for a thing may be hard yet not unassailable to one who breaks it. Then they say: 'azzahu ya'azzahu when he overpowered him.

Allah the Exalted said, regarding the story of Dawud (peace be upon him): ﴿and he overpowered me in speech﴾.

Overpowering is stronger than being unassailable, for a thing may be unassailable in itself, fortified against its enemy, yet not overpower others. So the overpowering is stronger than the unassailable. They gave it the strongest vowel, the damma, while the hard is weaker than the unassailable, so they gave it the weakest vowel, the fatha, and the unassailable, intermediate between the two ranks, takes the middle vowel.

A parallel to this is their saying dhabah (with kasra on its first letter) for the slaughtered place, and dhabh (with fatha on its first letter) for the act itself. There is no doubt that a body is stronger than an accident, so they gave the strong vowel to the strong and the weak to the weak. This is like their saying nahb and nahb, with kasra for the thing plundered and fatha for the act. And like their saying mil' and mal', with kasra for what fills a thing and fatha for the verbal noun, which is the act. And like their saying himl and haml: with kasra for what is strong and heavy on the bearer's back, head, or other limbs, and haml with fatha for what is light and not burdensome, like the load of an animal, and the load of a tree is more like it, so they gave it fatha.

Consider this in al-hubb and al-hubb. They made the initial kasra for the beloved himself, and the damma for the verbal noun, signifying the lightness of the beloved upon their hearts, the subtlety of his place in their souls, his sweetness to them, and the heaviness and persistence of bearing love, as the creditor persists upon his debtor. For this reason it is called gharam. Hence their descriptions of bearing it as hard and difficult are abundant, and their report that the greatest and hardest of created things, such as rock and iron, if it were carried, would melt the one carrying it and he could not bear it. This is abundant in the poetry and speech of the earlier and later poets. So it was best that the verbal noun here be given the strong vowel, and the beloved the vowel that is lighter than it.

From this: their saying qabad with a sukun in its middle for the act, and qabad with movement for the thing grasped. Movement is stronger than sukun, and the thing grasped is stronger than the verbal noun.

Its parallel is sabq with sukun for the act, and sabaq with fatha for the wager taken in this contract.

Consider their saying dar, dawaran; fara al-qidr, fawaran; and waghalat, ghalayanan: how they followed the vowels in these verbal nouns to match the movement of what is named.

Thus the word corresponds to the meaning.

Consider their saying hajar and hawa'. How they placed for the heavy, strong meaning these strong letters, and for the light meaning they placed al-hawaya, which is among the lightest of letters.

This is more than can be encompassed, and if Allah extends my life I shall compose a separate book on it, Allah willing.

Such meanings require subtlety of mind and delicacy of disposition. They are not attained with coarse hearts, nor by contentment with the rudiments of grammar and morphology, without reflecting upon them and pondering them, and considering the wisdom of the one who established the language, and surveying the secrets in this marvelous tongue which escape most minds. This is a field that alerts the discerning to what lies beyond it: ﴿And whomever Allah has not granted light, for him there is no light﴾.

Consider their naming the coarse, harsh man al-'utull, al-ja'zari, and al-jawwas, how you find these words calling out to the meanings beneath them.

Consider their naming the tall man al-'ashanniq. Reflect on how these letters entail and correspond to the meaning of tallness, and their naming the short man al-bahtar. Consider their use of three fathas in the name of the tall one, al-'ashanniq, and their use of two dammas with a sukun between them in al-bahtar. How the first word entails the opening of the mouth, the widening of the organs of speech, their extension, and the absence of one overlapping another, while in the name al-bahtar the matter is the opposite.

Consider their saying: tala al-shay' fahuwa tawil (the thing was long, so it is long), and kabura kabir (it was big, so it is big). If its length and size increase, they say tiwalan and kibaran, bringing the alif, which has more extension and is longer than the ya' in al-atwal. If the size of the thing increases and its weight in souls becomes heavier, they make its name heavier, saying kabbaran with the ba' doubled.

If we loosed the reins of the pen in this matter, its course would be long and it would resist control.

Let us return to what the discussion was about. We say: the mim is a labial letter, whose speaker brings together his lips. The Arabs assigned it as a sign of plurality. So they say for the singular: anta; and when they move to the plural they say: antum. They say for the singular absent: huwa; and when they move to the plural they say: hum. Likewise in the attached pronouns they say: darabtu, darabtum; iyyaka, iyyakum; iyyahu, iyyahum; and their parallels, such as bihi and bihim. They say of a blue thing, and when its blueness intensifies, gathers and becomes firm, they say zarqam. And they say of a large-buttocked person: istahum on the pattern of qunfudh.

Consider the words in which the mim occurs, how you find plurality bound to it, such as lamma al-shay' yalummuhu, when he gathers it. From it: Allah lamma shi'tahu, meaning He gathered what had been scattered of his affairs. From it: their saying dar lamumah, meaning one that gathers people together. From it: al-akl al-lumm, explained as: he eats his share and his companion's share. Its origin is from al-lamm, which is gathering, as one says lafahu yalfuhu. From it: alamma bi al-shay', when he came close to meeting it and reaching it.

From it: al-lamam, which is approaching the gathering with the major sins. From it: al-mulamma, which is the calamity that befalls the servant. From it: al-lammah, which is the hair that has gathered and contracted until it passes the lobe of the ear. From it: lamm al-shay' and what derives from it.

From it: badr al-tamm, when it is complete and its light gathers.

From it: al-tawam, for the two twins gathered in one womb.

From it: al-umm (the mother). The umm of a thing is its origin from which it branches. It is the one that gathers it together, and by it Makkah was named Umm al-Qura, and al-Fatihah Umm al-Qur'an, and the Preserved Tablet Umm al-Kitab.

Al-Jawhari said: umm al-shay' is its origin, and Makkah is Umm al-Qura. Umm mathwak is the companion of your dwelling, meaning the one to whom you retreat and with whom you gather. Umm al-dimagh is the membrane that gathers the brain, and it is called umm al-ras (mother of the head).

Allah the Exalted said concerning the clear verses: ﴿They are the mother of the Book﴾.

And al-ummah is a community equal in creation, or in time, or in language. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth nor bird that flies with its wings but they are communities like you﴾.

And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Were it not that dogs are a community among the communities, I would have ordered them to be killed."

From it: al-imam, whom those following gather around to follow.

From it: amma al-shay' ya'ummuhu, when he gathers his intent and aim toward it.

From it: ramma al-shay' yarummuhu, when he repairs it and gathers its scattered parts.

It has been said: from this the pomegranate was named, for the gathering and compactness of its seeds.

From it: damma al-shay' yadummuhu, when he gathers it.

From it: hamm al-insan and humumuh, which are his will and resolutions that gather in his heart.

From it: their saying to the black one: ahamm; a black coal: hamamah; and hamma ra'suhu, when his head turned black after being shaved entirely. This is because blackness is a color that gathers the sight and does not let it scatter.

For this reason, a black cloth or hair is placed over the eyes of one weak of sight, due to pain or otherwise, so that his sight may gather upon it and the seeing power be strengthened.

This is a long chapter, and we shall limit ourselves to this measure.

Now that this is known about the mim, they have attached it to the end of this name, "Allahumma," with which the servant asks his Lord, glorified is He, in every need and every state, signifying the gathering of His names and attributes. When the petitioner says, "Allahumma, inni as'aluka," it is as if he said: I call upon Allah, to whom belong the Most Beautiful Names and the Highest Attributes, by His names and attributes.

So he brought the mim, indicating plurality, at the end of this name, signifying his petition to Him, exalted is He, by all His names. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said in the authentic hadith: "No servant has ever been afflicted by distress or grief and then said: 'O Allah, I am Your servant, son of Your servant, son of Your maidservant; my forelock is in Your hand, Your judgment over me is executed, Your decree over me is just. I ask You by every name You have, by which You named Yourself, or sent down in Your Book, or taught to any of Your creation, or kept to Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen with You: that You make the Great Qur'an the spring of my heart, the light of my chest, the departure of my sorrow, and the removal of my worry and distress,' except that Allah removes his worry and distress and replaces them with joy." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall we not learn them?" He said: "Yes, whoever hears them should learn them."

So the supplicant is recommended to ask Allah by His names and attributes, as in the Greatest Name: "Allahumma inni as'aluka bi'anna laka al-hamd, la ilaha illa anta, al-Hannan al-Mannan, Badi' al-samawati wa al-ard, ya dha al-jalal wa al-ikram, ya Hayy ya Qayyum."

These words include the Most Beautiful Names, as mentioned in another place.

Supplication is of three kinds.

The first: that you ask Allah by His names and attributes. This is one of the two interpretations of His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾.

The second: that you ask Him by your need and your poverty and humility. You say: I am the poor, needy, wretched, humble servant seeking refuge, and the like.

The third: that you ask for your need without mentioning either of these two.

The first is more complete than the second, and the second is more complete than the third. When supplication combines the three matters, it is most complete.

This is the general character of the Prophet's (ﷺ) supplications.

In the supplication taught by the most truthful of this community, may Allah be pleased with him, the three categories are mentioned.

For he said at its beginning: "Allahumma, inni zalamtu nafsi zulman kathiran," which is the state of the supplicant. Then he said: "Wa innahu la yaghfiru al-dhunuba illa anta," which is the state of the One asked. Then he said: "Faghfir li," mentioning his need, and he concluded the supplication with two of the Most Beautiful Names that correspond to and entail what is sought.

This view which we have chosen has come from more than one of the early generation. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "Allahumma" is the gathering of supplication. Abu Raja' al-Utaridi said: the mim in His saying "Allahumma" contains ninety-nine of Allah's names. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: whoever says "Allahumma" has called upon Allah by all His names.

A group explained this view by saying that the mim here takes the place of the waw that signifies plurality, since it comes from its point of articulation. So the one who calls with it is as if saying: O Allah, to whom the Most Beautiful Names and the Highest Attributes belong. That is why it was doubled, to serve as a substitute for the sign of plurality, which is the waw and nun in "muslimun" and the like.

According to the method we have mentioned, namely that the mim itself signifies plurality, this explanation is not needed.

It remains to ask: why did they not combine "ya" with this mim, according to the correct view?

The answer: analogy requires that the vocative particle not enter this name, because of the alif and lam in it. They tolerated it in this case only because of their frequent use of its invocation, their need for it, and their appeal to it for help. Either they would have to remove the alif and lam from it, which is not permissible because they are obligatory, or they would have to reach it by means of "ayyu," which is also not permissible, since that is used only to address a common noun with the definite article, like al-rajul, al-rasul, and al-nabi, and not for proper names.

So they departed from their analogy in this name because of necessity. Since they placed the doubled mim at its end as a substitute for the plurality of the name, they made it a substitute for the vocative particle, and so they did not combine the two. And Allah knows best.

It is also called the Verse of Love.

Abu Sulayman al-Darani said: When hearts claimed the love of Allah, Allah sent down a trial for them: ﴿Say, "If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you"﴾.

Some of the early pious predecessors (al-salaf) said: A people claimed the love of Allah, so Allah sent down the verse of the trial: ﴿Say, "If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you"﴾.

He said: "﴿Allah will love you﴾" points to the evidence of love, its fruit, and its benefit. Its evidence and sign is following the Messenger, and its benefit and fruit is the love of the One who sent him for you. So if following has not been achieved, then your love for Him has not been achieved, and His love for you is absent.

The root of worship is the love of Allah, or rather devoting love to Him alone, so that all love is for Allah. One does not love anything alongside Him; rather one loves things for His sake and in Him, just as He loves His prophets, messengers, angels and friends. Our love for them is part of the completeness of His love, and it is not love alongside Him, unlike the love of one who takes rivals besides Allah and loves them as he loves Him.

Since love for Him is the very reality of servitude to Him and its essence, it is only realized by following His command and avoiding His prohibition. When one follows the command and avoids the prohibition, the reality of servitude and love becomes clear. For this reason, the Exalted made following His Messenger a sign of it and a witness for whoever claims it, saying, ﴿Say, "If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 31]. He made following His Messenger conditional upon their love for Allah, and a condition for Allah's love for them. The existence of the conditioned thing is impossible without the existence of its condition, and its realization is by the realization of its condition. Thus it is known that love is absent when following is absent. So the absence of their love for Allah necessarily follows from the absence of following His Messenger, and the absence of following entails the absence of Allah's love for them. Therefore it is impossible for their love for Allah to be established, or for Allah's love for them to be established, without following His Messenger.

It indicates that following the Messenger ﷺ is the love of Allah and His Messenger and obedience to his command. That is not sufficient for servitude until Allah and His Messenger are more beloved to the servant than anything else. So nothing is more beloved to him than Allah and His Messenger. Whenever he has something more beloved to him than both of them, this is the shirk that Allah will never forgive its owner, and Allah will not guide him. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿Say, "If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your kindred, the wealth you have acquired, the commerce you fear will decline, and the dwellings you are pleased with are more beloved to you than Allah and His Messenger and jihad in His cause, then wait until Allah brings His command. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people."﴾ [al-Tawbah: 24].

So whoever prefers the obedience of any of these over the obedience of Allah and His Messenger, or the word of any of them over the word of Allah and His Messenger, or the pleasure of any of them over the pleasure of Allah and His Messenger, or fear of any of them and hope in them and reliance upon them over the fear of Allah, hope in Him and reliance upon Him, or dealing with any of them over dealing with Allah, is one for whom Allah and His Messenger are not more beloved than anything else. If he says it with his tongue, it is a lie from him and a report contrary to what is in him. Likewise, whoever prefers the ruling of anyone over the ruling of Allah and His Messenger, that one is more beloved to him than Allah and His Messenger. However, the matter may become unclear to one who prefers the word, ruling or obedience of someone, or his pleasure, supposing that he does not command, rule, or say anything except what the Messenger said, so he obeys him, refers judgment to him, and accepts his sayings on that basis. Such a person is excused if he is unable to do otherwise. But if he is able to reach the Messenger, and knows that someone other than the one he follows has more right to be followed, absolutely or in some matters, and does not turn to the Messenger or to the one who has more right, then this is the one who is feared for, and he falls under the threat. If he considers it permissible to punish whoever opposes him and humiliates him, and does not agree with him in following his shaykh, then he is among the oppressive transgressors. Allah has set a measure for everything.

(Section)

Al-Hasan said: A people in the time of the Prophet ﷺ said, "Indeed we love our Lord," so Allah the Exalted sent down this verse: ﴿Say, "If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you"﴾.

Al-Junayd said: A people claimed the love of Allah, so Allah sent down the verse of love: ﴿Say, "If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you"﴾.

That is, following the Messenger is conformity to what your Beloved loves, for he is the one who conveys from Him what He loves and what He dislikes. His following is therefore agreement with God in doing what He loves and leaving what He dislikes.

Malik said regarding this verse: Whoever loves the obedience of Allah, Allah loves him and makes him beloved to His creation. Conformity to the beloved is evidence of love for him, because whoever loves a beloved must love what the beloved loves and hate what the beloved hates; otherwise he is not a true lover of him, a sincere love, but rather that contradicts it, and otherwise he would not be a lover of him, but a lover of his own aim: whether the beloved loves or dislikes it, and the beloved is for him a means to that aim, so if he obtains his share from someone else he departs from the beloved. This is corrupt, tainted love. When true love requires loving what the beloved loves and hating what the beloved hates, then he must conform to him in it.

But here is a matter in which many who claim love err: conformity to the beloved in his will does not mean his creational, cosmic will, for the entire cosmos is his will, and everything creatures do is by the necessity of His will and cosmic desire. If conformity to Him in this will were His love, He would have no enemy at all, and the devils, disbelievers and polytheists, worshippers of idols, the sun and the moon, would be His friends and beloved, exalted is Allah far above that.

This is only supposed by those of His enemies who deny His love and religion, who equate His friends with His enemies. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds as corrupters on earth? Or shall We treat the righteous as the wicked?﴾ [Sad: 28]. And Allah the Exalted said, ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds, equal in living and dying? Evil is their judgment.﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 21]. And Allah the Exalted said, ﴿Shall We treat the Muslims like the criminals? What is wrong with you? How do you judge?﴾ [al-Qalam: 35-36].

So He, glorified be He, denounced whoever equates the Muslims with the criminals, and the obedient with the corrupters, even though all of them fall under the cosmic will and general decree.

(Benefit)

Reflect on His saying, ﴿then follow me; Allah will love you﴾, meaning the matter is that Allah loves you, not that you love Him. This is not attained except by following the Beloved ﷺ.

(Another benefit)

Asceticism has five types: asceticism in this world, asceticism in the self, asceticism in status and leadership, asceticism in whatever is other than the Beloved, and asceticism in every will that contradicts the will of the Beloved. This is only attained through perfect following of the Beloved's Messenger.

Allah the Exalted said, ﴿Say, "If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ So He, glorified be He, made following His Messenger a cause of their love for Him, and for the servant to be beloved of Allah is higher than for him to be a lover of Allah. The matter is not that you love Allah, but that Allah loves you. Obedience to the beloved is the sign of his love, as it has been said:

Thou disobeyest God while claiming to love Him, This is a wondrous thing, impossible by reason.

Had your love been true, you would have obeyed Him, For the lover is obedient to the one he loves.

[Section on the meaning of āl (آل), its derivation and its rulings]

On this there are two opinions. The first is that its original form is ahl (أهل). The hāʼ was changed into a hamzah, so it became aʼl (أأل), and then it was softened according to the analogy of similar words, so it became āl (آل). They said: for this reason, when it is diminutive, it returns to its original form and becomes uhayl (أهيل). They said: since it is a branch of a branch, they restricted it to certain nouns that it is attached to. So they do not attach it to names of time or place, nor to non-proper nouns. They do not say āl rajul (آل رجل, "the family of a man") or āl imraʼah (آل امرأة, "the family of a woman"). Nor do they attach it to a pronoun, so one does not say ālahu or ālī. Rather, it is attached only to what is exalted, just as the tāʼ (ت) in oaths was a substitute for the wāw (و) and a branch of it, while the wāw is a branch of the verb of swearing, so they restricted the tāʼ to the most noble and greatest of names, which is the name of Allah, the Exalted.

This opinion is weak in several respects:

First, there is no proof for it.

Second, it entails an irregular change without a required cause, while contradicting the original form.

Third, ahl is attached to rational and non-rational beings, whereas āl is attached only to a rational being.

Fourth, ahl is attached to a proper noun and to an indefinite noun, whereas āl is attached only to an exalted person whose followers return to him.

Fifth, ahl is attached to a noun in the apparent form and to a pronoun, whereas among the grammarians some forbade attaching āl to a pronoun, and those who permitted it considered it irregular and rare.

Sixth, when a man is mentioned with his āl, he is included in it, as in the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Admit the family of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment﴾ [Ghafir 46].

And the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam and Noah and the family of Abraham and the family of ʻImrān over the worlds﴾ [Āl ʻImrān 33].

And the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿except the family of Lot; We saved them at dawn﴾ [al-Qamar 34].

And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Allah, send blessings upon the family of Abī Awfā."

This is when the one to whom āl is attached is not mentioned with it. But when he is mentioned with it, it may be said that he is mentioned separately and is included in āl, and it may be said that mentioning him separately is sufficient without mentioning him as an attachment. Ahl is the opposite of this. So when you say jāʼa ahl Zayd (جاء أهل زيد, "the people of Zayd came"), he is not included among them.

It was also said: rather, its origin is awl (أول). Ṣāḥib al-Ṣiḥāḥ mentioned it under the chapter of the hamzah, the wāw and the lām. He said: "Āl al-rajul are his family and dependants, and his āl are also his followers." According to these scholars, it is derived from āla yaʼūlu (آل يؤول), meaning "to return." So the āl of a man are those who return to him and are attached to him, and he governs them (yaʼūluhum), meaning he manages them, so their ultimate return (māʼal) is to him. From this comes al-iyālah (الإيالة), which is governance (al-siyāsah). So the āl of a man are those whom he governs and manages, and he himself is more entitled to this than anyone else. Thus he is more entitled to being included in his āl, but it is not said that he is exclusively of his āl; rather he is included among them. This root is established for the original essence of a thing and its reality. For this reason the reality of a thing is called its taʼwīl (تأويل), because it is its reality to which it returns.

From this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Do they await anything but its taʼwīl? On the day its taʼwīl comes, those who had forgotten it before will say: "The messengers of our Lord had indeed come with the truth."﴾ [al-Aʻrāf 53].

So the taʼwīl of what the messengers reported is the coming of its reality and seeing it directly. From this is the taʼwīl of a dream, which is its reality seen directly. From this is the taʼwīl of the external vision that is struck for the seer in the realm of imagination (ʻālam al-mithāl). From this is taʼwīl in the sense of outcome, as was said regarding the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and more excellent in outcome (taʼwīlan)﴾ [al-Nisāʼ 59].

It was said: "better in outcome," because the outcomes of matters are their realities to which they return. From this is taʼwīl in the sense of tafsīr (تفسير, exegesis), because the explanation of speech is the clarification of its meaning and its reality which is intended by it. They said: from this is al-awwal (الأول, "the first"), because it is the origin of the count and its foundation from which it branches. From this is āl in the sense of the person himself. The proponents of this view said, and the Arabs were bound to attach it: so it is not used alone except in rare speech, as in the statement of the poet:

"We are the āl of Allah in our land; we have remained āl upon the era of ʻĀd (Iram)."

They also were bound to attach it to the apparent noun, so it is not attached to a pronoun except rarely. Some grammarians considered attaching it to a pronoun a grammatical error, as Abū ʻAbd Allāh Ibn Mālik said. But the correct view is that it is not an error; rather it is from the speech of the Arabs, though rare. From this is the statement of the poet:

"I am the protecting horseman, and my father, and my āl; so who will protect the reality of your āl?"

ʻAbd al-Muṭṭalib also said regarding the Elephant and its companions:

"And grant victory over the āl of the Cross and its worshippers today, against your āl."

So he attached it to the yāʼ (ي) and the kāf (ك). Some grammarians claimed that it is attached only to the proper name of a rational being. This is what they said, and it is the more common case, but its attachment to a non-rational being has also come. The poet said:

"You escaped, and his divorce did not benefit me except the mare of al-Taqrīb from the āl of Aʻwaj."

Aʻwaj is the name of a horse. They said: among its rulings also is that it is not attached except to an exalted person who is followed, so one does not say āl al-ḥāʼik (the family of the weaver), nor āl al-ḥajjām (the family of the cupper), nor āl rajul.

As for its meaning, a group said: āl al-rajul means the man himself, and āl al-rajul also means whoever follows him, and his āl means his household and relatives. From the first is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when Abū Awfā came to him with his charity: "O Allah, send blessings upon the family of Abī Awfā."

And the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Peace be upon the family of Yāsīn﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 130].

And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Allah, send blessings upon Muḥammad and upon the family of Muḥammad, as You sent blessings upon the family of Abraham."

So the family of Abraham is Abraham himself, because the blessing sought for the Prophet (ﷺ) is blessing upon Abraham himself, and his āl follow him in it.

Others disputed this and said: āl can only mean followers and relatives. The evidences you have mentioned refer to relatives. As for the saying "as You sent blessings upon the family of Abraham," the family of Abraham here are the prophets, and what is sought from Allah, glorified is He, is that He bless His Messenger (ﷺ) as He blessed all the prophets among the descendants of Abraham, not Abraham alone. This is explicitly stated in some wordings: "upon Abraham and upon the family of Abraham."

As for the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Peace be upon Ilyāsīn﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 130], there are two readings. One is Ilyāsīn, on the pattern of Ismāʻīl, and there are two views on it. One is that it is a second name for the Prophet Ilyās, and Ilyāsīn is like Mīkāl and Mīkāʼīl. The second view is that it is a plural, and there are two views on this: one is that it is the plural of Ilyās, whose original form is Ilyāsiyyīn with two yāʼs, like ʻIbrāniyyīn, then one of the two yāʼs was lightened, so it became Ilyāsīn, and the intended meaning is his followers, as Sībawayh related: al-Ashʻarūn, and similarly al-Aʻjamūn.

The second is that it is the plural of Ilyās with the yāʼ omitted.

The second reading is ﴿Peace be upon Āl Yāsīn﴾, and there are several views on it. One: Yāsīn is the name of his father, so āl is attached to him as one says Āl Ibrāhīm. Two: the āl of Yāsīn is Ilyās himself, so āl is attached to Yā-Sīn, and the intended meaning of āl is Yāsīn himself, as the earlier scholars mentioned. Three: it is on the omission of the yāʼ of relation, so one says Yāsīn, and its original form is Yāsiyyīn as previously mentioned, and his āl are his followers in his religion. Four: Yāsīn is the Qur'an, and his āl are the people of the Qur'an. Five: it is the Prophet (ﷺ), and his āl are his relatives and followers, as will come.

All these views are weak. What led their proponents to them is their difficulty with attaching āl to Yāsīn, whose name is Ilyās or Ilyāsīn, and they saw it separated in the codex. Some readers read it as Āl Yāsīn. Then some of them said he has the names Yāsīn, Ilyāsīn and Ilyās. Another group said Yāsīn is the name of someone else. Then they differed: al-Kalbī said Yāsīn is Muḥammad (ﷺ), and Allah sent peace upon his āl. Another group said it is the Qur'an. All of this is manifest artificiality with no need for it. The correct view, and Allah knows best, is that the original expression is Āl Yāsīn, like Āl Ibrāhīm. The alif and lām at its beginning were dropped to avoid the gathering of similar sounds, and because the name indicates the place of the omitted part. This is frequent in their speech: when similar elements gather, they dislike pronouncing them all, so they omit what does not cause confusion when omitted. Yet they do not omit it in a place where similar elements do not gather. For this reason they do not omit the nūn from innī, annī, ka'annī, and lākinnī, nor do they omit it from laytanī. Since the lām in laʻalla resembles the nūn, they omitted the nūn with it, especially since the Arabs' practice is to use foreign names and change them, so they say sometimes Ilyāsīn, sometimes Ilyās, sometimes Yāsīn, and perhaps they say Yās. In one of the two readings, the peace falls upon the one greeted, and in the other reading upon his āl.

On this basis, the dispute between the proponents of the two views about āl is resolved: if āl appears alone, it includes the one to whom it is attached, as in the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Admit the family of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment﴾ [Ghafir 46], and there is no doubt that he is included in āl here.

And the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We certainly seized the family of Pharaoh with years of drought﴾ [al-Aʻrāf 130], and its like.

And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Allah, send blessings upon the family of Abī Awfā." There is no doubt that Abū Awfā himself is included in this. And his saying: "O Allah, send blessings upon Muḥammad and upon the family of Muḥammad, as You sent blessings upon the family of Abraham." This is the wording of most of al-Bukhārī's narrations, and Abraham here is included in his āl. Perhaps this is what those who said "āl al-rajul is the man himself" intended.

As for when a man is mentioned and then his āl are mentioned, he is not included among them. So a distinction is made between the bare and the conjoined. When you say aʻṭi li-Zayd wa-āl Zayd (give to Zayd and the family of Zayd), Zayd here is not included in his āl. But when you say aʻṭihi li-āl Zayd (give it to the family of Zayd), it includes Zayd and his āl. This has many parallels, which we have mentioned elsewhere. It is that the signification of a word varies with being bare or conjoined, like al-faqīr and al-miskīn: they are two categories when mentioned together, and one category when each is mentioned alone. For this reason they were two categories in zakāh and one category in expiations. Likewise īmān and islām, al-birr and al-taqwā, al-faḥshāʼ and al-munkar, al-fusūq and al-ʻiṣyān, and similar examples, which are numerous, especially in the Qur'an.

(Faidah)

People have differed over whether it is permissible to apply the title "sayyid" (master, lord) to human beings. A group prohibited it, and this view is reported from Malik. They argued that someone said to the Prophet ﷺ, "O our sayyid," and he said, "The sayyid is only Allah."

Another group permitted it, and they argued from the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Stand up for your sayyid."

This [second position] is more sound than the first hadith.

These people said: "Sayyid" is one of the things that is ascribed to Allah, so one does not say of a man from the tribe of Tamim that he is "sayyid of Kinda," nor say of Malik that he is "sayyid of mankind."

He said: On this basis, it is not permissible to apply this name to Allah.

But this requires consideration, for when "sayyid" is applied to Allah, the Exalted, it carries the meaning of the Owner (al-malik), the Master (al-mawla), and the Lord (al-rabb), and not the meaning in which it is applied to a created being. And Allah, glorified and exalted, knows best.

(Benefit/Note)

All of the Prophet's (ﷺ) children passed away before him except Fatimah, for she lived on six months after him. Because of her patience and her seeking reward from Allah, Allah raised her in ranks, so that she was preferred thereby over the women of the worlds.

Fatimah was the most excellent of his daughters without qualification.

It has been said: indeed she is the most excellent of the women of the worlds.

It has been said: rather, her mother Khadijah is (the most excellent).

It has been said: rather, Aishah is.

It has been said: rather, one should withhold judgment on this matter.

This is one of the things mentioned first because of its virtue, since prostration (sujud) is more excellent, and a servant is closest to his Lord when he is prostrating.

If it is said: bowing (ruku') comes before it by nature, by time, and by custom, since it is a movement from height to lowering, and height is by nature before lowering. Why then was bowing not mentioned first?

The answer is that it should be said:

Pay attention to the meaning of the verse, from His saying ﴿Bow down with those who bow down﴾, and He did not say "Prostrate with those who prostrate." He used prostration to refer to prayer, and He meant her praying in her house, because a woman's praying in her house is better than her praying with her people. Then He said to her, "﴿Bow down with those who bow down﴾," meaning pray with those who pray in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). He did not mean bowing alone, apart from the other parts of prayer. Rather, He used bowing to refer to prayer, as you say, "I performed two rak'as (units of prayer) and four rak'as," meaning prayer, not bowing by itself.

So the verse contains two prayers: her praying alone, which He referred to by prostration, because prostration is the most excellent state of the servant. Likewise, a woman's prayer in her house is better for her. Then her praying in the mosque He referred to by bowing, because it is lower in excellence than prostration.

Likewise, her praying with the worshippers, as opposed to her praying alone in her house in her prayer niche (mihrab).

This is a wondrous arrangement and a precise understanding of jurisprudence.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿O Mary, be devoutly obedient (qunut) to your Lord, prostrate, and bow with those who bow﴾, al-Suhayli went far astray in what he forced as a benefit of the order, and he brought forth what the wording does not bear.

Another said: prostration was in their religion before bowing. This speaker says what he has no knowledge of. What appears from the verse, and God knows best His intended meaning, is that it includes general worship and its details. He mentioned the more general first, then what is more specific than it, then what is more specific than that. He mentioned qunut first, which is continuous obedience, and it includes standing, remembrance, supplication, and all kinds of obedience. Then He mentioned what is more specific than that, which is prostration, which is legislated on its own, such as the prostration of gratitude (sujud al-shukr) and the prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa), and it is also legislated within prayer. So it is more specific than general qunut. Then He mentioned bowing, which is legislated only within prayer, so it is not recommended to perform it alone. So it is more specific than what came before it.

The benefit of this order is descending from the more general to the more specific, and then to what is more specific still. These are two well-known methods in speech: descending from the general to the specific, and its reverse, which is ascending from the specific to what is more general, and then to what is more general still. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, bow down and prostrate, worship your Lord, and do good﴾.

So He mentioned four things, the most specific of which is bowing, then prostration, which is more general than it, then worship, which is more general than prostration, then doing good in general, which includes all of that.

What makes this clearer is the discussion of what He mentioned after this verse, His saying: ﴿And purify My House for those who circumambulate it and those who stand [in prayer] and those who bow and prostrate﴾. He mentioned the most specific of these three, which is circumambulation, which is legislated only at the House itself. Then He moved from it to i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque), which is the standing mentioned in the context of Hajj, and it is more general than circumambulation, because it occurs in every mosque, and it is specific to mosques and does not go beyond them. Then He mentioned prayer, which covers all parts of the earth except what is prevented by an obstacle or excepted by the Shari'ah.

If you wish, you may say: He mentioned circumambulation, which is the act of worship most closely tied to the House, then i'tikaf, which takes place in all mosques, then prayer, which takes place in the whole city, indeed in every place.

This completes the discussion of the examples he mentioned, and may God have mercy on him, he has excellent precedence and superior priority.

(Benefit)

The places of prostration in the Qur'an are of two types: informative and imperative. The informative is a report from God, Exalted is He, about the prostration of His creatures to Him, in general or in particular. So it is sunnah for the reciter and the listener, whether obligatory or recommended, to imitate them when reciting or hearing a verse of prostration. The verses of commands are included by a stronger reason. There is no difference in this between one command and another. How then can His saying ﴿So prostrate to God and worship﴾ [al-Najm: 62] require prostration, but His saying ﴿O you who have believed, bow down and prostrate﴾ [al-Hajj: 77] not require it? The one who prostrates is either imitating those reported about, or complying with what he was commanded. Under either assumption, it is sunnah for him to prostrate at the end of al-Hajj just as it is sunnah for him to prostrate at its beginning. Since the sunnah equated them, sound analogy and true reasoning also equate them.

This prostration was legislated by God and His Messenger as an act of worship at the recitation and hearing of these verses, as a means of drawing near to Him, as humility before His greatness, and as submission before Him. Bowing being joined with some of His verses confirms and strengthens this, and does not weaken or undermine it. And God is the One sought for help.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, prostrate, and bow with those who bow﴾ [Al 'Imran: 43], it is not a place of prostration because it is a specific report about the words of the angels to a particular woman, that she should continue worship of her Lord through qunut and pray to Him with bowing and prostration. So it is a report of what the angels said to her, and an announcement from God, Exalted is He, to us that the angels said that to Mary.

Therefore the context of that is different from the context of the verses of prostration.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 3, verse 44:

Qatadah said: Maryam was the daughter of their imam and their leader. The Children of Israel disputed over her, so they cast lots with their arrows to determine which of them would take charge of her. Zakariyya drew the lot, and he was the husband of her sister, so he took her into his care. Similar is related from Mujahid.
