Ibn Abbas said: When Maryam was placed in the mosque, the people of the place of prayer (ahl al-musalla) cast lots over her, while they were writing down the revelation (al-wahy), and they cast lots with their pens to determine which of them would take charge of her. This is agreed upon among the scholars of tafsir (ahl al-tafsir).

Translation:

As for the scheming (makr) which He has attributed to Himself, it is His requital of those who scheme against His friends (awliya') and His messengers. He counters their evil scheming with His good scheming. Thus scheming from them is the most ugly of things, and from Him it is the most excellent of things, because it is justice and recompense. Likewise, deception (mukhada'a) from Him is a requital for the deception of His messengers and friends, so there is nothing more excellent than that deception and scheming.

As for a man who works the deeds of the people of Paradise until there remains between him and it only a cubit, and then the Decree (al-kitab) overtakes him, this is because such an act is the deed of the people of Paradise as it appears to people; yet if it were a righteous deed acceptable for Paradise, one that Allah loves and is pleased with, He would not nullify it for him.

His saying "until there remains between him and it only a cubit" poses a difficulty for this interpretation. It is said: since the deed was judged by its ending and conclusion, this worker did not persevere in his deed until it was completed for him. Rather, there was a hidden blight in him and a flaw by which he was forsaken at the end of his life, so that blight, that calamity and inner corruption, betrayed him at the time of need; he returned to its requirement and it did its work. And had there not been a hidden deceit and blight, Allah would not have turned his faith over; He would have brought him to it, despite his sincerity and devotion, without any cause from him that would call for its corruption. Allah knows of His servants what none of them knows of one another.

As for the matter of Iblis, Allah, glorified is He, said to the angels, ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾. The Lord, exalted is He, knew what was in Iblis's heart of disbelief, arrogance and envy, which the angels did not know. When they were commanded to prostrate, what was in their hearts of obedience, love, awe and submission became manifest, so they hastened to comply; and what was in the heart of His enemy of arrogance, deceit and envy became manifest, so he refused and was arrogant, and he was among the disbelievers.

As for the fear of His friends from His scheming, it is true, for they fear that He will forsake them because of their sins and wrongdoings, so they would come to wretchedness. Thus their fear is due to their sins, and their hope is in His mercy.

His saying ﴿Do they feel secure from the scheming of Allah?﴾ refers only to the wicked and the disbelievers. The meaning of the verse is: none feels secure from Allah's counter-scheming against him for the evil deeds of his scheming, except the people who are losers. What those who know Allah fear of His scheming is that He may delay the punishment of their deeds from them, so that a kind of delusion arises in them, they become at ease with sins, and the punishment comes upon them unexpectedly and in a state of heedlessness. Another matter is that they become oblivious of Him and forget His remembrance, so that He withdraws from them when they abandon His remembrance and obedience, and trial and affliction hasten toward them; thus His scheming against them is His withdrawal from them. Another matter is that He knows of their sins and faults what they do not know of their own selves, so the scheming comes upon them from where they do not perceive. Another matter is that He tests them and afflicts them with what they have no patience for, so they are tempted by it, and that is scheming.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 3, verse 59:

As for analogy by way of the effective cause ('illah), it appears in the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in several places. Among them is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like that of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾. So He informed that Jesus is a counterpart of Adam in creation, by the common factor (jami') of the meaning shared between them, which is the meaning upon which the existence of all other created things depends, namely their coming into being in obedience to His will and His creating. How, then, is the existence of Jesus without a father deemed strange by one who acknowledges the existence of Adam without a father or a mother, and the existence of Hawwa' (Eve) without a mother?

Adam and Jesus are therefore two counterparts, joined by the meaning upon which the bringing into being and the creating can rightly be made dependent.

(Section)

Among the Devil's manipulations of this wrathful nation is that when they see a command or prohibition, of what they were commanded or forbidden, as burdensome to them, they seek to escape it through all kinds of tricks. If tricks fail them, they say: "This was incumbent upon us only when we had kingship and leadership."

Among this: when two brothers dwell in one place, and one of them dies without leaving a son, the widow of the deceased may not go out to a foreign man; rather, the dead man's brother (the widow's brother-in-law) marries her. The first son born to whomever marries her is attributed to his deceased brother. If he refuses to marry her, she goes out complaining about him to the elders of his people, saying: "The brother-in-law has refused to preserve a name for his brother in Israel, and he has not wished to marry me." The judge there summons him and requires him to stand and say: "I did not wish to marry her." Then the woman takes his sandal, removes it from his foot, grasps him by the hand, spits in his face, and calls out: "Thus shall be done to the man who does not build up his brother's house." He is afterward called "the one whose sandal was removed," and his sons are called "the sons of the one whose sandal was removed."

All of this is, according to their claim, prescribed for them in the Torah.

In this there is a wisdom that compels a man to marry his deceased brother's wife: for when he knows that this will befall him if he does not marry her, he prefers marrying her to the alternative. But if he hates her and has no desire to marry her, or if she is unwilling to marry him and hates him, the jurists devise a trick by which he is freed from her and she is freed from him. They oblige her to appear before the judge in the presence of their elders, and they instruct her to say: "The brother-in-law has refused to raise a name for his brother in Israel; he has not wished to marry me." Thus they compel her to lie about him, for he did wish to marry her but she hated him. Once they have taught her these words, she says them, and they then order him to lie, and to stand and say: "I did not wish to marry her." This is likely what he wants and desires, yet they order him to lie. It was not enough for them that they lied about him; they obliged him to lie as well, until they empowered her to disgrace him and spit in his face. They call this matter "al-Bayama wal-Jalus."

Some of what suffices has already been mentioned regarding their tricks in making lawful for themselves the things God has forbidden.

So this people is the house of tricks, deceit and wickedness.

In the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) they varied in kinds of tricks, plots and deception against him and his companions, and God, glorified and exalted, returned all of that upon them.

They devised against him and attempted to kill him several times, while God protected him from their scheming.

They devised against him, climbed onto a roof and took a millstone, intending to drop it on him while he was sitting in the shade of a wall. Revelation came to him, so he rose and departed, and began to wage war against them and expel them.

They plotted against him and backed his enemies among the polytheists, so God granted him victory over them.

They plotted against him and began gathering the enemy against him, so God granted him victory over their leader, and he killed him.

They plotted against him and intended to kill him by poison, so God informed him of it and saved him from it.

They practiced sorcery against him, until it appeared to him that he was doing a thing when he was not doing it. God healed him and freed him.

They plotted against him in their saying: "Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end" (Qur'an 3:72).

They intended by this to cast doubt upon the Muslims regarding his prophethood, for when they embraced Islam at the start of the day, the Muslims were reassured by them and said: "They have followed the truth, and its proofs have become clear to them." Then they would disbelieve at the end of the day, deny his prophethood, and say: "We intended only the truth and to follow it, but when it became clear to us that he is not (the true prophet), we turned back from believing in him."

This is among the greatest of their wickedness and cunning.

They never ceased, persistent and striving in cunning and wickedness, until God disgraced them at the hand of His Messenger and his followers, may God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, and be pleased with them, with the greatest disgrace, tore them to every shred and scattered their gathering in every direction.

They used to make covenants with him, peace be upon him, and make treaties with him. Whenever he went out to fight their enemy, they broke his covenant.

When God deprived this nation of its kingdom and might, and humiliated them, and scattered them across the earth, they moved from managing by power and authority to managing by cunning and guile, treachery and deception. Likewise, every weak coward whose authority lies in his trickery, deception, slander and lying. For this reason, women have been a house of guile, deception, lying and treachery, as God, exalted is He, said concerning the witness of Joseph, peace be upon him, when he said: "Indeed, it is of your guile; surely, your guile is great" (Qur'an 12:28).

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 3, verse 93–95:

These verses contain a clear demonstration of their lie in denying abrogation (naskh). Indeed, Allah, glorified and exalted, informed that all food had been lawful for the Children of Israel before the Torah was sent down, except what Israel had forbidden to himself. It is known that the Children of Israel were upon the law and creed of their father Israel, and that what was lawful for them was only lawful by Allah's making it lawful, through the tongue of Israel and the prophets after him, until the time the Torah was sent down. Then the Torah came with the prohibition of many foods that had been lawful for the Children of Israel. This is pure abrogation.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Before the Torah was sent down﴾, meaning: they were lawful for them before the sending down of the Torah. And they know this. Then He, exalted is He, said: {Say, "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful."}

Do you find in it that Israel forbade to himself what the Torah has forbidden to you, or do you find in it the prohibition of what he singled out for prohibition, namely the flesh and milk of camels specifically? If he only forbade this, and everything else was lawful for him and his sons, while the Torah has forbidden much of it, then your lie and fabrication in denying the abrogation of laws, and your restriction of Allah, exalted is He, in abrogating them, have become manifest.

So reflect on this noble situation which most of the exegetes circled around, and what they reported. This argument is better than the argument of many of the people of kalam (ahl al-kalam, speculative theologians) against them, that the Torah forbade many things of marriages, slaughtered animals, actions and statements, and that this is abrogation by the ruling of original permissibility (al-bara'ah al-asliyyah, the presumption of continuity of the original state). For this debate is very weak, since the people did not deny the lifting of original permissibility through prohibition and obligation, as this is the nature of all laws. Rather, they denied the prohibition of what Allah had permitted, making it forbidden, and the permitting of what He had forbidden, making it permitted.

As for the lifting of original permissibility and istishab (the presumption of continuity), no one among the people of the religions has denied it.

**(Benefit)**

Is the chamber of the Prophet ﷺ better, or the Ka'bah?

Ibn 'Aqil said: "A questioner asked me, 'Which is better, the chamber of the Prophet ﷺ or the Ka'bah?'

I said: If you mean the chamber alone, then the Ka'bah is better. But if you mean that he ﷺ is in it, then, by God, no: not the Throne and those who carry it, nor the Garden of Eden, nor the revolving spheres. For in the chamber is a body which, if it were weighed against both worlds, would outweigh them."

**[Section: God's choosing, among places and lands, the best and most noble of them]**

Among this is that God, glory be to Him, chose from among places and lands the best and most noble of them, which is the Sacred City (al-Balad al-Haram). He chose it for His Prophet ﷺ, made its rites (manasik, the acts of worship performed there) for His servants, and obligated them to come to it from near and far, "from every deep mountain pass." So they enter it only humbly, submissively, and abjectly, with their heads uncovered and stripped of the clothing of the people of this world. He made it a sanctuary (haram) of safety, where no blood is shed, no tree is cut, and no game is startled. Its grass is not uprooted, and its lost property is not picked up for ownership, but only for announcing it. He made the intention to go there an expiation for past sins, an erasure of burdens, and a removal of wrongdoings. This is as in the two Sahihs (the Sahih of al-Bukhari and the Sahih of Muslim) from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said:

"Whoever comes to this House, does not engage in obscenity or sin, will return as on the day his mother bore him."

He did not accept for the one who intends it a reward less than Paradise. In the Sunan (collections of hadith) from the narration of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said:

"Follow up the Hajj (pilgrimage) with the 'Umrah (lesser pilgrimage), for they remove poverty and sins as the furnace removes the impurities of iron, gold and silver. And an accepted Hajj (hajj mabrur) has no reward but Paradise."

In the two Sahihs from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The 'Umrah to 'Umrah is an expiation for what is between them, and the accepted Hajj has no reward but Paradise." So if the Secure City (al-Balad al-Amin) were not the best of his lands and the most beloved to him and the one he chose among lands, he would not have made its open spaces rites for his servants, obligated them to intend it, made that among the most emphatic obligations of Islam, and sworn by it in two places in His Mighty Book. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And this secure city﴾ [At-Tin: 3], and He said: ﴿I swear by this city﴾ [Al-Balad: 1]. There is no spot on the face of the earth other than it to which every capable person must strive and around whose House he must circumambulate. There is no place on the face of the earth that is legislated to be kissed and touched, in which sins and burdens are dropped, except the Black Stone and the Yemeni Corner (al-Rukn al-Yamani).

It is established from the Prophet ﷺ that prayer in the Masjid al-Haram is worth one hundred thousand prayers. In the Sunan of al-Nasa'i and the Musnad (of Ahmad), with a sound chain, from Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "A prayer in this my mosque is better than a thousand prayers elsewhere, except the Masjid al-Haram. And a prayer in the Masjid al-Haram is better than a prayer in this my mosque by a hundred prayers." Ibn Hibban narrated it in his Sahih. This is explicit that the Masjid al-Haram is the best of the spots of the earth absolutely. For this reason, the journey to it is an obligation (fard), while journeys to other places are recommended but not obligatory. In the Musnad, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i, from Abdullah ibn 'Adi ibn al-Hamra', that he heard the Messenger of God ﷺ, while standing on his mount at al-Hazwarah in Makkah, say: "By God, you are indeed the best of God's lands and the most beloved of God's lands to God. Had I not been expelled from you, I would not have left." Al-Tirmidhi said: This is a hasan sahih hadith.

Moreover, among its distinctive features is that it is the qiblah (direction of prayer) for all the people of the earth. There is no other qiblah on the face of the earth.

Among its special features as well is that it is forbidden to face it or turn one's back to it when relieving oneself, unlike the rest of the spots of the earth.

The soundest of the positions on this issue is that there is no difference in this between open land and buildings, for there are more than a dozen proofs for this which have been mentioned elsewhere. The one who distinguishes has nothing that can withstand them at all, along with their contradictions regarding the extent of open land and buildings. This is not the place to fully present the arguments of both sides.

Among its special features as well is that the Masjid al-Haram is the first mosque placed on the earth, as in the two Sahihs from Abu Dharr, who said: "I asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about the first mosque placed on the earth. He said: 'The Masjid al-Haram.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'The Masjid al-Aqsa.' I said: 'How long between them?' He said: 'Forty years.'" This hadith has caused confusion for those who did not know its intended meaning. They said: "It is known that Sulayman ibn Dawud (Solomon) is the one who built the Masjid al-Aqsa, and between him and Ibrahim there are more than a thousand years." This is from the ignorance of this speaker. For Sulayman's role regarding the Masjid al-Aqsa was only its renewal, not its founding. The one who founded it was Ya'qub ibn Ishaq, may God's blessings be upon them and their families and grant them peace, after Ibrahim built the Ka'bah by this amount of time.

Among what indicates its superiority is that God, exalted is He, informed that it is Umm al-Qura (the Mother of Cities). All the cities are followers of it and branches of it, and it is the origin of the cities. Therefore it must not have an equal among the cities. Just as the Prophet ﷺ informed that al-Fatihah is Umm al-Qur'an (the Mother of the Qur'an), so too it has no equal among the divine Books.

Among its special features as well is that no one may enter it except in ihram (the state of ritual consecration for pilgrimage), except those with recurring needs. This is a distinction that no other land shares. This ruling was received by the people from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, with a chain not used as proof, as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) hadith: "No one enters Makkah except in ihram, whether from its people or from others." Abu Ahmad ibn 'Adi mentioned it, but al-Hajjaj ibn Artah is in its chain, and another before him, among the weak narrators.

The jurists have three positions on the matter: negation (that ihram is not required), affirmation (that it is required), and a distinction between one who is within the boundaries (mawaqit) and one who is before them. The one before them may not pass beyond them except in ihram, while the one within them has the ruling of the people of Makkah. This is the position of Abu Hanifah, while the first two positions are those of al-Shafi'i and Ahmad.

Among its special features as well is that one is punished in it for intending evil deeds, even if one does not carry them out. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation with wrongdoing, We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ [Al-Hajj: 25].

Reflect on how He used the verb "intend" (yurid) here with the particle bi (with), and one only says "aradtu bi-kadha" (I intended with such-and-such) when it implies the meaning of the verb "hamma" (to resolve), for one says "hammtu bi-kadha" (I resolved upon such-and-such). So He threatened those who resolve to do wrong therein with making them taste the painful punishment.

From this is that the measures of the bad deeds are multiplied therein, not their quantities. For a bad deed's recompense is a bad deed, but a great bad deed's recompense is its equivalent, and a small one's recompense is its equivalent. So a bad deed in the Sanctuary of God, in His land, and upon His carpet, is more emphatic and greater than it at one of the far ends of the earth. For this reason, the one who disobeys the king upon his own carpet of kingship is not like one who disobeys him in a distant place of his house and carpet. This is the decisive word on the multiplication of bad deeds, and God knows best.

The secret of this preference and distinction has become evident in the attraction of hearts, the yearning of souls, their inclination, and their love for this Secure City. Its pull on hearts is greater than the pull of a magnet on iron. It is the most fitting for the saying of the poet:

*"Its beauties are the primal matter of all beauty,*
*and a magnet for the hearts of men."*

For this reason He, glory be to Him, informed that it is a place of return (mathabah) for the people, meaning that they return to it across the passing years from all regions, and they never have their fill of it. Rather, the more they visit it, the more they long for it.

*"The gaze does not turn away from it when it looks upon it,*
*until the gaze returns to it longing."*

How many slain, despoiled and wounded there are for its sake! How much wealth and lives have been spent in its love! The lover accepts separation from the fruit of his liver, from family, beloveds and homeland, putting before him all kinds of fears, perils, hardships and difficulties. He savors and delights in all of it, and finds it, if the sovereignty of love has manifested in his heart, sweeter than the blessings of those who are adorned and their luxuries and pleasures.

*"He is not a lover who counts his hardship*
*a torment, when his beloved is pleased."*

All this is the secret of its being attributed to Him, glory be to Him, in His saying: ﴿And purify My House﴾ [Al-Hajj: 26]. This special attribution entails the same majesty, veneration and love that the attribution of His servant and messenger to Himself entails. Likewise, His attribution of the believing servants to Himself clothes them with the splendor, love and dignity that it clothes them with. So everything that the Lord, exalted is He, attributed to Himself has, by that, a distinction and special status over others that makes it chosen and selected. Then He clothes it, through this attribution, with an additional preference, specialization and sublimity beyond what it had before the attribution.

Whoever equated between essences, actions, times and places, and claimed that none of them has any superiority over another, and that there is only a mere preference without a preferrer, has not been granted understanding of this meaning. This view is false, and it is refuted by more than forty aspects which have been mentioned elsewhere. The falsity of this doctrine is sufficiently evident from its conception, for our position requires that the essences of the messengers be like the essences of their enemies in reality, and that preference is only through a matter that does not return to the particular essences having attributes and merits that others do not have. Likewise, the very spots of land are one in essence, and no spot has any superiority whatsoever over another spot. Rather, superiority is due to the righteous deeds that occur in them. Thus there is no superiority for the spot of the House, the Masjid al-Haram, Mina, 'Arafat, or the sacred sites over any spot of the earth you name. Rather, the preference is by consideration of a matter external to the spot that does not return to it or to a quality that subsists in it.

God, glory be to Him, has refuted this false view by His saying: ﴿And when a sign comes to them, they say: We will not believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of God﴾ [Al-An'am: 124]. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾, meaning: not everyone is fit or suitable to bear His message. Rather, there are specific places that are appropriate only for it and suitable only for it, and God knows best those places among you.

Had the essences been equal, as these people claim, there would have been no refutation of them in this. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus did We try some of them by means of others, that they might say: Are these the ones upon whom God has bestowed favor from among us? Is God not most knowing of the grateful?﴾ [Al-An'am: 53], meaning: He, glory be to Him, is most knowing of who thanks Him for His blessing, so He singles him out with His bounty and bestows favor upon him, and not upon one who does not thank Him. Not every place is fit for His thanks, for bearing His favor, or for being singled out with His honor.

So the essences of those He chose and preferred, whether objects, places, persons or others, comprise attributes and matters subsisting in them that are not in others, and for their sake God chose them. He, glory be to Him, is the One who favored them through those attributes and singled them out for choosing. So this is His creation, and this is His choosing: ﴿And your Lord creates what He wills and chooses﴾ [Al-Qasas: 67].

How clear is the falsehood of an opinion that holds that the place of the Sacred House is equal to all other places, that the essence of the Black Stone is equal to all other stones of the earth, and that the essence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is equal to the essence of anyone else. Preference lies only in external matters outside the essences and the attributes subsisting in them. These statements and their like are among the transgressions that the theologians (al-mutakallimun) committed against the Sharia (the divine law) and attributed to it, while it is innocent of them. They have no more than the sharing of essences in a general matter, and that does not necessitate their equality in reality, because things that differ may share a general matter while differing in their intrinsic attributes. God Most High never made equal the essence of musk and the essence of urine, nor the essence of water and the essence of fire, ever. The clear disparity between noble places and their opposites, and between virtuous essences and their opposites, is far greater than this disparity. Between the essence of Moses (peace be upon him) and the essence of Pharaoh there is a disparity greater than between musk and dung. Likewise, the disparity between the very Ka'bah and the house of the sultan is far greater than this disparity, by much. So how can the two spots be made equal in reality, when the preference is based on the acts of worship, remembrance and supplications that take place there?!

We did not intend to give an exhaustive refutation of this rejected, despised doctrine; we only intended to depict it. The judgment is to be referred to the discerning, just and intelligent person, and God and His servants do not regard anything else at all. God, glory be to Him, does not single out anything, nor prefer or favor it, except for a meaning that requires its specification and preference. Yes, He is the giver of that preponderance and its bestower. He is the One who created it, then chose it after its creation: ﴿And your Lord creates whatever He wills and chooses﴾.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 3, verse 97:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿In it are clear signs, the standing-place of Ibrahim; whoever enters it is safe. And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by people who are able to make their way to it. As for whoever disbelieves, God is Self-Sufficient, above the worlds.﴾ (3:97)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever enters it is safe﴾

This may be a report that carries the meaning of a command, because the Exalted's report cannot be broken.

It may be a report about His law and His religion, which He legislated for His sanctuary (haram).

It may be a report about the familiar, continuous situation of His sanctuary in the Jahiliyyah and in Islam, as the Exalted said: ﴿Do they not see that We made a secure sanctuary, while people are being snatched away from around them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 67], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they say, "If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land." Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary to which the fruits of everything are brought?﴾ [al-Qasas: 57].

Whatever goes beyond these is among the false sayings and is not to be paid attention to, such as the saying of some of them: ﴿And whoever enters it is safe﴾ from the Fire,

and the saying of some of them: "He is safe from death while not upon Islam," and the like. For how many have entered it while they were in the depths of Hellfire?

(Section)

﴿Hajj al-bayt﴾ (pilgrimage to the House) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is in one of the two prepositional phrases before it. What the meaning requires is that it be in His saying ﴿upon the people﴾, because it is an obligation, and obligation calls for "upon" (ʿala). It is also permissible that it be in His saying "to God" (li-llah), because that phrase includes both obligation and entitlement. This reading is strengthened by the fact that the predicate is the place of the benefit, and placing it first in this construction implies that it is to be delayed. The more deserving option was that it be "to God."

The first option is preferred, since saying "pilgrimage to the House is upon the people" is more common in the usage of obligation than saying "pilgrimage to the House is for God," meaning a right that is owed to God. Consider this carefully.

On this basis, the fronting of the first prepositional phrase, which is not the predicate, has two benefits:

The first: it names the thing that makes the pilgrimage obligatory, so it deserves to be placed before mention of the obligation. Thus the verse contains three matters arranged according to their occurrence. The first is the one who imposes this duty, and so it begins with mentioning him.

The second is the one who performs the obligation, which is the one on whom the duty is imposed, namely the people.

The third is the connection and the right associated with it, in terms of imposition and of the people's duty and performance, which is the pilgrimage.

The second benefit: since the prepositional phrase "to God" names the Exalted, it is required to give it priority, to magnify the sanctity of this obligation that He imposed, and to warn against neglecting it, since what God the Exalted imposes is not like what anyone else imposes.

As for His saying "whoever" (man), it is a substitute (badal). Some people have been drawn to say that it is the agent (fa'il) of the verbal noun, as if He had said, "that whoever is able to make their way to it should make pilgrimage to the House."

This view is weak for several reasons. Among them: pilgrimage is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn). If the meaning of the verse were what he mentioned, it would indicate a collective obligation (fard kifaya), because when those who are able perform the pilgrimage, the responsibility of others is cleared. The meaning would then return to "upon the people is that their able ones should make pilgrimage to the House." When the able ones perform the obligation, it no longer remains obligatory upon those who are not able. But that is not the case. Rather, pilgrimage is an individual obligation upon everyone, whether or not the able ones perform it. However, God the Exalted excuses the one who is unable, because of his inability to perform the obligation, so He does not hold him accountable for it and does not require him to perform it. If he makes pilgrimage, he discharges the duty from himself, but the pilgrimage of the able ones does not discharge the duty from the unable. For further clarification: if you say, "It is obligatory upon the people of this region that from among them a group able to fight should fight," then when that group fights, the obligation no longer attaches to the others. But if you say, "It is obligatory upon all people that from among them whoever is able should fight," then the obligation attaches to all of them, and the one who is unable is excused because of his inability. In the arrangement of the verse in this way, rather than saying "pilgrimage to the House is for the able ones," there is this marvelous subtlety. So consider it.

The second view: the idea of the verbal noun being attributed to its agent, when the agent is present, is preferable to attributing it to its object. One does not depart from this principle except on the basis of a transmitted proof. If the agent were "whoever," the verbal noun would be attributed to it, and it would be said, "upon the people is the pilgrimage to the House by whoever is able." To interpret it as an example of "I like Zayd's beating by 'Amr," where the verbal noun is separated from its agent (which is attributed to it) by the object and the adverbial phrase, is to take the less common and less preferred reading. This is like the reading of Ibn 'Amir, "the killing of their children by their partners" (with the word for "partners" in the genitive, separated from the verbal noun by the object). One should not turn to that.

When it is established that "whoever" is a substitute of part from the whole (badal ba'd min kull), there must be a pronoun in the sentence referring back to "the people," as if it were said, "whoever among them is able." Omitting this pronoun is not good in most speech. Its omission here is good for several reasons. Among them: "whoever" refers to rational beings, like the noun it substitutes, so it is connected to it. Among them also: the relative clause is more specific than the first noun. If the relative clause were more general, omitting the resumptive pronoun would be ugly. An example: if you say, "I saw your sisters who went to the market," meaning "who among them went," it would be ugly, because the one who went to the market is more general than the sisters. Likewise, if you say, "Wear the garments that are beautiful and elegant," meaning "of them," without mentioning the pronoun, it would be even less permissible, because the word "that are beautiful" is more general than "garments." The principle of substitution of part from the whole is that the substitute is more specific than what it substitutes. If the substitute is more general, and you attribute it to a pronoun or restrict it by a pronoun that refers back to the first noun, the generality is removed and only the specificity remains. Another reason the omission of the pronoun in this verse is good, besides what was previously mentioned, is the length of the speech through the relative clause and the relative pronoun.

As for the prepositional phrase in His saying "to it" (ilayhi), it may have two readings. The first: that it be in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from "way" (sabil), as if it were a qualifier of an indefinite noun that was placed before it. If it came after, it would be in the position of a qualifier of "way." The second: that it be linked to "way."

If it is said: how can it be linked to it when there is no sense of a verb in it?

It is said: "way" here refers to what conveys one to the House, such as provisions, supplies, and the like. It thus carries a trace of a verb, and it is not intended as "way" in the sense of "road." Therefore it is proper for the prepositional phrase to be linked to it, and the excellence of the arrangement and the inimitability of the wording required placing the prepositional phrase first, although its proper place is later, because it is a pronoun referring back to the House, and the House is what is intended with care. They place first in their speech what is more important to them. This explanation is that of al-Suhayli. But it is very far-fetched. Rather, the correct view concerning the complement of the prepositional phrase is another reading, better than these two and more suitable to the verse than either. It is the obligation understood from "upon the people," meaning that the pilgrimage is obligatory upon the people. So it is a binding, obligatory right. As for linking it to "way" or making it a circumstantial qualifier of it, that is extremely far-fetched. Consider this carefully.

Hardly does this occur to the mind from the verse. This is like one saying, "God has the pilgrimage owed from you" (li-llah 'alayka al-hajj), and "God has prayer and zakat owed from you."

Among the benefits and secrets of the verse is that when the Exalted mentions what He makes obligatory and what He prohibits, He mentions it with the wording of command and prohibition, which is most common, or with the wording of prescription, writing, and prohibition, such as: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾, ﴿Prohibited to you is carrion﴾, ﴿Say: Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has prohibited﴾. The arrangement of the verse and the emphasis of the obligation are as follows.

In the case of pilgrimage, He used this arrangement, which indicates the emphasis of the obligation, in ten respects:

The first: He placed His name first and attached to it the particle of entitlement and specification (li). Then He mentioned those upon whom He imposed it, with the general term (the people) introduced by the particle "upon" ('ala). Then He substituted for it "those who are able." Then He made "way" indefinite within a conditional context, to signal that pilgrimage is obligatory by whatever way is made easy, whether provisions or wealth. Thus the obligation is linked to the attainment of whatever is called a way. Then He followed this with the gravest threat of disbelief, saying: ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾, that is, by not committing to this obligation and abandoning it. Then He magnified the matter and emphasized the warning by informing that He is independent of it, and God the Exalted is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy. He has no need of anyone's pilgrimage. In mentioning His independence of it here there is an announcement of His hatred for the one who disbelieves, His wrath against him, and His turning His face away from him, which is among the greatest and most forceful threats. Then He emphasized this by mentioning the name "the worlds" in a general sense, and He did not say "God is independent of it," because if He is independent of all the worlds, then He has complete and perfect independence from every aspect, from everyone, in every respect. This is more indicative of the enormity of His hatred for the one who neglects His right which He imposed on him. Then He emphasized this meaning with the particle "indeed" (inna), which signals emphasis. These are ten respects that require the emphasis of this great purpose.

Consider the secret of the substitution in the verse, which requires the mention of the predication twice: once by attributing it to the general population of people, and once by attributing it to the specific group of those who are able. This is one of the benefits of substitution: strengthening the meaning and emphasizing it by repeating the predication. For this reason there is an intention of repeating and restating the governing element.

Then consider what the verse contains of clarification after ambiguity, and detail after generality, and how this includes presenting the speech in two forms and two arrangements, out of care for it and to emphasize its importance.

Then consider how this obligation begins with mention of the excellences of the House and the greatness of its status, in a way that moves souls to seek it and make pilgrimage to it, even if they were not commanded to do so. Thus He said: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for people is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds. In it are clear signs, the standing-place of Ibrahim; and whoever enters it is safe﴾. He described it with five attributes:

The first: it is the oldest of the houses of the world, the first established on earth.

The second: it is blessed. Blessing is the abundance and permanence of good. There is no house in the world more blessed than it, none with more good, none more lasting, and none more beneficial to creatures.

The third: it is guidance. He described it with the verbal noun itself, as an intensification, so that it is as if it were guidance itself.

The fourth: what it contains of clear signs, which exceed forty signs.

The fifth: safety for whoever enters it. In describing it with these attributes, rather than commanding that it be visited, there is something that stirs souls to make pilgrimage to it, even if the distances between them and the land are great and the regions are far apart from the visitors. Then He followed this with explicit obligation, reinforced by those emphases. This shows you the great care of the Exalted for this mighty House, the honoring of its mention, the magnifying of its importance, and the elevation of its status. Even if it had no honor except His attributing it to Himself, by His saying: ﴿And purify My House for those who circumambulate﴾, this attribution would suffice as excellence and honor. It is this attribution that drew the hearts of the worlds toward it and captured their souls with love for it and longing to see it. It is the place of return for lovers, who return to it and never fully satisfy their need of it. Every time they increase in it, they increase in love for it and longing for it. Neither union cures them nor separation strips them of it, as it has been said:

I circumambulate it, while my soul is longing for it, and what is after circumambulation but nearness?

And I kiss the Corner, seeking relief from what is in my heart of longing and of bewilderment.

By God, I do not increase except in ardor, and the heart does nothing but beat rapidly.

O Garden of Refuge, O goal of desires, O my wish beyond every security.

The overpowering of longing refused except to draw near to You, and for me there are no hands to reach You from afar.

My turning away from you was not the turning away of weariness, and I have witness from my eye and my tongue.

I called upon my patience to leave you in your absence, and weeping; but weeping answered, and patience disobeyed me concerning you.

They claim that the lover, when he is far away, will have his passion worn out after a long time.

If this claim were true, there would always be a cure for passion among people in every time.

Rather, patience wears away, while passion remains in its state, unworn by the two changing nights.

And this is a lover whom longing and passion have led, without a driver's reins or a rider's bridle.

He came to you despite the distance of the visit, even if his mount had tired and two legs had carried him.

(Section)

When the wakeful saw the might of this world over its people, the deceit of hope toward its devotees, Satan's mastery and the leading of souls, and they saw that the rule had passed to the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammarah), they took refuge in the fortress of humble supplication and seeking refuge, as a terrified slave seeks shelter in the sanctuary of his master. The desires of this world are like the play of imagination, and the gaze of the ignorant is confined to the outward. But the person of intellect sees what lies behind the veil. Desire showed itself to them, and when they stretched out their hands to grasp it, the snare of the trap became visible to the eyes of insight. They flew away on the wings of caution and aimed for the second departure: ﴿Would that my people knew﴾. They perceived the existence, understood the purpose, resolved on departure before the departure, and prepared themselves to travel the even path. People are busy with trifles while they are crossing the wastelands, and the sparrows of passion are in the bonds of the net, awaiting slaughter. Two foxes fell into a net. One said to the other, "Where shall we meet after this?" The other replied, "After two days, in the tannery." By God, the days were nothing but a dream. Let them awaken, for they have already obtained victory. What has passed of this world is dreams, what remains of it is wishes, and the time is lost between them.

How can one be safe when he has a wife who does not show him mercy, a child who does not excuse him, a neighbour he cannot trust, a companion who does not advise him, a partner who does not deal justly with him, an enemy who never sleeps from hostility toward him, a self that commands evil, a adorned world, a desire for beardless youths, an overpowering appetite, a dominating anger, an enticing Satan, and a weakness that prevails over him? If God takes him in charge and draws him to Himself, all of these are subdued for him. But if He abandons him and leaves him to himself, all of these gather against him, and destruction follows.

When people turned away from judging by the Book and the Sunnah, and from referring to them, and believed that they were not sufficient, and turned instead to opinions, analogy (qiyas, reasoning by analogy), juristic preference (istihsan, a preference for one ruling over another on grounds of benefit), and the sayings of shaykhs, there came upon them corruption in their natural disposition, darkness in their hearts, turbidity in their understanding, and deficiency in their intellects. These matters overtook them and prevailed over them, until the young grew up upon them and the old grew old in them. They did not regard them as deception. Then another dominion came upon them, in which innovations took the place of the Sunnahs, the self took the place of the intellect, desire took the place of right guidance, misguidance took the place of guidance, the reprehensible took the place of the recognised, ignorance took the place of knowledge, ostentation took the place of sincerity, falsehood took the place of truth, lying took the place of truthfulness, flattery took the place of sincere counsel, and oppression took the place of justice. Dominion and ascendancy passed to these matters, and their people became the ones pointed to, whereas before this the dominion belonged to their opposites, and their people were the ones pointed to.

So when you see the dominion of these matters advancing, their banners raised and their armies mounted, then the belly of the earth is better than its surface, the summits of mountains are better than the plains, and keeping company with wild beasts is safer than keeping company with people.

[Section: The Station of I'tisam (Holding Fast)]

Then the heart descends to the station of i'tisam (holding fast).

It has two kinds: holding fast to Allah, and holding fast to the rope of Allah. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah, and do not be divided﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103], and He says: ﴿And hold fast to Allah. He is your Protector; how excellent a Protector and how excellent a Helper!﴾ [al-Hajj: 78].

I'tisam is an ifti'al (reflexive form) derived from 'ismah (protection), meaning to cling to that which protects you and keeps you away from what is feared and dreaded. So 'ismah is protection (himyah), and i'tisam is seeking protection (ihtima'). From this, fortresses were called 'awasim (protectors) because of their defending and shielding.

The mainstay of happiness, both worldly and otherworldly, rests upon holding fast to Allah and holding fast to His rope. There is no salvation except for one who clings to these two protections.

As for holding fast to His rope, it protects from misguidance; and holding fast to Him protects from destruction. The one traveling toward Allah is like one traveling a road toward his destination: he needs guidance to the road and safety along it, and he will not reach his destination except after these two things are attained for him. The guide is responsible for protecting him from misguidance and for leading him to the road, while the provisions, strength and weapons are what give him safety from highway robbers and their harms.

So holding fast to the rope of Allah necessitates guidance and following the guide, and holding fast to Allah necessitates for him strength, provisions, weapons, and the supplies with which he equips himself on his path. This is why the expressions of the early scholars (salaf) differed regarding holding fast to the rope of Allah, though all of them pointed to this same meaning.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Hold fast to the religion of Allah."

Ibn Mas'ud said: it is the community (al-jama'ah). He said: "Keep to the community, for it is the rope of Allah which He commanded you to hold; what you dislike in the community is better than what you love in division."

Mujahid and 'Ata' said: it is the covenant of Allah. Qatadah, al-Suddi and many people of tafsir said: it is the Qur'an.

Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "This Qur'an is the rope of Allah, the clear light, the beneficial healing, a protection for whoever holds to it, and salvation for whoever follows it."

'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the Qur'an: "It is the firm rope of Allah, the tongues do not differ over it, it does not wear out through much repetition, and scholars are never satisfied with it."

Muqatil said: by the command of Allah and His obedience, and "do not be divided as the Jews and Christians were divided."

In the Muwatta', from the narration of Malik, from Suhayl ibn Abi Salih, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah is pleased with three things for you and displeased with three things for you. He is pleased that you worship Him and do not associate anything with Him, that you hold fast together to the rope of Allah, and that you advise those whom Allah has put in charge of your affairs. And He is displeased with qil wa qal (idle talk), wasting of wealth, and excessive questioning." Muslim narrated it in the Sahih.

The author of al-Manazil said: holding fast to the rope of Allah is preserving obedience to Him, while observing His command.

By "observing the command" he means performing acts of obedience because Allah commanded them and loves them, not merely out of habit or for some motive other than complying with the command. As Talq ibn Habib said about taqwa: it is acting in obedience to Allah upon a light from Allah, hoping for the reward of Allah, and abandoning disobedience to Allah upon a light from Allah, fearing the punishment of Allah.

This is the faith and ihtisab referred to in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), such as his saying: "Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward (iman wa ihtisaban)," and "Whoever stands in prayer on Laylat al-Qadr out of faith and seeking reward will be forgiven." So fasting and standing in prayer are obedience; faith and observing the command is that faith be the commander, and sincerity of motive is that faith be the sole commander with nothing else alongside it. Ihtisab is hoping for the reward of Allah.

So holding fast to the rope of Allah protects from innovation and from the harms of deeds, and Allah knows best.

(Section)

As for holding fast to Him, it is to rely upon Him, to seek refuge in Him, to take shelter in Him, and to ask Him to protect and shield the servant, guard him and ward off harm from him. The fruit of holding fast to Him is that He repels harm from the servant, as Allah says: ﴿Allah defends those who believe﴾. So He repels from His believing servant, when he holds fast to Him, every cause that leads to ruin, and shields him from it. He wards off from him doubts and desires, the open and hidden schemes of his enemy, and the evil of his own self, and He repels from him the consequences of the causes of evil once they have taken hold, in proportion to the strength and firmness of his holding fast to Him. So the causes of destruction are rendered absent in his case, and He repels their effects and their causes from him, repels His decree with His decree, and His will with His will, and grants him refuge in Himself from Himself.

Section.

As for the author of al-Manazil, he said: holding fast to Allah is ascending beyond every imagined thing (al-mawhum).

For him, the imagined (al-mawhum) is everything other than Allah the Exalted, and ascending beyond it is rising from witnessing the benefit, harm, giving, withholding, and influence of things up to Allah the Exalted. This is an indication of fana' (annihilation). His intent is ascending from witnessing what is other than Allah to Allah. Perfection in this is ascending from willing what is other than Allah to His will.

The Ittihadi (monist) interprets it as ascending from the existence of what is other than Him to His existence, such that he sees no existence for anything else at all, and sees the existence of every existent as His existence; so there is no existence for other than Him except in the false illusion in his view.

He said: it has three levels. The holding fast of the common people is through the report, submitting and yielding, by affirming the promise and the threat, glorifying the command and the prohibition, and founding their conduct upon certainty and fairness.

He means that the common people held fast to the report received from Allah, submitting without dispute, rather with faith and submission, and they yielded to glorifying the command and the prohibition and complying with both, affirming the promise and the threat, and they founded their conduct upon certainty, not upon doubt and hesitation, nor the way of caution, as the poet said:

"The astrologer and the physician both claim
that bodies are not resurrected. I say to both of you:
If your words are true, I am not losing;
if my words are true, the loss is upon you both."

This is the path of people of doubt and suspicion, who carry out commands and prohibitions out of caution. This path does not save one from the punishment of Allah, nor does it obtain happiness for its follower, nor bring him to safety.

As for the fairness upon which they founded their conduct, it is fairness in their dealings with Allah and with His creation.

Fairness in dealing with Allah is that one gives servanthood its due, and does not contend with his Lord over attributes of divinity which are not fitting for the servant nor appropriate for him, such as greatness, pride, and majesty.

And from fairness toward his Lord is that he does not thank other than Him for His blessings and forget Him, does not use them to disobey Him, does not praise other than Him for His provision, and does not worship other than Him, as in the divine report: "I, and the jinn and mankind, are in a great matter: I create and others are worshipped; I provide and others are thanked."

And in another report: "Son of Adam, you have not been fair to Me: My good comes down to you, and your evil ascends to Me. I show affection to you with blessings while I am free of you, and you show hatred to Me with sins while you are needy of Me. The noble angel continues to ascend to Me with an ugly deed from you."

And in another report: "Son of Adam, there is no new day but a new provision comes to you from Me, and the angels come to Me from you with an ugly deed. You eat My provision and disobey Me, you call upon Me and I answer you, you ask Me and I give you, and I call you to My Paradise and you refuse that." This is not fairness.

As for fairness toward the servants, it is that one treats them with the same treatment he loves to be treated with.

By the life of Allah, what was mentioned as the holding fast of the common people is in reality the holding fast of the elite of the elite. But the author (al-Shaykh) is among those for whom the banner of fana' was raised, so he exerted himself toward it, and no blame of a blamer deters him in it, and he sees no station more exalted than it.

Section.

He said: The holding fast of the elite is through detachment (al-inqita'), which is preserving the will by restraining it, letting one's character flow to creation by extending it, and abandoning attachments by resolve; and it is holding to the firmest handhold.

He means the detachment of the soul from its aims in these three aspects: it preserves its will and restrains it from what is other than Allah the Glorified. This resembles the state of Abu Yazid as he reported about himself when he was asked: "What do you want?" He said: "I want not to want."

Second: letting one's character flow to creation by extending it. This is the very reality of tasawwuf, for as Abu Bakr al-Kattani said: "Tasawwuf is character; whoever surpasses you in character surpasses you in tasawwuf."

Indeed, good character and purifying the soul with noble qualities indicate the breadth of its owner's heart, the generosity of his soul and disposition. In this description he restrains harm, bears harm and brings comfort; he turns his left cheek to one who slapped his right, gives his cloak to one who takes his shirt, and walks two miles with one who compels him to walk one mile. This is a sign of his detachment from the shares and aims of his own soul.

As for abandoning attachments by resolve, it is the complete determination to renounce attachments and leave them, outwardly and inwardly.

The root is cutting the attachments of the inner self. Whenever one cuts them, the attachments of the outer self do not harm him. Whenever wealth is in your hand and not in your heart, it does not harm you even if it is abundant; whenever it is in your heart, it harms you even if none of it is in your hand.

It was said to Imam Ahmad: "Can a man be an ascetic while having a thousand dinars?" He said: "Yes, on condition that he does not rejoice when it increases nor grieve when it decreases." For this reason the Companions were the most ascetic of the Ummah while possessing wealth in their hands.

It was said to Sufyan al-Thawri: "Can a man of wealth be an ascetic?" He said: "Yes, if when his wealth increases he is thankful, and when it decreases he is thankful and patient."

Cutting outward attachments is only praised in two situations: where one fears harm to his religion from them, or where there is no preponderant benefit in them. The perfection of this is cutting those attachments that become hooks on the Sirat that prevent one from crossing, and they are the hooks of desires and doubts; what is attached to him after these does not harm him.

Section.

He said: The holding fast of the elite of the elite is through connection (al-ittisal), which is witnessing the Truth as singular, after humbly submitting to Him in glorification, and occupying oneself with Him in nearness.

Since that detachment leads to this connection, that is for the intermediate ones (al-mutawassitin), while this is for the people of arrival (ahl al-wusul), in his view.

By "witnessing the Truth as singular" he means witnessing the Truth, glorified is He, alone and singular, with nothing alongside Him. This is due to the annihilation of the witness in the witnessing, and the transfer in this, according to the people, is through unveiling (kashf).

It has already been stated that this is not perfection, and that perfection is to pass away in His purpose from one's own purpose. As for his annihilation in witnessing from witnessing what is other than Him, it is lower in rank than this annihilation, as already mentioned.

When he says "after *al-istihdha'* (standing before Him) out of glorification," the Shaykh, because he so often uses metaphorical expressions (*al-isti'arat*), conveyed a subtle and great meaning through the word *al-istihdha'*. It is a form X (*istif'al*) derived from *al-muhadhah* (facing, being opposite), which is the kind of facing in which no part of the one facing is left outside what he faces, but he confronts it and meets it completely, with all of his parts. He intends by this nearness and the removal of the intermediaries that prevent it. There is no doubt that the servant draws near to his Lord, and the Lord draws near to His servant. As for the servant's nearness, it is like His saying, ﴿Prostrate yourself and draw near﴾ [al-'Alaq: 19], and His saying in the divine report: "Whoever draws near to Me a handspan, I draw near to him an arm's length." And like His saying: "My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues to draw near to Me with voluntary acts until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks. By Me he hears, by Me he sees, by Me he strikes, and by Me he walks." And in the authentic hadith: "The closest the Lord is to His servant is in the last third of the night." And in another hadith: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating." And in the authentic hadith, when the people raised their voices with *takbir* while travelling with the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "O people, be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent. Indeed, the One you call upon is All-Hearing and near, nearer to one of you than the neck of his mount."

So the Shaykh expressed the seeking of nearness to Him, and the rejection of the intermediaries that stand between the servant and the desired nearness, in which the eyes of His worshippers and friends are not comforted except by it, through *al-istihdha'*. Its reality is the servant's arrival in His presence, before Him, and between His hands, the opposite of the state of one who casts Him behind his back, turns away from Him, and distances himself from Him, like one who turns his back on the one he obeys and inclines his side away from him.

The meaning of this matter cannot be grasped except through experiencing it and tasting it. The best way to express it is by the Prophetic, Muhammadan expression, and the closest of the expressions of the people of the Path is that it is *al-taqrib* (drawing near) through the removal of intermediaries, by whose removal the servant attains the reality of glorification. Therefore he said "*al-istihdha'* before Him, out of glorification."

Whoever wishes to understand this as it should be understood, let him understand the Hidden Name of God (*al-Batin*) and understand His Name *al-Qarib* (the Near), with the heart filled with His love and the tongue constantly moving in His remembrance. From here the servant is led to the annihilation (*fana'*) toward which he strives and for which he works.

Therefore He singled out these people for success, to the exclusion of all others. And those who call to good are those who call to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, not those who call to the opinion of so-and-so and so-and-so.

[Section: The difference between sincere advice (nasihah) and rebuke (ta'nib)]

The difference between sincere advice and rebuke is that sincere advice is a kindness to the one you advise, in the form of mercy towards him, compassion for him, and zeal for him and over him. It is pure kindness, issuing from mercy and tenderness, and the one giving advice intends by it the countenance of Allah and His good pleasure, and benefit to His creation. So he is extremely gentle in offering it, and he bears the harm and blame of the one advised. He treats him as a wise, compassionate physician treats a patient afflicted with a disease: he endures his bad manners, his harshness and his aversion, and he strives gently, by every possible means, to get the medicine to him. This is the manner of the one giving sincere advice.

As for the rebuker, he is a man whose aim is reproach, humiliation, and disparagement of the one he admonishes, and insulting him, while wearing the guise of advice. He says to him, "O doer of such-and-such! O one deserving of blame and humiliation!", in the guise of a compassionate advisor. The sign of this is that if he sees someone he loves and treats well commit the same act as mine, or something worse, he does not say anything to him, but seeks out excuses for him. If he is overcome, he says, "I have guaranteed him freedom from error? A human being is prone to mistakes, his good qualities outnumber his faults, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful," and similar things. How strange! How is this for one he loves and does not hate, and how is it that his share from you is rebuke in the guise of advice, while this person's share from you is hope for pardon, forgiveness, and the seeking of excuses!

Among the differences between the advisor and the rebuker: the advisor does not become hostile to you if you do not accept his advice. He says, "My reward has fallen upon Allah, whether you accept or not," and he prays for you in your absence, does not mention your faults, and does not expose them among people. The rebuker is the opposite of this.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 3, verses 106–107:

﴿On the Day when some faces will turn bright and some faces will turn dark. As for those whose faces turn dark: "Did you disbelieve after your belief? Then taste the punishment for what you used to deny."﴾ (106)

﴿As for those whose faces turn bright, they will be in the mercy of Allah, abiding therein forever.﴾ (107)

Ibn ʿAbbas said: The faces of the people of the Sunnah and the community (ahl al-sunnah wa'l-jamaʿah) will turn bright, and the faces of the people of division and innovation (ahl al-firqah wa'l-bidʻah) will turn dark.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 3, verses 106–107:

﴿On the Day when some faces will turn bright and some faces will turn dark. As for those whose faces turn dark: "Did you disbelieve after your belief? Then taste the punishment for what you used to deny."﴾ (106)

﴿As for those whose faces turn bright, they will be in the mercy of Allah, abiding therein forever.﴾ (107)

Ibn ʿAbbas said: The faces of the people of the Sunnah and the community (ahl al-sunnah wa'l-jamaʿah) will turn bright, and the faces of the people of division and innovation (ahl al-firqah wa'l-bidʻah) will turn dark.

[Prohibiting the Evil and Its Conditions]

The first example: The Prophet ﷺ prescribed for his community the obligation of forbidding evil, so that through forbidding it there would be achieved some of the good that Allah and His Messenger love. Thus, if forbidding evil entails something that is more evil and more hateful to Allah and His Messenger, then it is not permissible to forbid it, even if Allah hates it and abhors its people. This is like denouncing rulers and governors by rising up against them, for that is the foundation of every evil and fitna until the end of time. "The Companions asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for permission to fight the commanders who delayed the prayer beyond its time, and they said: 'Shall we not fight them?' He said: 'No, as long as they establish the prayer.'" And he said: "Whoever sees in his ruler something he dislikes, let him be patient and not withdraw his hand from obedience to him." Whoever reflects upon what befell Islam in the great and small fitnas will see that it came from neglecting this principle and from impatience toward an evil, so one seeks to remove it and there arises from it something greater. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw in Makkah the greatest of evils and could not change them. Indeed, when Allah opened Makkah and it became a land of Islam, he resolved to change the House and restore it to the foundations of Ibrahim, but he refrained from doing so, though he had the power to do it, out of fear of something greater occurring, namely that the Quraysh would not bear it, given their recent conversion to Islam and that they were people of recent unbelief. For this reason he did not permit denouncing the rulers by the hand, because of what would follow from it of something greater, as has been found to be the case.

[Forbidding Evil Has Four Degrees]

Forbidding evil has four degrees. The first: that it is removed and its opposite replaces it. The second: that it is reduced, even if not entirely removed. The third: that something similar to it replaces it. The fourth: that something worse than it replaces it. The first two degrees are legislated, the third is a matter of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning), and the fourth is forbidden. So if you see the people of wickedness and sin playing chess, your denouncing them is from lack of understanding and insight, unless you move them from it to what is more beloved to Allah and His Messenger, such as archery and horse racing and the like. And if you see the sinners gathered in amusement and play, or listening to whistling and clapping, then if you move them from it to the obedience of Allah, that is the goal; otherwise, leaving them in that state is better than emptying them for something greater than that, since what they are engaged in keeps them occupied from that. Likewise, if a man is occupied with books of lewdness and the like, and you fear that moving him away from them will lead him to books of innovation, misguidance and sorcery, then leave him with his former books. This is a wide field. I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah sanctify his soul and illuminate his grave, say: "I passed, along with some of my companions, in the time of the Tatars, by a group of them who were drinking wine. One of those with me denounced them, and I denounced him, and I said to him: 'Allah only prohibited wine because it turns people away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer, but these people, wine is turning them away from killing souls, enslaving offspring and seizing property, so leave them.'"

(Benefit)

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Allah looked into the hearts of the servants and found the heart of Muhammad ﷺ to be the best of the hearts of the servants, so He chose him for His message. Then He looked into the hearts of the servants after him and found the hearts of his Companions to be the best of the hearts of the servants, so He chose them as his companions. Whatever the believers see as good is good in the sight of Allah, and whatever the believers see as evil is evil in the sight of Allah."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will not harm you except for some hurt﴾. The construction of this clause is clearer if it is read as: they will not inflict anything on you except hurt; as for real harm (ḍarr), they will never inflict it on you. ﴿And if you are patient and mindful of Allah, their scheme will not harm you at all﴾. So He negated that the harm of their scheme would reach them, even though they are not spared some hurt that comes to them from their scheming, whether by intimidation and speech, or by forcing them into fighting, and the hurt and fatigue they suffer from it. But that does not harm them. Thus there is a distinction between hurt (adhā) and harm (ḍarr).

This is a parable God has struck for those who spend their wealth in other than obedience to Him and seeking His pleasure. God, glorified is He, likens what these people spend of their wealth on noble deeds, glory, the acquisition of praise and a good reputation, not seeking thereby the Face of God, and what they spend to bar [people] from the way of God and from following His messengers, to a crop that its owner sowed, hoping for its benefit and good. Then a wind of extreme bitter cold struck it, whose cold burns whatever crop and fruit it passes over, and so it destroyed that crop and dried it out.

It has been differed over regarding ṣirr (a biting, freezing wind). It was said: it is severe cold. It was said: it is fire. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The fire was described as ṣirr only because of its sound (taṣriyah) when it blazes. It was also said: ṣirr is the sound that accompanies the wind from the intensity of its blowing. The three opinions are mutually related: it is a severe cold that burns by its dryness to the tilth just as fire burns it, and in it is a loud sound.

As for His saying: ﴿It struck the tilth of a people who wronged themselves﴾, it is an alert that the cause of its striking their tilth is their wrongdoing. It is He who set the aforementioned wind upon them until it destroyed their crop and dried it out. So their wrongdoing is the wind that destroyed their deeds and their expenditures and ruined them.

This is a parable God has struck for those who spend their wealth in other than obedience to Him and seeking His pleasure. God, glorified is He, likens what these people spend of their wealth on noble deeds, glory, the acquisition of praise and a good reputation, not seeking thereby the Face of God, and what they spend to bar [people] from the way of God and from following His messengers, to a crop that its owner sowed, hoping for its benefit and good. Then a wind of extreme bitter cold struck it, whose cold burns whatever crop and fruit it passes over, and so it destroyed that crop and dried it out.

It is He who set the aforementioned wind upon them until it destroyed their crop and dried it out. So their wrongdoing is the wind that destroyed their deeds and their expenditures and ruined them.

Al-Zuhri, 'Asim ibn 'Umar, Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hibban and others said: The Day of Uhud was a day of trial and purification (tamhis). Allah, Mighty and Majestic, tested the believers by it and exposed the hypocrites (munafiqun) among those who displayed Islam with their tongues while concealing disbelief. Allah honored whom He willed of the people of His guardianship (wilaya) with martyrdom on it. Among what was revealed of the Qur'an regarding the Day of Uhud were sixty verses of Surat Al 'Imran, the first of which is: ﴿And when you went out early from your family to station the believers at their positions for battle﴾ [Al 'Imran: 121], through to the end of the account.

[Section on the rulings and jurisprudence contained in this battle]

Among them: jihad becomes obligatory once one begins to undertake it. Even if a man puts on his armor, prepares its means and readies himself to set out, he is not permitted to turn back from the expedition until he fights his enemy.

Among them: when the enemy attacks Muslims in their homes, it is not obligatory for them to go out to meet him; rather, it is permissible for them to remain in their homes and fight there if that is more advantageous against their enemy, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ advised them on the Day of Uhud.

Among them: it is permissible for the imam to lead the army through part of the lands of his subjects when that happens to be on his route, even if the owner does not consent.

Among them: he does not permit those children who are not yet of age and cannot withstand fighting to take part; rather he sends them back when they come out, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent back Ibn 'Umar and those with him.

Among them: it is permissible to campaign with women and to seek their help in jihad.

Among them: it is permissible to plunge into the enemy's ranks, as Anas ibn al-Nadr and others did.

Among them: when the imam is struck by a wound, he may lead them in prayer seated, and they pray behind him seated, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did in this expedition, and his practice continued in this way until his death.

Among them: it is permissible for a man to supplicate that he be killed in the way of Allah and to wish for that, and this is not among the wishing for death that is prohibited, as 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh said: "O Allah, let me meet a man from the polytheists whose disbelief is great and whose fury is fierce; I will fight him, he will kill me for Your sake, take my spoils, then slit my nose and my ears. Then when I meet You, and You say, 'O 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, why were you mutilated?' I will say, 'For You, O Lord.'"

Among them: whoever kills himself is among the people of the Fire, due to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ concerning Quzman, who displayed great prowess on the Day of Uhud; when the wounds grew severe upon him, he slit his own throat, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "He is among the people of the Fire."

Among them: the sunnah regarding the martyr is that he is not washed, nor is funeral prayer offered over him, nor is he shrouded in other than his own garments; rather he is buried in them with his blood and wounds, unless they are stripped from him, in which case he is shrouded in other garments.

Among them: if he was in a state of major impurity (junub), he is washed, as the angels washed Handhala ibn Abi 'Amir.

Among them: the sunnah regarding the martyrs is that they be buried at the places where they fell and not moved to another place. Some of the Companions had transported their slain to Medina, so the herald of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ proclaimed the order to return the slain to their places of falling. Jabir said: "While I was among the watchers, my paternal aunt came bringing my father and my maternal uncle, loading them on a camel, and she entered Medina with them to bury them in our graveyard. A man came calling out: 'Indeed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ orders you to return the slain and bury them where they fell.' He said: So we returned with them and buried them among the slain where they had been killed. Then, during the caliphate of Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, a man came to me and said: 'O Jabir, by Allah, the agents of Mu'awiya have disturbed your father's grave.' So it became evident, and some of it appeared. He said: I came to him and found him in the same state in which I had left him; nothing about him had changed. He said: I reburied him, and so it became the sunnah regarding the martyrs that they be buried where they fell."

Among them: it is permissible to bury two or three men in one grave, for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ "used to bury two or three men in a grave and would say: 'Which of them has memorized more of the Qur'an?' When they pointed to a man, he would place him first in the lahd (niche)."

He also buried 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn Haram and 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh in one grave, because of the love that was between them, and he said: "Bury these two who loved one another in this world in one grave."

Then after a long time they were exhumed, and the hand of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn Haram was over his wound just as he had placed it when he was wounded; his hand was lifted from the wound and blood gushed forth, then it was returned to its place and the blood ceased.

Jabir said: "I saw my father in his grave when it was dug up; he appeared as if he were sleeping, and his condition had not changed in the slightest. It was said to him: 'Did you see his shroud?' He said: 'He was buried only in a woolen cloak (namira); his face was covered, and over his feet was idhkhir (sweet herb), and we found the cloak as it was, and the idhkhir upon his feet in its same form, and between that and then were forty-six years.'"
