He said: ﴿And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead; rather, they are alive with their Lord, receiving provision, rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty, and rejoicing for those who have not yet joined them from behind them, that there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve.﴾ [Al Imran: 169-170]. Thus He combined for them, along with everlasting life, the station of nearness to Him and that they are with Him, the continuous flow of provision upon them, their joy in what He has given them of His bounty, which is above contentment, indeed it is the perfection of contentment, and their rejoicing at their brothers who have not yet joined them, whose joy and bliss will be complete upon their gathering with them, and their rejoicing at what He renews for them at every moment of His blessing and generosity.

Allah, glorified is He, also reminded them, in the midst of this trial, of what is among the greatest of His favours and blessings upon them, which, if they set it against every trial that befalls them and every calamity, would make those vanish in comparison with this favour and blessing, leaving no trace of them whatsoever.

This is His favour upon them in sending to them a Messenger from among themselves, who recites to them His verses, purifies them, teaches them the Book and wisdom, and rescues them from the error in which they were before his sending to guidance, from wretchedness to success, from darkness to light, and from ignorance to knowledge. So every calamity and trial that befalls the servant after the attainment of this great good is a very small matter compared to the abundant good, just as the harm of rain that befalls people is small in comparison with the good they gain from it. He informed them that the cause of the calamity is from their own selves, so that they would be cautious; and that it is by His decree and destiny, so that they would affirm His unity, rely upon Him, and fear none but Him. He informed them of the wisdoms they contain, lest they accuse Him in His decree and destiny; and so that He would make Himself known to them through the various kinds of His names and attributes. He consoled them with what He gave them that is greater in rank and more momentous in weight than what they had missed of victory and spoils, and He comforted them for their slain with what they gained of His reward and generosity, so that they would compete for it and not grieve over them. So to Him belongs praise as He is worthy of it, and as befits the nobility of His Face and the might of His majesty.

[Section: Resolve (al-'Azm)]

When his intention becomes firmly established, it becomes a resolute determination (ʿazm jāzim), which necessitates setting out on the journey and is linked with reliance upon God. God, exalted, says: ﴿And when you have resolved, then rely upon God﴾ [Al ʿImran: 159].

ʿAzm (resolve) is: the firm intention that is connected with action. For this reason it has been said that it is the first beginning of movement in seeking the sought-after goal. The verified position is that the beginning of movement arises from resolve, and is not resolve itself; but because it is connected to it without any separation, one thinks that it is.

Its reality is: the gathering of the powers of will upon the act.

Resolve is of two kinds. The first is the resolve of the seeker (murid) to enter the path, and this belongs to the beginnings (bidayat). The second is a resolve during the journey itself, which is more specific than this, and it belongs to the stations (maqamat). We shall mention it in its place, God willing.

At this station, the wayfarer (salik) needs to distinguish what is his from what is upon him, so that he may keep what is his and discharge what is upon him. This is self-reckoning (muhasaba), and in rank it comes before repentance (tawba), for when he knows what is his and what is upon him, he begins to discharge what is upon him and to depart from it, which is repentance.

The author of the Manazil placed repentance before self-reckoning. The reason for this is that he regarded repentance as the first station of the traveller after his awakening, and repentance is not complete except by self-reckoning. So self-reckoning is the completion of the station of repentance, and what is meant by self-reckoning is the continuation in guarding repentance so that one does not depart from it, as if it were the fulfilment of the pledge of repentance.

Know that the ordering of these stations is not in the sense that the wayfarer cuts off a station, departs from it and moves on to the second, as in the stages of physical travel. This is impossible. Do you not see that wakefulness (yaqza) accompanies him in every station and does not leave him, and likewise insight (basira), will (irada) and resolve (ʿazm)? Likewise repentance: just as it is among the first of the stations, it is also among the last, indeed it accompanies him in every station. For this reason God, exalted, made it the last of the stations of His elect. He, exalted, said concerning the Expedition of Tabuk, which was the last of the expeditions, in which they crossed the valleys, the beginnings, the states and the ends: ﴿God has certainly turned in mercy to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a group of them had nearly swerved. Then He turned to them in mercy. Indeed, He is Kind and Merciful to them﴾ [al-Tawba: 117]. Thus He made repentance the first of their matter and its last. And He said in the surah of the death of the Messenger of God ﷺ, which is the last surah revealed: ﴿When the help of God and the victory come, and you see people entering the religion of God in multitudes, then glorify your Lord with His praise and seek His forgiveness; indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance﴾ [al-Nasr: 1-3].

In the Two Sahihs, from ʿAisha, may God be pleased with her, that the Messenger of God ﷺ did not pray any prayer after this surah was revealed to him except that he would say in his bowing and prostration: "Glory be to You, O God, our Lord, and praise be to You. O God, forgive me," interpreting the Qur'an (yatawwalu al-Qur'an).

Repentance is therefore the end of every wayfarer and every friend of God, and it is the goal toward which those who know God and His worship proceed, and what befits Him. God, exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, and they declined to bear it and feared it, but man bore it. Indeed, he was unjust and ignorant﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72] ﴿so that God may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women and the polytheist men and polytheist women, and that God may accept the repentance of the believing men and believing women. And God is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ahzab: 73]. Thus He, glorified be He, made repentance the goal of every believing man and believing woman.

Likewise patience (sabr): it does not separate from him in any station of the stations.

This ordering is only the ordering of the conditional, which depends on its condition that accompanies it. An example of this: contentment (rida) follows patience, because contentment depends upon it, and it is impossible for it to be established without it. So when it is said that the station or state of contentment, according to the disagreement among them, is it a station or a state, after the station of patience, it does not mean that one departs from patience and moves on to contentment. It only means that the station of contentment is not attained for him until the station of patience has preceded it. So understand this ordering within the stations of servanthood.

When this is so, you know that intention and resolve precede all the other stages, so there is no reason to delay them. And you know by this that self-reckoning precedes repentance in rank as well, for when the servant reckons with himself, he departs from what is upon him, and that is the reality of repentance. Also, the station of trust (tawakkul) precedes the station of turning back (inaba), because one trusts in God in attaining it: trust is the means, and turning back is the end. And the station of monotheism (tawhid) is the most fitting of the stations with which to begin, just as it is the first call of all the messengers. The Prophet ﷺ said to Muʿadh ibn Jabal when he sent him to Yemen: "Let the first thing you call them to be the testimony that there is no god but God." In another narration: "until they know God." And because no station and no state is valid except through it, there is no reason to make it the last of the stations. It is the key to the call of the messengers and the first obligation God imposed upon the servants. Whatever else is said is an error, like the saying of one who says: the first of the obligations is speculative reflection (nazar), or the intention to reflect, or knowledge (maʿrifa), or the doubt which necessitates reflection.

All these sayings are erroneous. Rather, the first of the obligations is the key to the call of all the messengers. It was the first thing that their first, Noah, called to, when he said: ﴿O my people, worship God; you have no god other than Him﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 59], and it was the first thing that their last, Muhammad ﷺ, called to.

Among the people of the path there is much disagreement regarding the number of the stations and their order. Each describes the stages of his journey and the condition of his travelling. They also differ over whether some of the stages of the journey belong to the category of states. The difference between them is that stations are acquired (kasbiyya), while states are bestowed (wahbiyya). Some say: states are results of stations, and stations are results of deeds. Thus whoever is more righteous in deed is higher in station, and whoever is higher in station is greater in state.

Among the matters on which they differed is contentment: is it a state or a station? There is a disagreement between the Khurasanis and the Iraqis about this.

Some of the shaykhs judged between them, saying: if it is attained through acquisition, it is a station; otherwise it is a state.

The correct position in this matter is that the incoming experiences (waridat) and the encounters (munazalat) have names according to their conditions. Thus they are flashes (lawami'), lightnings (bawariq) and gleams (lawaih) at their first appearance and emergence, just as lightning flashes and appears from afar. When they reach him and he engages with them, they are states (ahwal). When they take firm root in him and remain with him without departing, they are stations (maqamat). So they are flashes and gleams at their beginning, states in their middle, and stations at their ends. What was a lightning is itself the state, and what was a state is itself the station. These names apply to it according to its attachment to the heart, its manifestation to him, and its persistence in it.

The wayfarer may strip himself of his station as one strips off a garment, and descend to what is below it. Then he may return to it, or he may not.

Among the stations are some that comprise two stations. Among them are some that comprise more than that. Among them are some into which all the stations are folded, so that its possessor does not deserve its name except when he has gathered all the stations within it.

Repentance comprises the station of self-reckoning and the station of fear. Its existence cannot be conceived without these two.

Trust (tawakkul) comprises the station of entrusting (tafwid), seeking help (isti'ana) and contentment. Its existence cannot be conceived without them.

Hope (raja') comprises the station of fear and will (irada).

Fear (khawf) comprises the station of hope and will.

Turning back (inaba) comprises the station of love (mahabba) and awe (khashya). A servant is not turning back except by the combination of these two.

Humility (ikhbat) comprises the station of love, lowliness and submission. Neither of them is complete as humility without the other.

Asceticism (zuhd) comprises the station of desire (raghba) and dread (rahba). One is not an ascetic who does not desire what he hopes will benefit him, and dread what he fears will harm him.

The station of love comprises the station of knowledge (ma'rifa), fear, hope and will. Love is a meaning composed of these four, and through them it is realized.

The station of khashya (reverential fear) comprises the station of knowledge of God and the station of knowledge of the true right of His servanthood. Whenever one knows God and knows His right, his fear of Him intensifies, as God, exalted, said: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ [Fatir: 28]. So the knowers of Him and of His command are the people of His fear. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I am the most knowledgeable of you about God, and the most fearful of you of Him."

The station of awe (haiba) comprises the station of love, reverence and veneration.

The station of gratitude (shukr) comprises all the stations of faith. For this reason it is the highest and loftiest of them. It is above contentment, and it includes patience without the reverse being true, and it includes trust, turning back, love, humility, submission and hope. So all the stations are folded into it. Its possessor does not deserve its name absolutely except by gathering the stations within it. For this reason faith is two halves: half patience and half gratitude, and patience is included within gratitude, so all of faith returns to gratitude. And the grateful are the fewest of the servants, as God, exalted, said: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba': 13].

The station of modesty (haya') comprises the station of knowledge and vigilance (muraqaba).

The station of intimacy (uns) comprises the station of love together with nearness. If the lover is far from the beloved, he does not feel intimacy with him; and if he is near a man but does not love him, he does not feel intimacy with him either, until love for him is combined with nearness to him.

The station of sincerity (sidq) comprises sincere devotion (ikhlas) and resolve. By the combination of these two the station of sincerity is valid for him.

The station of vigilance (muraqaba) comprises knowledge together with fear. By the measure of these two the station of vigilance is valid.

The station of tranquillity (tuma'nina) comprises turning back, trust, entrusting, contentment and submission. It is a meaning composed of these matters: when they are gathered, its possessor becomes one of tranquillity, and whatever is lacking from them diminishes the tranquillity.

Likewise, desire and dread: each of them is composed of hope and fear, and hope predominates over desire, and fear predominates over dread.

For each of these stations, the wayfarers relative to it are of two kinds: the righteous (abrar) and the near ones (muqarrabun). The righteous are in its skirts, and the near ones are at the summit of its hump. So too are all the levels of faith. Each of the two kinds cannot count their differences in rank, and the excellence of their degrees, except God.

Their division into three categories—the general, the elite, and the elite of the elite—arose only from making annihilation (fana') the goal of the path, and from the knowledge of the people which they strove toward. We shall mention what is in that, and the divisions of annihilation, praiseworthy and blameworthy, excellent and inferior, for the allusion of the people to it, God willing, and their focus is upon it.

Moreover, the ordering that every arranger of the stations alludes to is not free from arbitrariness and unsupported claim, for when the servant commits himself to the contract of Islam and enters into it entirely, he has committed himself to its outward and inward requirements, its stations and its states. In every pledge of it and every obligation of it he has states and stations, and he does not fulfil that pledge or obligation except by them. Whenever he fulfils one obligation, he looks toward another obligation after it, and whenever he crosses one station, he faces another.

It may happen that he is granted the highest of the stations and states at the very beginning of his journey, so that there is opened to him from the state of love, contentment, intimacy and tranquillity what has not yet been attained by a wayfarer at his end. This wayfarer at his end needs matters of insight, repentance and self-reckoning more than the beginner needs them. So there is no universal necessary order for the journey.

We have mentioned that repentance, which they placed among the first of the stations, is the goal of the knowers and the end of the near friends of God. And there is no doubt that their need for self-reckoning at their end is greater than their need for it at their beginning.

al-Tustari, Abu Talib al-Makki, al-Junayd ibn Muhammad, Abu Uthman al-Nisaburi, and Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi; and of a rank higher than these, such as Abu Sulayman al-Darani and Awn ibn Abd Allah, who was called Hakim al-Ummah (the Wise Man of the Community), and their likes. They spoke about the deeds of the hearts and the states (ahwal) in a detailed, comprehensive, clear and unrestricted manner, without ordering them or confining the stations (maqamat) to a fixed number. For they were far greater than this, and their concern was loftier and more noble. They were only intent on acquiring wisdom and knowledge, the purity of the hearts, the purification of the souls, and the correction of conduct (mu'amalah). For this reason, their speech is little but blessed, while the speech of the later scholars is abundant, lengthy, and little in blessing.

But it is necessary to address the people of the age in their own terminology, since they lack the strength to strive toward receiving

The root meaning of khidhlan (abandonment) is leaving and forsaking. It is said of a cow or a sheep that falls behind with its young in the pasture and is left by its companions: khadhul.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said concerning this verse: "If Allah helps you, no one among the people can overcome you, and the abandonment of those who abandon you will not harm you. And if He abandons you, no one will help you after Him." That is, do not leave my command to the people, and turn away from the people for my command.

Khidhlan is that Allah leaves a servant between himself and his own self and entrusts him to it. Tawfiq (divine success) is its opposite: that He does not leave him and his self, nor entrust him to it, but rather takes charge of him, is gentle with him, helps him, defends him, and watches over him with the watchfulness of a compassionate father over a child who cannot care for himself. Whoever is left by Him between himself and his own self has perished utterly.

For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) used to supplicate:

"O Living, O Self-Subsisting, O Originator of the heavens and the earth, O Possessor of majesty and honour, there is no god but You. By Your mercy I seek help: set right all of my affairs, and do not leave me to myself even for the blink of an eye, nor to anyone of Your creation."

So the servant is placed between Allah and His enemy Iblis. If Allah takes charge of him, his enemy cannot prevail over him; but if He abandons him and turns away from him, Satan seizes him, as the wolf seizes the sheep.

If it is said: What is the fault of the sheep when the shepherd leaves it between itself and the wolf? Can it overpower the wolf and escape from it?

It is said: By the life of Allah, Satan is the wolf of man, as the Truthful and Believed one (ﷺ) said. But Allah has not given this accursed wolf authority over this sheep despite its weakness. When it submits itself, makes peace with the wolf, answers its call, obeys its command, does not hold back, but comes toward it quickly and obediently, and leaves the protected pasture of the shepherd, over which wolves have no way, and enters the domain of the wolves, whoever enters it becomes their prey. Is the wolf anything other than the sheep's destroyer? How much more so when the shepherd warns it, frightens it, and admonishes it, and has shown it the fate of the sheep that separated from the shepherd and entered the valley of the wolves?

Ahmad ibn Marwan al-Maliki said in the book al-Mujalasa: I heard Ibn Abi al-Dunya say: Allah, glory be to Him, has knowledge beyond counting, and He gives each one of His servants what He does not give to others. Abu Abd Allah Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Sa'id al-Qattan narrated to us: Ubayd Allah ibn Bakr al-Sahmi narrated to us from his father: that a group of people were on a journey, and among them was a man who would pass by a bird and say: "Do you know what this is saying?" They would say: "No." He would say: "It says such and such," and he would thus inform us of something we could not know whether it was true or false. Then they passed by a flock in which there was a sheep that had stayed behind with its lamb, bending its neck toward it and bleating. He said: "Do you know what this sheep is saying?"

We said: "No." He said: "It is saying to the lamb: 'Come along, lest the wolf eat you as it ate your brother last year in this place.'"

He said: "We came to the shepherd and said to him: 'Was this sheep born before this year of yours?'"

He said: "Yes, it bore a lamb last year, and the wolf ate it in this place." Then we came upon a people among whom was a woman in a litter on her camel, and the camel was groaning and bending its neck toward her. He said: "Do you know what this camel is saying?" We said: "No." He said: "It is cursing its rider and claims that her saddle is sewn badly and is on its hump." He said: "We came to them and said: 'O people, this companion of ours claims that this camel curses its rider, and claims that her saddle is badly sewn and is on its hump.'" He said: "They made the camel kneel and unloaded it, and it was just as he had said."

So this is a sheep that warned its lamb of the wolf once, and it took warning. Allah, glory be to Him, has warned the son of Adam of his wolf again and again, yet he refuses except to answer its call when it summons him, and it spends the night with him and rises with him. [Quran 14:22 quoted:] ﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided: Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I broke my promise to you. I had no authority over you, except that I invited you and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me. Indeed, I disbelieved in your association of me with Allah before. Indeed, for the wrongdoers is a painful punishment.﴾

(Benefit)

Reliance upon Allah (tawakkul) is of two kinds. The first is reliance upon Him for obtaining the servant's worldly needs and portions, or for repelling his worldly hardships and calamities. The second is reliance upon Him for attaining what He loves and is pleased with: faith, certainty, jihad, and calling to Him. Between the two kinds there is virtue that none but Allah can count. Whenever the servant relies upon Him in the second kind with true reliance, the first kind suffices him completely. Whenever he relies upon Him in the first kind without the second, it also suffices him, but he will not have the outcome of one who relies upon Him in what He loves and is pleased with. So the greatest reliance upon Him is reliance in guidance, the purification of monotheism, following the Messenger, and striving against the people of falsehood. This is the reliance of the messengers, and especially of their followers.

Reliance is sometimes compulsory reliance, of necessity and helplessness, where the servant finds no refuge or shelter but reliance, as when the means are closed to him and his soul is constricted and he thinks there is no refuge from Allah except with Him. Relief and ease never fail to follow this, without exception.

And sometimes it is reliance by choice, which is reliance together with the existence of a means leading to the desired end. If the means is commanded, abandoning it is blameworthy; and if the means is in place but reliance is abandoned, that is also blameworthy, for it is obligatory by the consensus of the Muslim community and the text of the Qur'an, and what is obligatory is to perform both and combine them. If the means is forbidden, it is unlawful to engage in it, and reliance becomes the single means for him, for reliance is among the strongest means for attaining what is desired and repelling what is disliked; indeed it is the strongest of all means absolutely. If the means is permissible, consider: does performing it weaken your reliance or not? If it weakens it, dividing your heart and scattering your resolve, then leaving it is better. If it does not weaken it, then engaging in it is better, because the wisdom of the Most Wise of judges requires linking the effect to it, so do not nullify His wisdom as long as you are able to uphold it, especially if you do it as an act of worship. Thus you will have performed the worship of the heart through reliance and the worship of the limbs through the means, intended as drawing near to Allah. What confirms reliance is performing the means commanded, so whoever neglects them, his reliance is not sound, just as performing the means that lead to good fulfills one's hope; whoever does not perform them, his hope is mere wishful thinking. Likewise, whoever neglects them, his reliance is incapacity, and his incapacity is reliance.

The secret and reality of reliance is the heart's dependence upon Allah alone. Engaging in means does not harm it when the heart is free of dependence upon and inclination toward them, just as the words "I have relied upon Allah" do not benefit one whose heart depends upon another and trusts in another. The reliance of the tongue is one thing, and the reliance of the heart is another, just as repentance of the tongue alongside persistence of the heart is one thing, and repentance of the heart, even if the tongue does not speak, is another. The servant's saying "I have relied upon Allah" while his heart depends on another is like his saying "I repent to Allah" while he persists in his sin and commits it.

[Section on the virtue of the martyr]

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, no one is wounded in the way of Allah – and Allah knows best who is wounded in His way – except that he will come on the Day of Resurrection with his colour the colour of blood and his scent the scent of musk."

In al-Tirmidhi, from him (ﷺ): "There is nothing more beloved to Allah than two drops or two marks: a drop of tears out of fear of Allah, and a drop of blood shed in the way of Allah. As for the two marks, there is a mark in the way of Allah and a mark in one of the obligations of Allah."

It is authentically related from him (ﷺ) that he said: "No servant dies who has with Allah a good reward, and who would not wish to return to the world and have the world and all that is in it, except the martyr, because of what he sees of the virtue of martyrdom; he wishes to return to the world and be killed again." And in another wording: "he will be killed ten times, because of the honour he sees."

He (ﷺ) said to the mother of Harithah bint al-Nu'man, whose son had been killed with him on the day of Badr, when she asked him where he was: "He is in al-Firdaws al-A'la (the highest paradise)."

He (ﷺ) also said: "The souls of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds, which have lanterns suspended beneath the Throne. They roam freely in Paradise wherever they wish, then they return to those lanterns. Their Lord looked down upon them with a look and said: 'Do you desire anything?' They said: 'What could we desire, when we roam freely in Paradise wherever we wish?' He did this with them three times. When they saw that they would not be left alone unless they asked, they said: 'O Lord, we wish that You return our souls to our bodies until we are killed in Your way a second time.' When He saw that they had no further need, they were left alone."

He (ﷺ) also said: "For the martyr with Allah there are qualities: he is forgiven at the first gush of his blood; he is shown his seat in Paradise; he is adorned with the adornment of faith; he is married to the wide-eyed houris; he is protected from the punishment of the grave; he is safe from the greatest terror; a crown of dignity is placed upon his head, a single ruby of which is better than the world and all that is in it; he is married to seventy-two of the wide-eyed houris; and he may intercede for seventy of his relatives." Ahmad related it and al-Tirmidhi authenticated it.

He (ﷺ) said to Jabir: "Shall I not inform you what Allah said to your father?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Allah has not spoken to anyone except from behind a veil, but He spoke to your father face to face. He said: 'O My servant, ask of Me and I will give you.' He said: 'O Lord, bring me back to life so that I may be killed in You a second time.' He said: 'It has already preceded from Me (that they will not return to it).' He said: 'O Lord, then convey to those behind me.' So Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse: ﴿And do not think of those who have been killed in the way of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive, with their Lord, being provided for.﴾"

He (ﷺ) also said: "When your brothers were struck at Uhud, Allah placed their souls in the crops of green birds, which come to the rivers of Paradise, eat of its fruits, and return to lanterns of gold in the shade of the Throne. When they found the goodness of their food and drink and the excellence of their resting place, they said: 'Would that our brothers knew what Allah has done for us, so that they would not lose desire for jihad or shrink from war.' Allah said: 'I will convey it to them on your behalf.' So Allah revealed to His Messenger these verses: ﴿And do not think of those who have been killed in the way of Allah as dead.﴾"

In al-Musnad, marfu': "The martyrs are at the edge of a river at the gate of Paradise, in a green dome; their provision comes out to them from Paradise morning and evening."

He (ﷺ) said: "The earth is not dry of the blood of the martyr before his two wives hasten to him, like two birds who have lost their young, with a garment in each of their hands better than the world and all that is in it."

In al-Mustadrak and al-Nasa'i, marfu': "That I be killed in the way of Allah is more beloved to me than that I should have the people of the cities and the tents (i.e., all the people)."

In both of them: "The martyr feels from being killed only as much as one of you feels from a pinch."

In al-Sunan: "The martyr intercedes for seventy of his household."

In al-Musnad: "The best of the martyrs are those who, when they meet the enemy in the line, do not turn their faces away until they are killed. Those are they who will recline in the upper chambers of Paradise, and your Lord laughs at them. When your Lord laughs at a servant in this world, there is no reckoning for him."

Also in it: "The martyrs are four: a believer of excellent faith who meets the enemy, is true to Allah until he is killed – this is the one to whom people raise their necks [to look], and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raised his head until his cap fell off; a believer of excellent faith who meets the enemy, as though his skin were being struck with thorns of the acacia, an arrow of unknown origin strikes and kills him – he is in the second rank; a believer of excellent faith who mixed good deeds with other bad deeds, who meets the enemy and is true to Allah until he is killed – that one is in the third rank; and a believer who greatly transgressed against himself, who meets the enemy and is true to Allah until he is killed – that one is in the fourth rank."

In al-Musnad and Sahih Ibn Hibban: "The slain are three: a believer who strove with his wealth and himself in the way of Allah, and when he met the enemy fought them until he was killed – that is the martyr tested in the tent of Allah beneath His Throne; the prophets do not surpass him except by the rank of prophethood. A believer who feared for himself because of his sins and transgressions, who strove with himself and his wealth in the way of Allah, and when he met the enemy fought until he was killed – that is a purification that wiped away his sins and transgressions; indeed the sword erases transgressions, and he may enter by whichever gate of Paradise he wishes, for it has eight gates, and Hell has seven gates, some of which are better than others. And a hypocrite who strove with himself and his wealth, and when he met the enemy fought in the way of Allah until he was killed – that is in the Fire; indeed the sword does not erase hypocrisy."

It is authentically related from him (ﷺ): "A disbeliever and his killer will never be together in the Fire forever."

He was asked which jihad is best. He said: "One who strives against the polytheists with his wealth and himself." It was said: "Then which killing is best?" He said: "One whose blood is shed and whose horse is hamstrung in the way of Allah."

In Sunan Ibn Majah: "Among the greatest jihad is a word of justice before an unjust ruler." It is in Ahmad and al-Nasa'i as a mursal (report).

It is authentically related from him (ﷺ): "A group of his community will never cease fighting for the truth; those who forsake them will not harm them, nor those who oppose them, until the Hour comes." In another wording: "until their last fights the Messiah, the Dajjal."

Section

In this station the life of the martyrs is known, and that they are with their Lord being provided for, and that this life is more complete than their life in this world, and more perfect and better, even if their bodies have been reduced to dust, their flesh torn apart, their joints scattered, and their bones decayed. The concern is not with the empty encampment; the matter is with the one who dwells in it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not think of those who have been killed in the way of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive, with their Lord, being provided for.﴾ And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, "They are dead." Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 154]. If the martyrs attained this life only by following the Messengers and through them, then what is to be thought of the life of the Messengers in the barzakh (intermediate state)? The poet said well:

"Life is sleep, and death is wakefulness, and a man between them is a passing phantom."

So for the Messengers, the martyrs and the truthful ones, of this life, which is a waking from the sleep of this world, there is its most complete and perfect form. In proportion to a servant's life in this world is his longing for that life, his striving, and his eagerness to attain it. And Allah is the One sought for help.

In al-Musnad: "The best of the martyrs are those who, when they meet the enemy in the line, do not turn their faces away until they are killed. Those are they who will recline in the upper chambers of Paradise, and your Lord laughs at them. When your Lord laughs at a servant in this world, there is no reckoning for him."

Also in it: "The martyrs are four: a believer of excellent faith who meets the enemy, is true to Allah until he is killed – this is the one to whom people raise their necks [to look], and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raised his head until his cap fell off; a believer of excellent faith who meets the enemy, as though his skin were being struck with thorns of the acacia, an arrow of unknown origin strikes and kills him – he is in the second rank; a believer of excellent faith who mixed good deeds with other bad deeds, who meets the enemy and is true to Allah until he is killed – that one is in the third rank; and a believer who greatly transgressed against himself, who meets the enemy and is true to Allah until he is killed – that one is in the fourth rank."

In al-Musnad and Sahih Ibn Hibban: "The slain are three: a believer who strove with his wealth and himself in the way of Allah, and when he met the enemy fought them until he was killed – that is the martyr tested in the tent of Allah beneath His Throne; the prophets do not surpass him except by the rank of prophethood. A believer who feared for himself because of his sins and transgressions, who strove with himself and his wealth in the way of Allah, and when he met the enemy fought until he was killed – that is a purification that wiped away his sins and transgressions; indeed the sword erases transgressions, and he may enter by whichever gate of Paradise he wishes, for it has eight gates, and Hell has seven gates, some of which are better than others. And a hypocrite who strove with himself and his wealth, and when he met the enemy fought in the way of Allah until he was killed – that is in the Fire; indeed the sword does not erase hypocrisy."

It is authentically related from him (ﷺ): "A disbeliever and his killer will never be together in the Fire forever."

He was asked which jihad is best. He said: "One who strives against the polytheists with his wealth and himself." It was said: "Then which killing is best?" He said: "One whose blood is shed and whose horse is hamstrung in the way of Allah."

In Sunan Ibn Majah: "Among the greatest jihad is a word of justice before an unjust ruler." It is in Ahmad and al-Nasa'i as a mursal (report).

It is authentically related from him (ﷺ): "A group of his community will never cease fighting for the truth; those who forsake them will not harm them, nor those who oppose them, until the Hour comes." In another wording: "until their last fights the Messiah, the Dajjal."

Section

In this station the life of the martyrs is known, and that they are with their Lord being provided for, and that this life is more complete than their life in this world, and more perfect and better, even if their bodies have been reduced to dust, their flesh torn apart, their joints scattered, and their bones decayed. The concern is not with the empty encampment; the matter is with the one who dwells in it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not think of those who have been killed in the way of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive, with their Lord, being provided for.﴾ And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, "They are dead." Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 154]. If the martyrs attained this life only by following the Messengers and through them, then what is to be thought of the life of the Messengers in the barzakh (intermediate state)? The poet said well:

"Life is sleep, and death is wakefulness, and a man between them is a passing phantom."

So for the Messengers, the martyrs and the truthful ones, of this life, which is a waking from the sleep of this world, there is its most complete and perfect form. In proportion to a servant's life in this world is his longing for that life, his striving, and his eagerness to attain it. And Allah is the One sought for help.

In the sound hadith about the man who had a dispute with another man, he said, "Ḥasbiya Allāh wa-ni'ma al-wakīl" (God is sufficient for me, and He is the best Guardian). The Prophet said, "Indeed God blames helplessness, but upon you is shrewdness (al-kays). When something overcomes you, then say: Ḥasbiya Allāh wa-ni'ma al-wakīl."

Here, the man said "Ḥasbiya Allāh wa-ni'ma al-wakīl" after he had become helpless in regard to shrewdness, which, had he practised it, would have secured him the judgment against his opponent. So if he had taken the means by which he would have been shrewd, and then was overcome and said "Ḥasbiya Allāh wa-ni'ma al-wakīl," the phrase would have been placed in its proper position. Likewise Abraham, the Friend (al-Khalīl), when he took the means that he had been commanded to take, and did not fall short by abandoning them or any part of them, and then his enemy overcame him and they threw him into the fire, he said in that state, "Ḥasbiya Allāh wa-ni'ma al-wakīl." The phrase was thus placed in its proper position, settled in its appropriate place, had its effect, and its consequence followed from it.

[Tawakkul (trust in God)]

Likewise the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his Companions on the day of Uhud. When it was said to them after they had withdrawn from Uhud, ﴿Indeed the people have gathered against you, so fear them⦆, they prepared themselves and went out to meet their enemy, and they gave the enemy their shrewdness from their own selves. Then they said, ﴿Ḥasbunā Allāh wa-ni'ma al-wakīl (God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Guardian)⦆, and the phrase had its effect and brought about its requirement. For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever fears God, He will make for him a way out, and will provide for him from where he does not expect. And whoever trusts in God, then He is sufficient for him⦆. So He made trust (tawakkul) follow taqwā (God-consciousness), which is the carrying out of the means that have been commanded. Then, if he trusts in God, He is sufficient for him. As He said in another place: ﴿And fear God, and upon God let the believers rely [al-Ma'idah: 11]⦆. Therefore trust and reliance without carrying out the commanded means is pure helplessness. If it is mixed with some kind of trust, it is the trust of helplessness. So a servant should not make his trust into helplessness, nor make his helplessness into trust. Rather, he should make his trust one of the commanded means, without which the goal is not achieved, all of them together.

From here two groups of people went astray. The first group claimed that trust alone is an independent sufficient cause for the attainment of what is sought. So the means that the wisdom of God had prescribed as leading to their effects were nullified by them. Thus they fell into a kind of negligence and helplessness, in proportion to what they neglected of the means. Their trust was weakened, since they thought its strength lay in standing alone apart from the means. So they gathered all their concern and made it one concern. Although this has strength from one aspect, it has weakness from another. Whenever the side of trust is strengthened by being isolated, negligence in the means, which is the locus of trust, weakens it. For trust has the means as its locus, and its perfection lies in trusting God while using them. This is like the trust of the farmer who ploughs the earth and casts the seed into it, then trusts God for its growth and sprouting. He has given trust its due, and his trust is not weakened by leaving the land idle and abandoned. Likewise is the trust of the traveller who covers the distance while striving in his journey, and the trust of the shrewd in being saved from God's punishment and in winning His reward, together with their striving in His obedience. This is the trust whose effect follows from it, and God is sufficient for whoever stands by it.

As for the trust of helplessness and negligence, its effect does not follow, and God is not sufficient for its possessor. God is sufficient only for the one who trusts in Him when he fears Him, and his God-consciousness is doing the commanded means, not wasting them.

The second group is the one that stood by the means, and saw that the effects are tied to them by Law and by Decree, but turned away from the side of trust. Although this group attained what it attained through the means it carried out, it does not have the strength of the people of trust, nor God's help for them, His sufficiency for them, and His defence of them. Rather, it is forsaken and powerless, in proportion to what it has lost of trust.

So all strength lies in trusting God, as one of the early pious predecessors (al-Salaf) said: "Whoever wishes to be the strongest of people, let him trust in God." Strength is guaranteed to the one who trusts, along with sufficiency, support and defence. Whatever of that diminishes for him is only in proportion to what diminishes of his God-consciousness and trust. Otherwise, when he is truly committed to both, God must make for him a way out of everything that has become constricted for people, and God will be his sufficiency and protector.

The point is that the Prophet (ﷺ) guided the servant to what contains the utmost of his perfection and the attainment of his aim: that he should be eager for what benefits him, exert his effort in it, and then precaution benefits him, and the saying "Ḥasbiya Allāh wa-ni'ma al-wakīl" benefits him. This is unlike the one who was helpless and negligent, until his interest escaped him, and then said "Ḥasbiya Allāh wa-ni'ma al-wakīl." In that case God blames him, and God is not his sufficiency in this state. For God is only the sufficiency of the one who fears Him and trusts in Him.

**[Section on the Station of Fear]**

Among the stations (*manazil*) of ﴿You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5] is the station of fear (*khawf*).

It is among the most noble stations of the path and the most beneficial for the heart, and it is an obligation upon everyone. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me, if you are believers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 175]. He says: ﴿And fear Me alone﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40]. He says: ﴿So do not fear the people, but fear Me﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44]. He praised its people in His Book and commended them, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are apprehensive out of fear of their Lord﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 57], up to His words: ﴿It is those who hasten to good deeds, and they are foremost in them﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 61].

In the *Musnad* and at-Tirmidhi, it is related from 'Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that she said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, regarding the saying of Allah: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 60], is it the one who commits zina, drinks wine, and steals?' He said: 'No, O daughter of as-Siddiq, rather it is the man who fasts, prays, and gives charity, and fears that it will not be accepted from him.'"

Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, they worked hard at acts of obedience and strove in them, and yet they feared that these would be rejected from them. Indeed, the believer combines good deeds with fear, while the hypocrite combines evil deeds with feeling secure."

*Al-wajal* (trepidation), *al-khawf* (fear), *al-khashyah* (awe-fear), and *al-rahbah* (dread) are closely related words, but they are not synonyms.

Abu al-Qasim al-Junayd said: "Fear is the anticipation of punishment at every passing breath."

It has been said: "Fear is the agitation and movement of the heart at the remembrance of what is feared."

It has been said: "Fear is the strength of knowledge of the pathways of the rulings. This is the cause of fear, not fear itself."

It has been said: "Fear is the heart's fleeing from the descent of what is disliked, upon sensing it."

*Al-khashyah* is more specific than *al-khawf*, for *al-khashyah* belongs to those who have knowledge of Allah. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28]. Thus it is fear joined with knowledge. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, I am the most aware of you of Allah, and the most fearful of Him."

Fear is movement, while *khashyah* is contraction, restraint, and stillness. The one who sees an enemy, a flood, or the like has two states. The first is movement to flee from it, which is the state of fear. The second is his stillness and settling in a place where it cannot reach him, which is *khashyah*. From this comes *inkhasha al-shay'* (the thing was contracted/settled), and the doubled and the weak-lettered forms are sister words, like *taqaddi al-bazi* and *taqaddada*.

As for *al-rahbah*, it is extreme fleeing from what is disliked. It is the opposite of *al-raghbah*, which is the heart's journey in seeking what is desired.

Between *al-rahab* and *al-harab* (fleeing) there is a correspondence in both wording and meaning, joined by *al-ishtiqaq al-awsat* (the middle derivation), which is the arrangement of the permutations of a word upon one comprehensive meaning.

As for *al-wajal*, it is the trembling and splitting of the heart at the remembrance of one whose authority and punishment are feared, or at seeing him.

As for *al-hayba*, it is fear accompanied by veneration and reverence, and it most often occurs together with love and knowledge. *Al-ijlal* is veneration joined with love.

Fear belongs to the general body of believers, *khashyah* to the knowing gnostics, *hayba* to the lovers, and *ijlal* to those brought near. The degree of fear and *khashyah* follows the degree of knowledge and gnosis, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, I am the most knowledgeable of you about Allah, and the most fearful of Him." In another narration it is "the most fearful (*khawfan*)." He also said: "If you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much, and you would not enjoy women on beds, and you would go out to the open ground crying out to Allah the Exalted."

The one who fears seeks refuge in fleeing and restraint, while the one who has *khashyah* seeks refuge in holding fast to knowledge. Their example is like that of one who has no knowledge of medicine and that of the skilled physician: the first seeks refuge in dietary restraint and flight, while the physician seeks refuge in his knowledge of medicines and diseases.

Abu Hafs said: "Fear is the whip of Allah, with which He straightens those who stray from His door." He also said: "Fear is a lamp in the heart, by which one sees what is in it of good and evil. Everyone from whom you fear, you flee from, except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for when you fear Him, you flee to Him."

So the one who fears is fleeing from his Lord to his Lord.

Abu Sulayman said: "Fear has never left a heart without its ruin." Ibrahim ibn Sufyan said: "When fear settles in hearts, it burns the places of desires within them and drives the world out of them." Dhu al-Nun said: "People remain on the path as long as fear has not departed from them. When fear departs from them, they lose the path." Hatim al-Asamm said: "Do not be deceived by a good place, for there is no better place than Paradise, yet Adam encountered what he encountered there. Do not be deceived by abundant worship, for Iblis, after long worship, encountered what he encountered. Do not be deceived by abundant knowledge, for Bal'am ibn Ba'ura encountered what he encountered, and he knew the Greatest Name. Do not be deceived by meeting the righteous and seeing them, for there is no person more righteous than the Prophet (ﷺ), yet his enemies and the hypocrites did not benefit from meeting him."

Fear is not intended for its own sake. Rather, it is intended for something else, as a means. For this reason it departs when the feared thing departs, for the people of Paradise have no fear upon them, nor do they grieve.

Fear is related to actions, while love is related to the Essence and the Attributes. For this reason the love of the believers for their Lord increases when they enter the abode of bliss, and no fear reaches them there. Therefore, the station and rank of love are higher and loftier than the station and rank of fear.

True, praiseworthy fear is that which stands between its bearer and the prohibitions of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. If it goes beyond that, then despair and hopelessness are feared from it.

Abu 'Uthman said: "The sincerity of fear is abstaining from sins, outwardly and inwardly."

I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah sanctify his spirit, say: "Praiseworthy fear is that which restrains you from the prohibitions of Allah."

The author of *al-Manazil* said: "Fear is being uprooted from the tranquility of security through contemplating the report." He means: leaving the stillness of security by keeping in mind what Allah has informed of, of promise and threat.

He said: "It has three degrees. The first degree is fear of punishment, which is the fear by which faith is sound. It is the fear of the common people, and it arises from affirming the threat, remembering the offense, and watching the outcome."

Fear is preceded by awareness and knowledge, so it is impossible for a person to fear something of which he has no awareness.

Fear has two objects. The first is the disliked thing itself whose occurrence is feared. The second is the cause and the path that leads to it. According to the degree of his awareness that the cause leads to the feared thing, and according to the degree of the threat, his fear will be. Whatever decreases of his awareness of either of these two decreases his fear accordingly.

So whoever does not believe that such-and-such a cause leads to such-and-such a feared outcome will not fear that cause. Whoever believes that it leads to some disliked thing but does not know its extent will not feel that particular fear. But when he knows the extent of what is feared and is certain that the cause leads to it, fear arises in him.

This is the meaning of its arising from affirming the threat, remembering the offense, and watching the outcome.

As for watching the outcome, it is an increase in keeping the feared thing in mind and setting it before one's eyes, so that one does not forget it. For even if he knows it, forgetfulness and lack of watchfulness come between the heart and fear. For this reason fear is a sign of the soundness of faith, and its departure from the heart is a sign that faith has departed from it. And Allah knows best.

**[Section]**

He said: "The second degree: the fear of cunning (*makr*) amid the passing of breaths that are wholly absorbed in wakefulness, mixed with sweetness."

He means that whoever attains wakefulness without heedlessness, and his breaths are wholly absorbed in it, finds that sweet. Indeed, nothing is sweeter than presence during wakefulness. Therefore he should fear cunning, and that this presence, wakefulness, and sweetness be taken from him. How many a person envied for his state has had his state reversed upon him, and has gone from good conduct to ugly deeds, so that he begins to turn his palms over and strike one hand upon the other in regret? While the full moon of his conditions was shining in the nights of fullness, the eclipse struck him and he entered darkness. So intimacy was replaced by loneliness, presence by absence, approach by aversion, nearness by distance, and gathering by dispersion, as it has been said:

*You thought well of your days when they were good, and did not fear the evil that fate might bring.*

*The nights were at peace with you, so you were deceived by them, yet at the clearness of the nights, turbidity arises.*

He said: "The third degree [the degree of the elect]. In the station of the people of special closeness there is no loneliness of fear, except the awe of majesty (*hayba al-jalal*), which is the highest degree pointed to in the utmost of fear."

He means that the loneliness of fear occurs only with severance and wrongdoing. The people of special closeness are people who have arrived at Allah and drawn near to Him, so their fear is not the fear of loneliness like the fear of the wrongdoers who are cut off, because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is with them in the attribute of turning toward them and loving them. This is unlike the awe of majesty, for it is connected to His Essence and Attributes. The more the servant knows Him and draws near to Him, the greater His awe and veneration become in his heart. This is higher than the degree of fear of the common people.

He said: "It is an awe that confronts the one who unveils during times of intimate conversation (*munajat*), protects the one who converses intimately during the intimate talk (*musamarah*), and breaks the one who beholds with the shock of might."

He means that awe is most often present during times of intimate conversation, which is the time of the servant's ingratiating himself to his Lord, humbling himself before Him, seeking His compassion, and praising Him for His favors, names, and attributes, or conversing with Him through His speech. This is what the people of the path mean by *munajat*.

This intimate conversation brings about the lifting of the veil between the heart and the Lord, and the removal of the barrier that prevents the heart from encountering the lights of His names and attributes and their manifestation upon it. Awe confronts him during these times, so his conversation flows according to the strength of what comes to him.

As for protecting the one who converses intimately during the intimate talk: *musamarah* among them is more specific than *munajat*. It is the heart addressing the Lord in the manner of a lover to his beloved. If the awe of His majesty does not accompany it, it takes the one engaged in it into expansiveness and presumption. Thus awe comes to protect the one who converses intimately in his intimacy from being stripped of the courtesy of servanthood.

As for its breaking the one who beholds with the shock of might: *al-fasm* means severing, that is, it nearly kills him and obliterates him with the shock of the might of Lordship, in its three meanings: the might of inaccessibility, the might of strength and power, and the might of dominion and subjugation. When it strikes the one who beholds, it nearly breaks him and erases his trace, for nothing can stand before the might of Lordship. And Allah knows best.

**(Section)**

*O you who are deceived by wishful hopes, cursed Iblis and was cast down from the abode of honor for abandoning a single prostration he was commanded to make. He expelled Adam from Paradise for a morsel he ate. He withheld from the murderer the sight of the one he killed after witnessing it, with a handful of blood. He commanded that the adulterer be put to the most grievous death for inserting a fingertip's length into what is not lawful. He commanded that the back be lashed with whips for a word of slander or a drop of intoxicant. He severed one of your limbs for three dirhams. So do not feel safe that He will imprison you in the Fire for one of His acts of disobedience, ﴿and He does not fear its consequence﴾ [ash-Shams: 15].*

*A woman entered the Fire over a cat. A man speaks a word without paying it any mind, and it plunges him into the Fire farther than the distance between east and west. A man may work at obedience to Allah for sixty years, and then at the time of death he deviates in his bequest, and is concluded with evil deeds, and enters the Fire. Life is judged by its end, and deeds by their conclusion. Whoever breaks his wudu' before the salam, the prayer he has already performed is nullified. Whoever breaks his fast before sunset, his fast is lost in vain. Whoever does evil at the end of his life meets his Lord in that state.*

*If only you had sent forward a morsel, you would have found it. But greed harms you. How many times has reward come running to you, then stood at the door, and the doorkeeper of "later," "perhaps," and "maybe" turned it away. How can success be achieved between incomplete faith and excessive hope, a sickness with no physician and no one to visit it, desire that is awake while the intellect sleeps, heedless in its delusion, bewildered in its intoxication, swimming in the surge of its ignorance, estranged from its Lord, and at ease with creation. Remembrance of people is its fruit and sustenance, while the remembrance of Allah is its prison and its death. Allah has from it only a small part of its outward self and its heart, and its certainty belongs to others.*

*May there never be anyone other than You in whom remains a trace by which blame finds its way to him.*

This verse is among the treasures of the Qur'an. In it Allah, the Exalted, draws attention to His wisdom, which requires the distinguishing of the wicked from the good, and that this distinguishing does not take place except through His messengers. He chooses from among them whom He wills and sends him to His servants, so that through their message the wicked is distinguished from the good, the friend from the enemy, and those fit for His nearness, His company and His honour from those fit only for the Fire (al-wuqud, fuel).

In this there is an admonition concerning the wisdom behind the sending of the Messengers: that it is necessary, and that it is not fitting for Allah, the Exalted, to neglect it. Whoever denies the message of His messengers has not measured Allah with His true measure, nor known Him with His true knowledge, and has attributed to Him what is not fitting for Him, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they did not measure Allah with His true measure when they said, "Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being."﴾

So contemplate this passage with true contemplation, and give it its share of reflection. Even if this book contained nothing but it, it would be among the most beneficial things to be gained from it.

And Allah is the Guide to the path of rectitude.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 3, Verse 185:**

(Section: The worldly life is like a prostitute who does not remain faithful to one husband. She only woos suitors so that they will admire her, and so she does not accept being a cuckold (*dayyatha*, tolerating dishonour).)

*I distinguished between her beauty and her deeds, and then her charm was not sufficient to cover her ugliness.*

*She swore to us that she would not betray her pledges, yet it is as if she swore to us that she would not keep them.*

Pursuing her is a journey through a land full of predators, and swimming in her is swimming in a pool of crocodiles. The one who rejoices in her is the same one whose pains she causes, her sufferings are born of her pleasures, and her sorrows come from her joys.

*The desires that were in the youth of her people were a torment, and then in old age they became a greater torment.*

The bird of nature sees the grain, while the eye of reason sees the snare, except that the eye of desire is blind.

*And the eye of contentment is blind to every fault, just as the eye of anger reveals every flaw.*

Desires were adorned for the eyes of natures, so turn away from them. ﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾ (2:3). Those who followed them fell into the desert of regrets. About the first it is said: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾ (2:5). About the second it is said: ﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves briefly; indeed you are criminals﴾ (77:46).

When the successful (*al-Muwaffaqun*) recognised the worth of the worldly life and the brevity of stay in it, they killed their desires in it, seeking the life of eternity. When they awoke from the sleep of heedlessness, they recovered with diligence what the enemy had seized from them in the time of idleness. When the road grew long for them, they glimpsed the goal, so the distant became near to them. Whenever life appeared sweet to them, they remembered ﴿This is your day which you were promised﴾ (21:103).

*And a company that travelled through the night, whose tent was pitched over every dusty horizon, standing firm.*

*They drove their resolves, between which lands were lost, so their night journey became the rising of determinations.*

*The stars of the night show them what they follow, upon the shoulder of al-Shi'ra and the head of al-Na'a'im.*

*When they charged into the battlefield of earnestness, they shattered the spears of gifts in the chests of nobility.*

(Section)

As for patience regarding sins, its requirement is clear. What helps most in it is cutting off habitual things, parting from those who assist one in them through sitting together and conversation, and breaking off customary habits, for habit is a distinct natural disposition. When desire is added to habit, two troops of the army of Satan support each other, and the motive of religion cannot prevail against the two of them.

(Section)

The second category is that which does not fall under one's choice, and the servant has no means of repelling it, such as calamities in which the servant has no part: the death of someone dear to him, the theft of his property, his illness, and the like. This is of two kinds:

The first is that in which the human servant has no part.

The second is that which afflicts him from another human being like himself, such as abuse, beating, and other things.

For the first kind, the servant has four stations. The first is the station of helplessness, which is the station of anxiety, complaint, and discontent. This is not done except by the least of people in intellect, religion, and manliness, and it is the greater of the two calamities.

The second station: the station of patience, either for God's sake or for human dignity.

The third station: the station of contentment (ridā), which is higher than the station of patience. There is dispute over its obligation, while the consensus of the Salaf holds it to be obligatory.

The fourth station: the station of gratitude, which is higher than the station of contentment, for one witnesses the affliction as a blessing and thanks the One who tested him for it.

As for the second kind, that which afflicts him from people, he has these same stations, and four more are added to them. The first is the station of pardon and forgiveness. The second is the station of the heart's soundness from desire for revenge and retaliation, and its freedom from the pain of constantly dwelling on the offence and being distressed by it. The third is the station of witnessing divine decree: that although the one who inflicts this harm upon you is a wrongdoer, He who decreed it for you and caused it to pass through the hand of this wrongdoer is not a wrongdoer. Harm from people is like heat and cold, which admit of no means of repelling. Whoever is resentful of the harm of heat and cold is not a man of sound judgment, and all of it proceeds by decree, though its paths and causes differ. The fourth station is the station of doing good to the one who does evil, and answering his evil with your goodness. In this station there are benefits and interests that none knows but God. If the servant misses this lofty station, let him not be content for himself with the lowest and most base of stations.

Section: The third category is that whose occurrence is through one's own choice. Once it has taken hold, one has neither choice nor means of repelling it. This is like passionate love: its beginning is by choice and its end is by compulsion. It is also like exposing oneself to the causes of sicknesses and pains that have no remedy once their causes have been engaged, just as there is no way to avert intoxication once one has consumed an intoxicant. Such a person's duty was to be patient at the outset, and once he failed in that, his duty remains to be patient at the end, and not to obey the call of his desire and his self. Here Satan has a remarkable deception: he makes him imagine that consuming some of what was forbidden may become obligatory for him, or be permitted to him by way of treatment. Its utmost is that it would be like treating oneself with wine or impurity, which many jurists have permitted. This is among the greatest ignorance, for such treatment does not remove the disease but increases and strengthens it. How many have treated themselves with that and their religion and worldly life were ruined by that remedy! Rather, the beneficial remedy for this disease is patience and piety, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And if you are patient and mindful of God, indeed that is of the determination of affairs﴾, and He said: ﴿Indeed, whoever is mindful of God and patient, then indeed God does not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾. Thus patience and piety are the cure for every disease of the religion, and neither of the two can do without the other.

If it is said: Is one rewarded for patience in this category if he was a disobedient, negligent person who pursued its causes, and is he punished for what arose from it, though it was not within his choice?

It is said: Yes. If he is patient for the sake of God Most High and repents of the forbidden cause he pursued, he is rewarded for his patience, because it is a striving by him against his own self, and it is a righteous deed, and God does not waste the reward of one who does good work.

As for his punishment for what arose from it: he deserves punishment for the cause and for what arose from it, just as the drunkard is punished for what he committed while intoxicated. When the cause is forbidden, the drunkard is not excused. God, glorified is He, punishes for forbidden causes and for what arises from them, just as He rewards for commanded causes and for what arises from them. This is why whoever calls to an innovation and misguidance bears a burden like the burdens of those who follow him, because their following him arose from his act. For this reason the son of Adam who killed his brother bears a share of the sin of every killer until the Day of Resurrection. God the Exalted said: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge﴾, and He the Exalted said: ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾.

The Lord, exalted is He, calls His servants in the Qur'an to know Him by two paths.

The first is contemplation of His acts (maf'ulat), and the second is reflection upon His signs (ayat) and pondering them. These are His visible signs and those are His audible, intelligible signs. The first kind is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day, and the ships which run through the sea with that which benefits people﴾ until the end of it.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day, are signs for those of understanding﴾.

This is abundant in the Qur'an. The second is like His saying: ﴿Will they not then reflect upon the Qur'an?﴾ And His saying: ﴿Have they not pondered the word?﴾ And His saying: ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses﴾. This too is abundant.

As for the acts, they indicate the actions, and the actions indicate the attributes. For the act indicates the one who performed it, and that necessitates His existence, His power, His will and His knowledge, because it is impossible for a voluntary act to proceed from one who is non-existent, or from an existent who has no power, no life, no knowledge and no will. Then, the diverse specifications found in the acts indicate the will of the Doer, and that His act is not by nature such that it would be uniform and unchanging. What is found in them of benefits, wisdom and praiseworthy ends indicates His wisdom, exalted is He. What is found in them of benefit, kindness and goodness indicates His mercy. What is found in them of seizing, vengeance and punishment indicates His anger. What is found in them of honouring, drawing near and special care indicates His love. What is found in them of humiliation, distancing and forsaking indicates His hatred and abhorrence. What is found in them of the beginning of a thing in utmost deficiency and weakness, then driving it to its completion and its end, indicates the occurrence of the Return (ma'ad). What is found in them of the conditions of plants and animals and the movement of waters is evidence for the possibility of the Return. What is found in them of the appearance of the effects of mercy and blessing upon His creation is evidence for the truth of prophethood. What is found in them of perfections, which if they were absent it would be deficient, is evidence that the Giver of those perfections is more worthy of them. So His acts are among the most indicative of anything of His attributes and of the truthfulness of what His messengers related about Him. Thus the created things bear witness, confirming the audible signs, and direct attention to reasoning from the signs of created things. The Exalted said: ﴿We shall show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth﴾, meaning that the Qur'an is the truth. He informed that He will surely show them from His visible signs what makes clear to them that His recited signs are true. Then He informed that His testimony is sufficient for the truth of His report, by what He has established of proofs and demonstrations for the truthfulness of His Messenger. So His signs bear witness to his truthfulness, and He is the witness to the truthfulness of His Messenger through His signs. He is the Witness and the one witnessed for, He is the proof and the thing proved. Thus He is the proof by Himself over Himself. As some of the knowers said: "How can I seek a proof for One who is the proof of everything? Whatever proof I seek for Him, I find Him more manifest than it." For this reason the messengers said to their peoples: ﴿Is there doubt about God?﴾ So He is more known than every known thing and clearer than every proof. Things are known through Him in reality, though He is known through them in reflection and in inferring from His acts and His judgments.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 3, verse 191:**

**(A Great Principle)**

The root of good and evil lies in reflection (*tafakkur*), for reflection is the source of will and pursuit, of renunciation (*zuhd*) and abandonment, of love and hatred. The most beneficial reflection is reflection on the interests of the Hereafter (*al-ma'ad*), on the ways of attaining them, on warding off the harms of the Hereafter, and on the ways of avoiding them. These are four kinds of reflection, and they are the noblest of all reflections. After them come four more: reflection on the interests of this world and the ways of obtaining them, and reflection on the harms of this world and the ways of guarding against them. The thoughts of intelligent people revolve around these eight categories.

The head of the first category is reflection on the bounties and favours of God, on His command and His prohibition, and on the ways of knowing Him, His names and His attributes, through His Book, the Sunnah of His Prophet, and what is related to them. This reflection produces in its possessor love and knowledge. When he reflects on the Hereafter, its nobility and its permanence, and on this world, its baseness and its perishing, it produces in him desire for the Hereafter and asceticism regarding this world. Whenever he reflects on the shortness of hope and the narrowness of time, this brings him earnestness, striving, and the exertion of his utmost effort in seizing the time. These reflections raise his aspiration, revive it after its death and its lowliness, and place him in one valley while people are in another.

Opposed to these reflections are the base thoughts that roam the hearts of most of this creation, such as reflection on what one is not obliged to reflect upon and what one is not given the capacity to comprehend, which is among the superfluous knowledge that does not benefit, like reflection on the modality of the Lord's Essence and His attributes, which is beyond the reach of the intellects. Among them is reflection on delicate crafts that do not benefit but harm, like reflection on chess, music, and various kinds of forms and pictures. Among them is reflection on sciences which, even if they were sound, reflection on them would not give the soul perfection or nobility, like reflection on the subtleties of logic, mathematics, and natural science, and most of the sciences of the philosophers, which, even if a person reached their furthest point, he would not thereby be perfected or purify his soul. Among them is reflection on desires and pleasures and the ways of obtaining them. Although this may give the soul some pleasure, it has no good outcome, and its harm in the outcome of this world, before the Hereafter, is many times greater than its delight. Among them is reflection on what has not happened, on how it would be if it had happened, like reflection on what one would do, how one would act, and how one would take, give, and avenge, if one became a king, or found a treasure, or owned an estate, and similar base thoughts. Among them is reflection on the particular circumstances of people, their comings and goings, their entrances and exits, and what follows from that, the reflection of souls that are void, empty of God, His Messenger, and the Last Abode. Among them is reflection on the subtle tricks and deceits by which one reaches his aims and desires, whether they are permissible or forbidden. Among them is reflection on the kinds of poetry, its turns and its varieties, in praise, satire, love poetry, elegies, and the like, for it occupies a person from reflecting on what holds his happiness and his everlasting life. Among them is reflection on mental assumptions that have no existence outside and for which people have no need at all, and this is found in every science, even in the science of jurisprudence, the principles of jurisprudence, and medicine. So all these thoughts have harm that outweighs their benefit, and their harm is sufficiently evident in that they occupy a person from reflecting on what is more fitting for him and more beneficial to him, both in the immediate and in the deferred.

**(Section)**

It is related from some of the early Muslims (*salaf*) that he said: "An hour of reflection is better than sixty years of worship."

A man asked Umm al-Darda' (may God be pleased with her), after her husband's death, about his worship. She said: "His whole day was spent in the wilderness of reflection."

Al-Hasan said: "An hour of reflection is better than a night of standing in prayer."

Al-Fadl said: "Reflection is a mirror that shows you your good deeds and your bad deeds."

It was said to Ibrahim: "You reflect for a long time?" He said: "Reflection is the marrow of the intellect."

Sufyan frequently recited:

*"When a man has a capacity for reflection,*
*there is a lesson for him in everything."*

Al-Hasan, commenting on God's words, ﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant in the earth without right﴾, said: "He will prevent them from reflecting upon them."

Some of the knowers of God said: "If the hearts of the God-fearing looked with their reflection at what has been decreed in the veils of the unseen of the good of the Hereafter, a life would not be pleasant for them in this world, and their eyes would not be cooled by it."

Al-Hasan said: "Prolonged solitude is more complete for reflection, and prolonged reflection is a sign of the path to Paradise."

Wahb said: "A reflection never lasted long for anyone except that he gained knowledge, and no one ever gained knowledge except that he acted."

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: "Reflection on the favours of God is among the best of worship."

'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak, seeing one of his companions in reflection, said to him: "How far have you reached?" He said: "The Path (*al-sirat*)."

Bishr said: "If people reflected on the greatness of God, they would not disobey Him."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Two moderate units of prayer with reflection are better than a night of standing in prayer without a heart."

Abu Sulayman said: "Reflection on this world is a veil from the Hereafter and a punishment for the people of spiritual closeness, while reflection on the Hereafter produces wisdom and polishes the hearts."
