Ibn 'Abbas said: "Reflection on good calls to acting upon it."

Al-Hasan said: "The people of knowledge have never ceased to return remembrance to reflection and reflection to remembrance, and to make the hearts speak, until they spoke with wisdom."

Among the sayings of al-Shafi'i: "Seek help in speech through silence, and in deduction through reflection." This is because reflection is the work of the heart, while worship is the work of the limbs, and the heart is nobler than the limbs, so its work is nobler than the work of the limbs. Moreover, reflection brings its possessor to faith in a way that bare action does not, for reflection makes manifest to him the unveiling and clear appearance of the realities of matters, the distinguishing of their ranks in good and evil, the knowledge of the superior from the inferior and the ugly from the beautiful, the knowledge of the causes that lead to them, what opposes those causes and repels their effect, and the distinction between what ought to be striven for in attaining it and what ought to be striven for in removing its causes, and the difference between illusion and imagination, which prevents most souls from seizing opportunities after they are possible, and the actual cause that prevents, so that one occupies himself with it rather than with the first. Nothing cuts a servant off from his perfection, his success, and his happiness, both immediate and deferred, more than the illusion that dominates the soul and the imagination that is its vehicle, indeed its sea in which it never ceases to swim. This obstacle is cut off only by sound reflection and a truthful resolve by which one distinguishes between illusion and reality. Likewise, when one reflects on the outcomes of matters and his thought passes beyond their beginnings, he places them in their proper places and knows their ranks. So when the impulse of sin and desire comes upon him, his reflection passes beyond its pleasure and the soul's delight in it to its evil outcome and what follows from it of pain and sorrow, which cannot withstand that pleasure and joy, and whoever reflects in this way hardly ever proceeds to it. Likewise, when there comes upon his heart the impulse of comfort, ease, indolence, and shrinking from the hardship of acts of obedience and their toil, until his reflection passes over to what follows from them of pleasures, goods, and joys, which overwhelm the pains found at their beginnings in comparison with the perfection of their outcomes, and the more his reflection plunges into this, the more his desire for them grows and their endurance becomes easy for him, so he welcomes them with vigour, strength, and resolve. Likewise, when he reflects on the furthest end of what enslaves him of wealth, status, and forms, and looks at its final end with the eye of his reflection, he is ashamed before his intellect and his soul that he should be a slave to that, as it was said:

*"If the lover reflected on the furthest end*
*of the beauty that captivates him, he would not be captivated."*

Likewise, when he reflects on the end of the most prized foods over which the souls of the beast-like creatures (*ashbah al-an'am*) are consumed, and on what their matter comes to when they leave the body, his aspiration rises above devoting itself to them and making them the idol of his heart, the one he turns to, is pleased or angry for, strives for, toils for, and befriends or opposes for, as has come in the Musnad from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said:

"Indeed God has made the food of the son of Adam a parable for this world, and though its salt may be sharpened, he knows where it will end up."

Or as he said.

So when his reflection falls upon its outcome and its final end, and his soul is free, its owner's (i.e., the soul's) refusal is that it should make itself a slave to what ends in the most foul, most wicked, and most vile thing.

**Section:** When this is understood, reflection is the bringing together of two knowledges in the heart so that a third knowledge may be derived from them. An example of this is when he brings into his heart the immediate world, its life, its delights, the afflictions attached to it, its cessation and its passing, then brings into his heart the Hereafter, its delights, its lastingness, and its superiority over the delights of this world, and is certain of these two knowledges. This produces in him a third knowledge, namely that the Hereafter and its excellent and everlasting bliss are more deserving, in the judgment of every intelligent person, of being preferred over the immediate world, which is cut off and turbid. Then he has two states regarding knowledge of the Hereafter. The first is that he has heard this from another without his heart having been touched by the coolness of certainty about it, and his heart has not come into direct contact with the reality of the Hereafter. This is the state of most people, and two calls pull at him: one is the call of the immediate world and preferring it, which is the stronger of the two calls for him, because it is witnessed by him and perceived by the senses; and the call of the Hereafter, which is the weaker of the two for him, because it is a call based on hearsay that has not touched his heart with certainty, nor has its scientific reality confronted him. So when he leaves the immediate world for the Hereafter, his soul shows him that he has abandoned what is known for what is conjectural, or what is certain for what is imagined. The state of affairs calls out to him: "I will not leave a dinar in hand for a pearl promised." This affliction is what has prevented souls from preparing for the Hereafter and from striving for it as it should be striven for, and it arises from weakness of knowledge of it and of certainty about it. Otherwise, with complete conviction in which no doubt stirs in the heart, there would be no negligence regarding it and no lack of desire for it. This is why, if a man were served a food of the utmost goodness and delight, and he was in great need of it, and then it was said to him that it was poisoned, he would not approach it, because he knows that the evil consequence of eating it outweighs the pleasure of the meal. So what is the matter with faith in the Hereafter that it does not hold this position in his heart? That is only due to the weakness of the tree of knowledge and faith in the heart and its failure to take firm root in it. Likewise, when a man is travelling on a road and it is said to him that there are brigands and thieves on it who kill whomever they find and take his goods, he will not take it except in one of two ways: either he does not believe the informant, or he is confident of his own strength to overcome them and prevail over them. But if, along with his belief in the report, a belief that admits no doubt, he also knows in himself that he is too weak to resist them, he will not take that road. If these two knowledges were present to him in what he undertakes of preferring this world and its desires, he would not proceed to that. So it is known that preferring the immediate world and abandoning preparation for the Hereafter never occurs at all together with complete belief and faith.

The second state is that he is certain and convinced, with a conviction free of doubt, that there is for him an abode other than this abode, and a return that has been created for him, and that this abode is a path to that return and a station among the stations of those journeying to it. He also knows that it is lasting, and its bliss and its punishment do not cease, and there is no comparison between this immediate bliss and punishment and that one, except as when a man dips his finger into the sea and then withdraws it. What clings to the finger from it is like this world in comparison with the Hereafter. This knowledge produces in him preference for the Hereafter, seeking it, complete readiness for it, and striving for it as it should be striven for. This striving is reflection, remembrance, looking, contemplation, consideration, pondering, and insight. These are closely related meanings, which meet in one respect and differ in another. It is called reflection because it is the employment of thought in this matter and bringing it before him. It is called remembrance because it is the bringing of the knowledge that must be observed back to mind after its forgetting and absence. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who are mindful of God, when an impulse from Satan touches them, remember, and then they are seeing clearly.﴾

It is called looking (*nazar*) because it is the turning of the heart toward what is looked at. It is called contemplation (*ta'ammul*) because it is returning to the looking again and again until it becomes clear to him and is unveiled to his heart. It is called consideration (*i'tibar*), which is a form derived from crossing over (*al-'ubur*), because one crosses over through it to something else; he crosses over from what he has reflected upon to a third knowledge, which is the purpose of consideration. For this reason it is called *'ibrah* (lesson), and it is in the pattern of states, like *jilsah* (a sitting), *rukbah* (a riding), and *qitlah* (a killing), signifying that this knowledge and recognition have become a state for its possessor, by which he crosses over to its intended object. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for whoever fears.﴾ And He said: ﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for those of insight.﴾ It is called pondering (*tadabbur*) because it is looking at the backs (*adbar*) of matters, which are their ends and their outcomes. From this comes pondering the word, and God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have they not pondered the word?﴾ and ﴿Do they not ponder the Qur'an? And if it had been from other than God, they would have found in it much discrepancy.﴾

The pondering of speech is to look at its beginning and its end, then to repeat the looking time after time. For this reason it is in the pattern of *tafa''ul*, like *tajarru'* (sipping), *tafahhum* (understanding), and *tabayyun* (clarifying). It is called insight (*istibsar*), which is a form derived from *tabassur*, which is the clarification of a matter and its unveiling and its becoming manifest to the inner sight.

Each of remembrance and reflection has a benefit different from the other. Remembrance results in the repetition of what the heart has known and recognized, so that it becomes firmly established in it and does not fade, its trace not vanishing from the heart entirely. Reflection results in increasing knowledge and drawing in what is not already present in the heart. Reflection acquires it, and remembrance preserves it. For this reason al-Hasan said: "The people of knowledge have never ceased to return remembrance to reflection and reflection to remembrance, and to make the hearts speak, until they spoke with wisdom." Thus reflection and remembrance are the seed of knowledge, and its watering is conversing with it and discussing it, and its fertilizing is discussing it, as one of the early Muslims said: "Meeting men is a fertilization of their minds." So discussion is the fertilization of the intellect. Goodness and happiness are in a treasury whose key is reflection, for there must be reflection, and knowledge whose outcome is reflection, and a state that arises in the heart from that knowledge. For whoever does any beloved or hated thing, there must remain in his heart a state, and he is dyed with the dye of his knowledge, and that state necessitates a will, and that will necessitates the occurrence of the action.

So here there are five matters: reflection, whose fruit is knowledge; the fruit of both is the state that arises in the heart; the fruit of that is will; and the fruit of will is action. Reflection, then, is the beginning and the key to all goods. This reveals to you the excellence and nobility of reflection, and that it is among the best of the heart's works and the most beneficial to it, so much so that it was said: "An hour of reflection is better than a year of worship." Reflection is what transfers a person from the death of discernment to the life of wakefulness, from hateful things to beloved things, from desire and greed to asceticism and contentment, from the prison of this world to the expanse of the Hereafter, from the narrowness of ignorance to the breadth and spaciousness of knowledge, from the sickness of desire and clinging to this abode to the healing of turning to God and withdrawing from the abode of delusion, from the calamity of blindness, deafness, and muteness to the blessing of sight, hearing, and understanding from God and understanding of Him, and from the diseases of doubts to the coolness of certainty and the serenity of hearts.

In sum, the root of every act of obedience is reflection, and likewise the root of every act of disobedience arises from the side of reflection, for Satan finds the land of the heart empty and void, so he sows in it the love of base thoughts, from which wills and resolutions arise, and from those arises action. But when he finds the land of the heart occupied with sowing beneficial thoughts about what it was created for, what it was commanded to do, what it was prepared for, and what everlasting bliss or painful punishment awaits it, he finds no place for his seed. This is as it was said:

*"Her passion came to me before I knew passion,*
*and found a heart empty, so it took root."*

The meaning: "Grant us what You promised us through the tongues of Your messengers, of entry into Paradise."

Another group said the meaning is: "Grant us what You promised us for believing in Your messengers."

It is not easy to omit both the noun and the particle together unless one estimates it as "to confirm Your messengers and obey Your messengers." In that case the two estimates are equal, and the first is preferred, because their statement has already preceded: ﴿Our Lord, we have heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we have believed.﴾ This is explicit in belief in the Messenger and the One who sent him. Then they sought a means to Him through their belief, that He would give them what He promised them through the tongues of the messengers, since they only heard of His promise to them through the messengers. This also includes affirming those messengers, and that they conveyed His promise to them, so they affirmed it and asked Him to give them it. This is what the early scholars (al-salaf) and later scholars (al-khalaf) mentioned regarding the verse.

It was also said: the meaning is "Grant us what You promised us of victory and triumph through the tongues of the messengers." The first is more general and more complete.

Reflect on how their belief included belief in Him, belief in His command and prohibition, His messengers, His promise and threat, His names and attributes, His acts, the truthfulness of His promise, fear of His threat, and their obedience to His command. Through the totality of this, they became believers in their Lord, the Exalted. Thereby their means to ask for what He promised them, and salvation from His punishment, became valid.

Some people were perplexed by their asking that He fulfil for them what He had promised them, given that He will certainly do so.

He answered that this is pure worship (ta'abbud mahd), like His saying: ﴿My Lord, judge with truth﴾ and the angels' saying: ﴿So forgive those who have repented and followed Your way﴾. These people overlooked that the promise is conditional upon things, among them turning to Him, the Exalted, and asking Him to fulfil it for them, just as it is conditional upon faith and their dying in it, and that nothing reaches them that would nullify it. So when they ask Him, the Exalted, to fulfil for them what He promised them, that includes His granting them success, steadfastness, and help in the means through which He fulfils His promise to them. This supplication is among the most important and most beneficial supplications, and they are more in need of it than of many other supplications.

As for His saying ﴿My Lord, judge﴾, this is a request to Him, the Exalted, to give them victory over their enemies, so that He judges in their favour against them with victory and dominance.

Likewise, the angels' request to their Lord that He forgive those who repent is among the means by which forgiveness becomes incumbent for them. He, the Exalted, has established means through which He does what He wills with His friends and enemies, and made them causes for His will, just as He made them causes for the occurrence of His purpose. So from Him are both the cause and the effect. If this is unclear to you, then look at His creating the causes which necessitate His love and His anger. He loves, is pleased, becomes angry and displeased through the causes He created and willed. All is from Him and by Him. It originates from His will and returns to His wisdom alone. This is a great door among the doors of monotheism (tawhid), which none enters except those who know Allah.

A parallel to this verse in asking for what was promised is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Say: "Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity which the righteous have been promised? It will be for them a reward and a destination. For them therein is whatever they wish, abiding forever. It is upon your Lord a promise sought."﴾

His believing servants ask Him for it, and His angels ask it for them. The Garden asks its Lord for its people, its people ask Him for it, the angels ask it for them, and the messengers ask it for them and for their followers. On the Day of Resurrection He, the Exalted, will stand them before Him, and they will intercede before Him for His believing servants. In this is the completeness of His dominion, the manifestation of His mercy, His benevolence, His generosity, His kindness, and His giving what is asked. This is among the requirements of His names and attributes, and their demand for their effects and their objects. It is not permissible to nullify them from their effects and rulings. The Lord, the Exalted, is Generous, and all generosity belongs to Him. He loves to be asked, to be sought, and to be longed for. So He created one who asks Him, inspired him to ask, and created for him what he asks. He is the Creator of the asker, the asking, and the thing asked. This is because of His love for His servants' asking Him, their longing for Him, and their seeking from Him. He becomes angry when He is not asked:

"Allah becomes angry if you abandon asking Him,
while the son of Adam becomes angry when he is asked."

The one most beloved to Him among His creation is the one who asks Him most and best. He loves those who insist in supplication, and whenever a servant insists upon asking Him, He loves him, draws him near, and gives to him.

A hadith says: "Whoever does not ask Allah, Allah becomes angry with him."

So there is no god but Him. What a crime false foundations have committed against faith, barring hearts from knowing their Lord, His names, His attributes of perfection, and His descriptions of majesty. ﴿Praise be to Allah who guided us to this, and we would not have been guided had Allah not guided us.﴾

Abu Nu'aym al-Fadl said: Yunus narrated to us, that is Ibn Abi Ishaq: Yazid ibn Abi Murthid narrated to us, he said: Anas ibn Malik said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No Muslim asks Allah for Paradise three times except that Paradise says: 'O Allah, admit him into Paradise.' And whoever seeks refuge with Allah from the Fire three times, the Fire says: 'O Allah, protect him from the Fire.'"

It was narrated by al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, from Hannad ibn al-Sarri, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abu Ishaq, from Yazid with it. Al-Hasan ibn Sufyan said: Uthman ibn Abi Shayba narrated to us: Jarir narrated to us, from Layth, from Yunus ibn Hayyan, from Abu Hazim, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No servant asks Allah for Paradise seven times in a day except that Paradise says: 'O Lord, your servant so-and-so asks me, so admit him into it.'"

Abu Ya'la al-Mawsili said: Abu Khaythama Zuhayr ibn Harb narrated to us: Jarir narrated to us, from Yunus, from Abu Hazim, from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No servant seeks refuge from the Fire seven times except that the Fire says: 'Your servant so-and-so has sought refuge from me, so protect him.' And no servant asks Paradise seven times except that Paradise says: 'O Lord, your servant so-and-so has asked me, so admit him into Paradise.'"

Its chain is on the condition of the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim).

Abu Dawud said in his Musnad: Shu'ba narrated to us, Yunus ibn Hayyan narrated to me, he heard Abu 'Alqama, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says, 'I ask Allah for Paradise,' seven times, Paradise says: 'O Allah, admit him into Paradise.'"

Al-Hasan ibn Sufyan said: al-Muqaddami narrated to us: Umar ibn Ali narrated to us, from Yahya ibn Abdullah, from his father, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Increase your asking Allah for Paradise and seek refuge with Him from the Fire, for they are two intercessors whose intercession is accepted. When the servant increases his asking Allah for Paradise, Paradise says: 'O Lord, this servant of Yours who asked me, so settle him with me.' And the Fire says: 'O Lord, this servant of Yours who sought refuge with You from me, so protect him.'"

Some of the early scholars would not ask Allah for Paradise, and they said: "It is enough for us that He protect us from the Fire." Among them was Abu al-Sahba' Sila ibn Ashyam, who prayed through the night until dawn, then raised his hands and said: "O Allah, protect me from the Fire, or would one like me dare to ask You for Paradise?"

Among them was 'Ata' al-Sulami, who would not ask for Paradise. Salih al-Murri said to him: "Aban narrated to me, from Anas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: "Look into the register of My servant; whomever you see asking Me for Paradise, I will give it to him, and whoever seeks refuge in Me from the Fire, I will protect him."' 'Ata' said: 'It is enough for me that He protect me from the Fire.'" Abu Nu'aym mentioned it.

Abu Dawud, in his Sunan, narrated from the hadith of Jabir concerning the story of Mu'adh's prayer and his lengthening it for them, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the young man, meaning the one who complained about him: "How do you do it, my nephew, when you pray?" He said: "I recite al-Fatiha, ask Allah for Paradise, and seek refuge with Him from the Fire. I do not know what your murmuring is, and the murmuring of Mu'adh." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Myself and Mu'adh, we murmur around it."

In the Sunan of Abu Dawud, from the hadith of Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir, from Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Nothing is to be asked by the Face of Allah except Paradise."

He narrated it from Ahmad ibn Amr al-'Asfari: Ya'qub ibn Ishaq narrated to us: Sulayman ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, from Muhammad, and mentioned it.

It has already been mentioned at the beginning of the book the hadith of al-Layth, from Mu'awiya, from Salih, from Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Bashir, raised as a hadith: "There is no day except that Paradise and the Fire are asked. Paradise says: 'O Lord, my fruits are good, my rivers are flowing, and I long for my friends, so hasten to me with my people.'" The hadith continues.

So Paradise seeks its people by its very nature and draws them to it with a pull, and so does the Fire. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has commanded us that we never cease to remember them both and never forget them, as Abu Ya'la al-Mawsili narrated in his Musnad: Ishaq ibn Abi Israil narrated to us: Ayyub ibn Abi Shabib al-San'ani narrated to us, saying: "Among what we presented to Rabah ibn Zayd was: Abdullah ibn Numayr narrated to me: I heard Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid say: I heard Abdullah ibn Umar say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Do not forget the two great ones.' We said: 'And what are the two great ones, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Paradise and the Fire.'"

Abu Bakr al-Shafi'i mentioned, from the hadith of Kulayb ibn Harb, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Seek Paradise with your utmost effort, and flee from the Fire with your utmost effort, for the seeker of Paradise does not sleep, and the one fleeing from the Fire does not sleep. The Hereafter today is surrounded by hardships, and this world is surrounded by pleasures and desires, so let them not distract you from the Hereafter."

[A section on the difference between expiation of misdeeds (takfir al-sayyi'at) and forgiveness of sins (maghfirat al-dhunub)]

The mention of both has come in the Book of Allah, paired together, and each mentioned separately from the other. The paired form is like His saying, relating from His believing servants: ﴿Our Lord, forgive us our sins and expiate from us our misdeeds, and cause us to die with the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 193]. The single form is like His saying: ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds, and believed in what was sent down to Muhammad, and it is the truth from their Lord, He expiates from them their misdeeds and sets right their affairs﴾ [Muhammad: 2]. And His saying about forgiveness: ﴿And for them therein is every kind of fruit and forgiveness from their Lord﴾ [Muhammad: 15], and like His saying: ﴿Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excess in our affair﴾ [Al 'Imran: 147], and their likes.

So here there are four matters: sins (dhunub), misdeeds (sayyi'at), forgiveness (maghfirah), and expiation (takfir).

The sins (dhunub) are meant to be the major sins (kaba'ir), and the misdeeds (sayyi'at) are meant to be the minor sins (saghair), which are those in which expiation (kaffarah) operates, such as error and what is similar to it. For this reason expiation was made for them, and from it the term kaffarah was derived. For this reason they have no power or effect over major sins in the more correct of the two opinions. So they do not operate in premeditated murder, nor in the perjurious oath (al-yamin al-ghamus), according to the apparent position of the madhhab of Ahmad and Abu Hanifa.

The evidence that the misdeeds are the minor sins and that expiation is for them is His saying: ﴿If you avoid the major sins which you are forbidden, We will expiate from you your misdeeds and admit you to an honourable entrance﴾ [al-Nisa': 31]. In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: "The five prayers, and Friday to Friday, and Ramadan to Ramadan, are expiations for what is between them, if the major sins are avoided."

The term forgiveness is more complete than the term expiation. For this reason it was for the major sins, and expiation is with the minor sins. The term forgiveness includes protection and preservation, while the term expiation includes covering and removal. When mentioned singly, each of them enters into the other, as has preceded. So His saying ﴿He expiated from them their misdeeds﴾ [Muhammad: 2] encompasses their minor and major sins, erasing them and protecting from their evil. Rather, expiation when mentioned alone encompasses the worst of deeds, as the Exalted said: ﴿So that Allah may expiate from them the worst of what they did﴾ [al-Zumar: 35].

When this is understood, the secret of the promise regarding calamities, worries, griefs, fatigue and illness is understood as expiation and not forgiveness, as in His saying in the authentic hadith: "Nothing afflicts the believer of worry, grief, or harm, even a thorn that pricks him, except that Allah expiates from his sins through it." For calamities do not by themselves suffice for forgiving sins, and sins are not all forgiven except by repentance, or by good deeds in which sins shrink and vanish. So they are like the sea, which is not changed by carrion, and when water reaches two qullatayn, it does not carry impurity.

So for the people of sins there are three great rivers in which they are purified in this world. If these do not suffice for their purification, they will be purified in the river of the Furnace (Jahim) on the Day of Resurrection: the river of sincere repentance (tawba nasuh), the river of good deeds which overwhelm the burdens and surround them, and the river of great calamities which expiate. When Allah wills good for His servant, He admits him into one of these three rivers, so he arrives on the Day of Resurrection pure and clean, and he does not need the fourth purification.

Therefore He commanded them to be patient (ṣabr), which is the state of the one who is patient within himself.

Muṣābara (mutual endurance) is to withstand the opponent on the field of patience. It is a form of mufā'ala, which requires standing between two parties, like mutual reviling or mutual striking. It is thus the state of the believer in patience with his adversary.

Murābaṭa (steadfast guarding) is steadfastness, constancy, and remaining firm in patience and endurance.

A servant may be patient without being enduring toward his adversary, or he may endure without guarding his post, and he may be patient without enduring, and guard without being devoted to taqwa.

So He informed, glorified is He, that the pivot of all of this is taqwa, and that success (falāḥ) depends upon it. He said: ﴿And fear Allah, that you may be successful.﴾

Just as murābaṭa is holding the frontier that the enemy might attack from outwardly, it is also holding the frontier of the heart, lest desire and Satan enter through it and remove him from his kingdom.

It has been said regarding His words, exalted is He: ﴿Be patient, endure, and remain on guard﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 200] that it is a movement from the lower to the higher: patience is below endurance, and endurance is below murābaṭa. Murābaṭa is a form of mufā'ala from ribṭ, which means binding. The one on guard is called murābiṭ because the guards tie their horses, awaiting alarm. Then every person who awaits, having bound himself to an obedience he awaits, is called murābiṭ. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Shall I not inform you of what Allah erases sins by and raises ranks by? Performing wuḍū' thoroughly in difficult conditions, walking much to the mosques, and waiting for the prayer after the prayer: that is ribāṭ, that is ribāṭ."

And he (ﷺ) said: "A day of ribāṭ in the way of Allah is better than the world and all that is in it."

It has also been said: Be patient with your selves upon obedience to Allah; endure with your hearts upon trials in Allah; and remain on guard with your inner secrets upon longing for Allah.

It has also been said: Be patient for Allah, endure by Allah, and remain on guard with Allah.

It has also been said: Be patient in times of blessing, endure in hardship and adversity, remain on guard in the land of enemies, and fear the God of earth and heaven, that you may be successful in the abode of permanence.

So patience is with your self, endurance is between you and your enemy, and murābaṭa is steadfastness and preparing equipment. Just as ribāṭ is holding the frontier lest the enemy attack through it, so too ribāṭ is holding the frontier of the heart lest Satan attack it, take possession of it, and ruin or disorder it.

It has also been said: Swallow patience; if it kills you, it kills you as a martyr, and if it keeps you alive, it keeps you alive honored.

It has also been said: Patience for Allah is sufficiency; by Allah is survival; in Allah is trial; with Allah is fidelity; from Allah is estrangement. Patience in pursuit is the sign of victory, and patience in afflictions is the sign of relief.

It has also been said: The servant's state with Allah is his ribāṭ, and whatever is other than Allah is his enemies.

In the Kitāb al-Adab of al-Bukhārī: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about faith, and he said: patience and generosity." He narrated it from Mūsā ibn Ismā'īl, who said: Suwayd narrated to us, who said: ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr narrated to us, from his father, from his grandfather, and he mentioned it.

This is among the most comprehensive of statements and the greatest in proof, and the most inclusive of the stations of faith from its beginning to its end.

For the soul is required to do two things: to give what it is commanded to give, and to abstain from what it is forbidden. What drives it to the first is generosity (samāḥa). What drives it to abandon and distance itself from what it is forbidden is patience (ṣabr).

Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has commanded in His Book beautiful patience (al-ṣabr al-jamīl), beautiful forgiveness (al-ṣafḥ al-jamīl), and beautiful avoidance (al-hajr al-jamīl). I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah sanctify his spirit, say: beautiful patience is that in which there is no complaint, nor with it. Beautiful forgiveness is that with which there is no reproach. Beautiful avoidance is that with which there is no harm.

In an Israʾīlī report: Allah revealed to one of His prophets: I sent down My trial upon My servant, and he called upon Me, but I delayed answering him, so he complained against Me. I said: My servant, how can I have mercy on you from something by which I show mercy to you?

Ibn ʿUyayna said regarding His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient﴾ [al-Sajda: 24]: They took hold of the head of the matter, so He made them leaders.

It has been said: The best patience of the worshippers is that it be guarded, and the best patience of the lovers is that it be cast aside, as it was said:
"It became clear on the day of parting that his resolve to be patient was among the false suspicions."

Complaint to Allah, mighty and majestic is He, does not contradict patience. Ya'qūb, peace be upon him, pledged beautiful patience, and a prophet does not break his promise. Then he said: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and grief to Allah﴾ [Yūsuf: 86]. Likewise Ayyūb, of whom Allah reported that He found him patient, despite his saying: ﴿Harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 83].

What contradicts patience is complaining about Allah, not complaining to Allah. As one of them saw a man complaining to another of poverty and need, and said: "O you, you complain of One who has mercy on you to one who has no mercy on you?" Then he recited:
"If calamity befalls you, be patient with it as a noble person is patient, for He knows you best.
And if you complain to a son of Adam, you are only complaining of the Merciful to one who does not show mercy."

[Section: Sins are a fierce enemy]

Among their punishments: they are a supply from the human being by which his enemy is reinforced against him, and an army by which he strengthens him in his war. That is because Allah, glorified is He, afflicted this human with an enemy who does not leave him for the blink of an eye, does not sleep or become heedless of him, sees him and his tribe from where he cannot see them, exerts his utmost effort in opposing him in every state, and leaves no scheme by which he can reach him without reaching him. He seeks help against him from his own kind, from the satans of the jinn and others from the satans of mankind. He has set snares for him, sought his ruin, spread nets around him, set traps and nets for him, and said to his helpers: "Take your enemy and the enemy of your father; he will not escape you. His portion is Paradise and your portion is the Fire; his share is mercy and your share is curse. You know that what befell me and you of disgrace and distance from Allah's mercy was because of him and on his account. So exert your utmost effort that they become our partners in this affliction, since we have lost partnership with their righteous ones in Paradise." Allah, glorified is He, has informed us of all of this about our enemy and commanded us to take up its readiness and prepare its equipment.

When He, glorified is He, knew that Ādam and his descendants had been tested with this enemy, and that he had been empowered over them, He supplied them with armies and troops to meet him with, and He also supplied their enemy with troops and armies to meet them with. He established the market of jihad in this abode, during the span of life which, in comparison with the Hereafter, is like a single breath of its breaths. He purchased from the believers their selves and their wealth in exchange for Paradise: they fight in the way of Allah, so they kill and are killed. He informed that this is a promise binding upon Himself in His most noble books, which are the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an. He informed that none is more faithful to His covenant than He, glorified is He. Then He commanded them to rejoice in this transaction. Whoever wishes to know its value, let him look at who the Buyer is, at the price paid for this commodity, and at who conducted this contract. What victory is greater than this? And what trade is more profitable than it?

Then He, glorified is He, emphasized this matter to them by saying: ﴿O you who believe, shall I guide you to a trade that will save you from a painful punishment? You believe in Allah and His Messenger and strive in the way of Allah with your wealth and your selves. That is better for you, if you only knew. He will forgive you your sins and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence. That is the great achievement. And another you love: victory from Allah and an imminent conquest. So give good tidings to the believers﴾ [al-Ṣaff: 10–13].

He, glorified is He, did not empower this enemy over His servant, the believer, who is the most beloved of creatures to Him, except because jihad is the most beloved thing to Him, and its people are the highest of creation in rank with Him and the nearest to Him in means. So He, glorified is He, raised the banner of this war over the essence of His creation, which is the heart, the locus of His knowledge and love, worship and sincerity toward Him, reliance upon Him and turning to Him. He entrusted to it the command of this war, and supported it with an army of angels who never leave it: ﴿For him are successive angels before him and behind him, guarding him by the command of Allah﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11].

They follow one another; whenever one departs, another replaces it. They make him firm, command him to good, urge him toward it, promise him the honor of Allah, and encourage him to patience, saying: "It is only the patience of an hour, and you have rested the rest of eternity."

Then He, glorified is He, supported him with another army of His revelation and speech. He sent to him His Messenger (ﷺ) and sent down to him His Book, so his strength increased upon his strength, his support upon his support, and his equipment upon his equipment. Along with that, He supported him with reason as a vizier and manager, with knowledge as an advising counselor who gives him sincere counsel, with faith as one who makes him firm, strengthens him, supports and helps him, and with certainty as one who unveils to him the reality of the matter, until it is as if he witnesses what Allah promised His allies and party for the jihad against their enemies. So reason manages the affairs of his army, knowledge arranges for him the matters of war, its causes and its proper places, faith makes him firm, strengthens him, and gives him patience, and certainty makes him advance and carry out true charges.

Then He, glorified is He, supported the one carrying out this war with the outward and inward faculties. He made the eye his scout, the ear the bearer of his news, the tongue his interpreter, and the two hands and two feet his helpers. He established His angels and the bearers of His Throne to seek forgiveness for him and to ask that He protect him from evil deeds and admit him into the gardens. He, glorified is He, Himself undertook the repelling and defense on his behalf, and said: "These are My party, and the party of Allah are the successful." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are the party of Allah. Unquestionably, the party of Allah are the successful﴾ [al-Mujādila: 22].

And these are My army: ﴿And indeed, Our army will be the victorious﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 173].

He taught His servants the manner of this war and jihad, gathering it for them in four words, saying: ﴿O you who believe, be patient, endure, remain on guard, and fear Allah, that you may be successful﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 200].

The matter of this jihad is not complete except with these four matters. Patience is not complete except with enduring the enemy, which is confronting him and grappling with him. When he endures against his enemy, he needs another matter, which is murābaṭa: holding and guarding the frontier of the heart so that the enemy does not enter through it, and holding the frontiers of the eye, ear, tongue, belly, hand, and foot. These frontiers are where the enemy enters, roams through the homes, and corrupts whatever he can. So murābaṭa is holding these frontiers, and one does not leave their place empty, lest the enemy find the frontier vacant and enter through it.

These were the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the best of creation after the prophets and messengers, and the greatest in protection and guarding against Satan. Yet they vacated the position they were commanded to hold on the day of Uhud, so the enemy entered through it, and what happened, happened.

The sum of these three and their pillar upon which they stand is the taqwa of Allah, exalted is He. Patience, endurance, and murābaṭa profit nothing except with taqwa, and taqwa does not stand except upon the leg of patience.

The meeting of the two armies. Now look at yourself: the meeting of the two armies, the clash of the two hosts, and how you are sometimes overpowered and sometimes overpower the enemy. The king of the disbelievers came with his troops and soldiers, and found the heart sitting in its fortress on the throne of its kingdom. Its command was binding over its helpers, and its soldiers surrounded it, fighting on its behalf and defending its territory. They could not attack it except through the treachery of some of its commanders and soldiers against it. So he asked about the soldier closest to it and nearest to it in rank, and he was told: "It is the self (al-nafs)." He said to his helpers: "Enter upon it through its desire, look for the places of its love and what its beloved is, promise it that, and hold out hope to it of that. Engrave the image of the beloved in it, both in its waking and its sleeping. When it feels at ease with him and settles with him, cast upon it the hooks and grapnels of desire, then drag it toward you. When it turns against the heart and becomes with you against it, you will have taken the frontier of the eye, the ear, the tongue, the mouth, the hand and the foot. So guard these frontiers with complete vigilance. Whenever you enter through them into the heart, it will be slain, taken captive, or wounded and overwhelmed by wounds. Do not leave these frontiers, and do not allow a detachment to enter through them to the heart and expel you from it. If you are defeated, strive to weaken the detachment and its strength, so that it does not reach the heart. If it does reach it, it will arrive weak and will avail it nothing."

The frontier of the eye. When you have taken control of these frontiers, prevent the frontier of the eye from looking with consideration (i'tibar, reflection), and make its looking merely a diversion, a pleasure and a distraction. If it steals a glance seeking a lesson, then spoil that lesson for it with a look of heedlessness, approval and desire, for that is closer to it, cleaves more to its self, and is lighter for it. Take hold of the frontier of the eye, for through it you will attain your aim. I have never corrupted the children of Adam with anything like the gaze, for I sow with it the seed of desire in the heart, then water it with the water of wishful thinking. I do not cease to promise and hold out hope to it until I strengthen its resolve and lead it by the rein of desire to breaking loose from protection. So do not neglect the matter of this frontier; corrupt it as far as you are able, make its matter seem light to it, and say to it: "A glance is only a moment that calls you to glorify the Creator and to contemplate the wonder of His making, and the beauty of this form, which was created only so that the beholder might be guided by it. God did not create your two eyes in vain, and God did not create this form to veil it from sight." If you find him of little knowledge and corrupt intellect, say to him: "This form is a manifestation of the Real (al-Haqq) and one of its mirrors." Invite him to speak of union (al-ittihad, the claim that God and creation are one), and if he does not accept, then speak of indwelling (al-hulul), general or specific. Do not be content with less than that from him, for by it he will become one of the brothers of the Christians. Then order him at that point to chastity, self-restraint, worship and asceticism in this world, and hunt the ignorant through him and with him. This is among my closest successors and greatest soldiers; indeed, I am one of his troops and helpers.
